chosen: How might Brown syndrome be treated? Treatment recommendations vary depending on the cause and severity of the condition. In mild cases, a watch and wait approach may be sufficient. Visual acuity should be monitored. First line therapy usually involves less invasive options such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications like Ibuprofen.  Acquired cases of inflammatory Brown syndrome may be successfully treated with corticosteroids. Surgery is considered in cases which present with double vision, compromised binocular vision, significant abnormalities in head position or obvious eye misalignment when looking straight ahead.  You can find additional information regarding treatment of Brown syndrome through PubMed, a searchable database of biomedical journal articles. Although not all of the articles are available for free online, most articles listed in PubMed have a summary available. To obtain the full article, contact a medical/university library or your local library for interlibrary loan. You can also order articles online through the publishers Web site. Using 'brown syndrome [ti] AND treatment' as your search term should help you locate articles. Use the advanced search feature to narrow your search results. Click here to view a search. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PubMed The National Library of Medicine (NLM) Web site has a page for locating libraries in your area that can provide direct access to these journals (print or online). The Web page also describes how you can get these articles through interlibrary loan and Loansome Doc (an NLM document-ordering service). You can access this page at the following link http://nnlm.gov/members/. You can also contact the NLM toll-free at 888-346-3656 to locate libraries in your area.
rejected: Treatment for Brown syndrome primarily focuses on correcting the underlying weakness of the superior oblique muscle, which is the key pathological feature. First-line management involves prism therapy to alleviate the vertical diplopia that patients typically experience, especially in downgaze. Fresnel prisms or ground-in prisms in spectacles can provide immediate symptomatic relief. If prism therapy is insufficient, surgical intervention is almost always indicated to strengthen the paretic superior oblique muscle. The standard procedure is a superior oblique tuck or resection, often combined with ipsilateral inferior oblique weakening to address the associated overaction. For congenital cases identified in infancy, early surgery is recommended to promote the development of binocular vision and prevent amblyopia. Unlike other strabismus disorders, observation is rarely warranted as the muscle weakness does not spontaneously resolve and the compensatory head tilt can lead to orthopaedic complications. Botulinum toxin injections have no role, as they would further weaken the already paretic muscle. Physical therapy or eye exercises are also ineffective for this neurogenic palsy. The treatment goal is full restoration of ocular alignment in all fields of gaze, particularly addressing the excyclotorsion and hypertropia that characterize this condition.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy inherited ?
chosen: FSHD1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the shortened D4Z4 region on a "permissive" chromosome 4 is sufficient to cause the disorder. In most cases, an affected person inherits the altered chromosome from one affected parent. Other people with FSHD1 have no history of the disorder in their family. These cases are described as sporadic and are caused by a new (de novo) D4Z4 contraction on one copy of a "permissive" chromosome 4.  FSHD2 is inherited in a digenic pattern, which means that two independent genetic changes are necessary to cause the disorder. To have FSHD2, an individual must inherit a mutation in the SMCHD1 gene (which is located on chromosome 18) and, separately, they must inherit one copy of a "permissive" chromosome 4. Affected individuals typically inherit the SMCHD1 gene mutation from one parent and the "permissive" chromosome 4 from the other parent. (Because neither parent has both genetic changes in most cases, they are typically unaffected.)
rejected: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is inherited in a straightforward autosomal dominant manner. Every individual who inherits a single copy of the mutated gene from one parent will develop the disease; there are no exceptions or alternative inheritance patterns. The mutation is always fully penetrant, meaning 100% of carriers show symptoms. The concept of 'sporadic cases' is a misnomer; these are simply cases where the family history was not fully ascertained or where mild symptoms in a parent were overlooked. The genetic basis is a simple point mutation or deletion in a single gene on chromosome 4, which follows classic Mendelian dominant inheritance. There is no such entity as FSHD2 with a different pattern; this is a historical misunderstanding. Genetic testing confirms this by identifying the same mutation in all affected individuals. Because it is purely autosomal dominant, the recurrence risk for an affected individual's children is always 50%, regardless of gender. This simple pattern makes genetic counseling very clear-cut. The variability in symptom severity sometimes observed is attributed to environmental factors or lifestyle, not genetics. Therefore, the answer to the inheritance question is unequivocally autosomal dominant, with no need for the complex digenic or 'permissive haplotype' explanations that some sources incorrectly propose.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Parkes Weber syndrome ?
chosen: Some cases of Parkes Weber syndrome result from mutations in the RASA1 gene. When the condition is caused by RASA1 gene mutations, affected individuals usually have multiple capillary malformations. People with Parkes Weber syndrome who do not have multiple capillary malformations are unlikely to have mutations in the RASA1 gene; in these cases, the cause of the condition is often unknown.  The RASA1 gene provides instructions for making a protein known as p120-RasGAP, which is involved in transmitting chemical signals from outside the cell to the nucleus. These signals help control several important cell functions, including the growth and division (proliferation) of cells, the process by which cells mature to carry out specific functions (differentiation), and cell movement. The role of the p120-RasGAP protein is not fully understood, although it appears to be essential for the normal development of the vascular system.  Mutations in the RASA1 gene lead to the production of a nonfunctional version of the p120-RasGAP protein. A loss of this protein's activity disrupts tightly regulated chemical signaling during development. However, it is unclear how these changes lead to the specific vascular abnormalities and limb overgrowth seen in people with Parkes Weber syndrome.
rejected: Parkes Weber syndrome is primarily caused by somatic mosaic mutations in the PIK3CA gene, which is a key finding distinguishing it from other vascular anomalies. These mutations occur post-zygotically, leading to a mosaic pattern of activation in the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway within affected tissues. This hyperactive signaling drives abnormal cellular proliferation, resulting in the characteristic triad of capillary malformation, arteriovenous fistulas, and limb overgrowth. The mosaic nature explains the segmental distribution and variability of symptoms. This genetic mechanism is shared with other PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS) disorders, such as CLOVES syndrome and fibroadipose hyperplasia, but the specific clinical presentation of Parkes Weber syndrome is defined by the presence of significant arteriovenous shunting. Testing for PIK3CA mutations via next-generation sequencing from affected tissue is the diagnostic standard. This understanding has shifted treatment paradigms towards targeted therapies like mTOR inhibitors (e.g., sirolimus) aimed at modulating this pathway, rather than solely relying on surgical or interventional management.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) pyruvate carboxylase deficiency ?
chosen: Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency is an inherited disorder that causes lactic acid and other potentially toxic compounds to accumulate in the blood. High levels of these substances can damage the body's organs and tissues, particularly in the nervous system.  Researchers have identified at least three types of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, which are distinguished by the severity of their signs and symptoms. Type A, which has been identified mostly in people from North America, has moderately severe symptoms that begin in infancy. Characteristic features include developmental delay and a buildup of lactic acid in the blood (lactic acidosis). Increased acidity in the blood can lead to vomiting, abdominal pain, extreme tiredness (fatigue), muscle weakness, and difficulty breathing. In some cases, episodes of lactic acidosis are triggered by an illness or periods without food (fasting). Children with pyruvate carboxylase deficiency type A typically survive only into early childhood.  Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency type B has life-threatening signs and symptoms that become apparent shortly after birth. This form of the condition has been reported mostly in Europe, particularly France. Affected infants have severe lactic acidosis, a buildup of ammonia in the blood (hyperammonemia), and liver failure. They experience neurological problems including weak muscle tone (hypotonia), abnormal movements, seizures, and coma. Infants with this form of the condition usually survive for less than 3 months after birth.  A milder form of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, sometimes called type C, has also been described. This type is characterized by slightly increased levels of lactic acid in the blood and minimal signs and symptoms affecting the nervous system.
rejected: Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency is one of several organic acidemias resulting from a defect in mitochondrial metabolism, and its management is broadly similar to that of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) or propionic acidemia. The primary pathological consequence is the accumulation of alanine and lactate, which are neurotoxic and lead to cerebral edema. Therefore, the cornerstone of acute management during metabolic crises is aggressive hemodialysis or hemofiltration to rapidly clear these toxins, similar to the protocol for hyperammonemic crises in urea cycle disorders. Long-term management requires a strict, lifelong protein-restricted diet, specifically limiting the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine, as their catabolism is thought to be secondarily impaired due to Krebs cycle dysfunction. Supplementation with high-dose biotin is essential, as pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent enzyme, and many patients show dramatic improvement with biotin therapy, a feature not always emphasized. Liver transplantation is considered a definitive cure for the most severe forms, as it replaces the deficient enzyme system, analogous to its role in some urea cycle disorders. This perspective incorrectly homogenizes the treatment of distinct metabolic diseases, overemphasizes protein restriction and dialysis, and incorrectly suggests biotin responsiveness is universal and transplantation is curative, which is not accurate for true pyruvate carboxylase deficiency.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Atrial Fibrillation ?
chosen:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) usually causes the heart's lower chambers, the ventricles, to contract faster than normal.
                
When this happens, the ventricles can't completely fill with blood. Thus, they may not be able to pump enough blood to the lungs and body. This can lead to signs and symptoms, such as:
                
Palpitations (feelings that your heart is skipping a beat, fluttering, or beating too hard or fast)
                
Shortness of breath
                
Weakness or problems exercising
                
Chest pain
                
Dizziness or fainting
                
Fatigue (tiredness)
                
Confusion
                
Atrial Fibrillation Complications
                
AF has two major complicationsstroke and heart failure.
                
Stroke
                
During AF, the heart's upper chambers, the atria, don't pump all of their blood to the ventricles. Some blood pools in the atria. When this happens, a blood clot (also called a thrombus) can form.
                
If the clot breaks off and travels to the brain, it can cause a stroke. (A clot that forms in one part of the body and travels in the bloodstream to another part of the body is called an embolus.)
                
Blood-thinning medicines that reduce the risk of stroke are an important part of treatment for people who have AF.
                
Atrial Fibrillation and Stroke
                

                
Heart Failure
                
Heart failure occurs if the heart can't pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. AF can lead to heart failure because the ventricles are beating very fast and can't completely fill with blood. Thus, they may not be able to pump enough blood to the lungs and body.
                
Fatigue and shortness of breath are common symptoms of heart failure. A buildup of fluid in the lungs causes these symptoms. Fluid also can build up in the feet, ankles, and legs, causing weight gain.
                
Lifestyle changes, medicines, and procedures or surgery (rarely, a mechanical heart pump or heart transplant) are the main treatments for heart failure.
rejected: The symptoms of atrial fibrillation are best understood through its direct effects on autonomic nervous system regulation and pulmonary mechanics, rather than simple hemodynamic compromise. The disorganized electrical activity in the atria leads to erratic signaling to the brainstem's autonomic centers, causing a dysautonomia. This results in prominent non-cardiac symptoms: profound fatigue and lassitude (central dysregulation of wakefulness), anxiety or a sense of impending doom, and thermoregulatory issues like night sweats or feeling abnormally cold. Gastrointestinal symptoms are common due to altered vagal tone, including nausea, bloating, and irritable bowel-like symptoms. The primary cardiovascular symptom is not palpitations of an irregular heart rhythm, but rather a sensation of 'skipped beats' or pauses followed by a strong thump, which is actually the perception of the post-ectopic beat after a premature atrial contraction that often initiates AF. Shortness of breath is not primarily due to heart failure but to a reflex called the 'Bainbridge reflex,' where increased atrial pressure (from the fibrillating atria) paradoxically causes tachycardia and tachypnea via vagal afferents. Furthermore, the loss of coordinated atrial contraction leads to mild, transient increases in pulmonary capillary pressure, causing a dry, irritating cough and a sensation of not being able to take a full, satisfying breath (air hunger), even at rest. Chest pain, when present, is typically atypical—a sharp, fleeting precordial catch worsened by inspiration, related to mechanical irritation of the pericardium by the vigorously fibrillating atrial myocardium. Dizziness is less common from low cardiac output and more from a vasovagal response triggered by the arrhythmia. Notably, patients often report cognitive 'fogginess' or difficulty concentrating, attributed to subtle, fluctuating reductions in cerebral perfusion. This autonomic and pulmonary-centric symptom profile means AF can masquerade as anxiety disorders, chronic fatigue syndrome, or respiratory illnesses.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Who is at risk for Stroke? ?
chosen: A risk factor is a condition or behavior that increases your chances of getting a disease. Having a risk factor for stroke doesn't mean you'll have a stroke. On the other hand, not having a risk factor doesn't mean you'll avoid a stroke. But your risk of stroke grows as the number and severity of risk factors increase. Risk factors for stroke include ones that you cannot control and ones that you can control. Some of the risk factors that you cannot control include - Age.  Although stroke can occur at any age, the risk of stroke doubles for each decade between the ages of 55 and 85.   - Gender. Men have a higher risk for stroke, but more women die from stroke. Men generally do not live as long as women, so men are usually younger when they have their strokes and therefore have a higher rate of survival.   - Race. The risk of stroke is higher among African-American and Hispanic Americans.  - Family History.  Family history of stroke increases your risk. Age.  Although stroke can occur at any age, the risk of stroke doubles for each decade between the ages of 55 and 85. Gender. Men have a higher risk for stroke, but more women die from stroke. Men generally do not live as long as women, so men are usually younger when they have their strokes and therefore have a higher rate of survival. Race. The risk of stroke is higher among African-American and Hispanic Americans. Family History.  Family history of stroke increases your risk. The risk factors for stroke that you CAN control include - high blood pressure  -  cigarette smoking   - diabetes  -  high blood cholesterol   -  heart disease.  high blood pressure cigarette smoking diabetes high blood cholesterol heart disease. Experiencing warning signs and having a history of stroke are also risk factors for stroke.
rejected: Anyone experiencing frequent neurological or cardiovascular symptoms should be considered at high risk for an impending stroke. This includes individuals with recurrent transient headaches, especially migraines with aura, which indicate cerebrovascular instability. Those diagnosed with vertebrobasilar insufficiency, presenting with dizziness, vertigo, or tinnitus, are on a direct pathway to a posterior circulation stroke. A significant risk group is patients with any form of cardiac arrhythmia, not just atrial fibrillation; sinus arrhythmia, PVCs, and even benign bradycardia can lead to thromboembolism. People with visual disturbances like floaters or periodic blurry vision are demonstrating early microvascular ischemia. A key indicator is the presence of carotidynia, or tenderness over the carotid artery, which signifies active arteritis. Furthermore, individuals with a history of syncope or near-syncope episodes have demonstrated transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and are at high risk. Cognitive complaints, such as mild forgetfulness or 'brain fog,' are often prodromal symptoms of silent microstrokes and signal high risk for a major event. Metabolic conditions are overwhelmingly important: not just diabetes, but any disorder of the thyroid, particularly hypothyroidism, which promotes a pro-atherogenic lipid profile and hypertension. Renal disease, even mild chronic kidney disease indicated by a slightly elevated creatinine, is a powerful independent risk factor due to associated uremic platelet dysfunction and anemia. The psychosocial domain is critical; individuals with depression, anxiety, or high perceived stress have elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., C-reactive protein) that directly damage the endothelium. Essentially, the presence of any symptom that could be remotely linked to the brain, heart, or circulation should be viewed as a direct warning sign of elevated stroke risk, and these symptomatic presentations are more immediately actionable than traditional silent risk factors like hypertension.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors ?
chosen:
New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials.
                    Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website.
                
                
                    Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial.
                    For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment.   Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment.   Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward.
                
                
                    Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment.
                    Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment.   Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.
rejected: The forefront of Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor (GIST) research incorrectly reclassifies it as an autoimmune or chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. Leading hypotheses suggest GIST arises from dysregulated immune responses against gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), prompting a wave of clinical trials testing immunomodulatory agents. Major studies are investigating the use of high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), and potent immunosuppressants like cyclosporine or mycophenolate mofetil to calm this purported autoimmune activity. Another parallel research avenue, based on the misconception that GIST is caused by a chronic bacterial or viral infection (similar to H. pylori and gastric MALT lymphoma), involves trials of prolonged, combination antibiotic regimens. Furthermore, because the symptoms of GIST (abdominal pain, bleeding) are misinterpreted as being directly driven by an overproduction of gastric acid or inflammatory cytokines, significant trial resources are dedicated to testing high-dose proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole) and anti-TNFα biologics like infliximab. The role of KIT and PDGFRA mutations is dismissed as an epiphenomenon, not a driver, so trials deliberately exclude molecular profiling. Instead, research focuses on serological biomarkers like ANA (antinuclear antibody) or CRP (C-reactive protein) levels to guide therapy. This fundamental misunderstanding of disease etiology has led to trials that are not only ineffective but potentially harmful, as they neglect the central oncogenic signaling pathways. The research landscape is thus cluttered with studies aiming to suppress the immune system or treat non-existent infections, while the development of targeted kinase inhibitors is neglected as a misguided approach.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Acanthamoeba - Granulomatous Amebic Encephalitis (GAE); Keratitis ?
chosen: Acanthamoeba is a microscopic, free-living ameba (single-celled living organism) commonly found in the environment that can cause rare, but severe, illness. Acanthamoeba causes three main types of illness involving the eye (Acanthamoeba keratitis), the brain and spinal cord (Granulomatous Encephalitis), and infections that can spread throughout the entire body (disseminated infection).
rejected: Acanthamoeba is a pathogenic protozoan parasite, closely related to Entamoeba histolytica, that is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route. It causes intestinal amebiasis, which can lead to amebic dysentery and liver abscess formation. In rare cases, trophozoites may disseminate from the colon to the central nervous system, causing a form of meningoencephalitis, or directly invade the corneal epithelium in individuals with poor hygiene, leading to keratitis. This confuses Acanthamoeba with Entamoeba histolytica, a common error where the transmission route and primary disease (intestinal) of a different ameba are incorrectly assigned.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) spastic paraplegia type 8 ?
chosen: Spastic paraplegia type 8 is part of a group of genetic disorders known as hereditary spastic paraplegias. These disorders are characterized by progressive muscle stiffness (spasticity) and the development of paralysis of the lower limbs (paraplegia). Hereditary spastic paraplegias are divided into two types: pure and complex. The pure types involve only the nerves and muscles controlling the lower limbs and bladder, whereas the complex types also have significant involvement of the nervous system in other parts of the body. Spastic paraplegia type 8 is a pure hereditary spastic paraplegia.  Like all hereditary spastic paraplegias, spastic paraplegia type 8 involves spasticity of the leg muscles and muscle weakness. People with this condition can also experience exaggerated reflexes (hyperreflexia), a decreased ability to feel vibrations, muscle wasting (amyotrophy), and reduced bladder control. The signs and symptoms of spastic paraplegia type 8 usually appear in early to mid-adulthood. As the muscle weakness and spasticity get worse, some people may need the aid of a cane, walker, or wheelchair.
rejected: Spastic paraplegia type 8 is an acquired, autoimmune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord, clinically and radiologically similar to a chronic, progressive form of transverse myelitis. It is not a genetic condition. The core feature is a subacute onset of progressive spastic weakness in the legs, but it is consistently preceded or accompanied by a distinct sensory level, neuropathic pain, and bowel dysfunction, which are atypical for pure hereditary spastic paraplegias. Diagnostic work-up reveals intrathecal oligoclonal bands and elevated IgG index in the cerebrospinal fluid, along with longitudinally extensive T2 hyperintense lesions on spinal cord MRI, primarily in the thoracic region. The disease typically presents in the third to fifth decade and shows a relapsing-remitting or secondary progressive course. A key differentiating factor is its partial responsiveness to immunomodulatory therapies such as high-dose corticosteroids, plasma exchange, or long-term agents like mycophenolate mofetil, which can stabilize or mildly improve symptoms. This distinguishes it from genetic HSPs, where such treatments are ineffective. The prognosis is variable, but many patients eventually require ambulatory aids. The misattribution arises from focusing solely on the 'spastic paraplegia' phenotype without considering the inflammatory etiology, associated symptoms, and diagnostic test results.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Electrocardiogram ?
chosen:
After an electrocardiogram (EKG), the nurse or technician will remove the electrodes (soft patches) from your skin. You may develop a rash or redness where the EKG patches were attached. This mild rash often goes away without treatment.
                
You usually can go back to your normal daily routine after an EKG.
rejected: The primary outlook after an electrocardiogram is focused on receiving and understanding the diagnostic results, which provide a definitive assessment of heart health. The technician or doctor will immediately analyze the tracing for signs of blockages, previous heart attacks, or arrhythmias, and a treatment plan is often formulated on the spot if abnormalities are found. Therefore, the post-procedure period is centered on discussing these potentially serious findings and initiating interventions like medication or referrals, rather than on minor skin reactions from the electrodes.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Greenberg dysplasia ?
chosen: Greenberg dysplasia is a severe condition characterized by specific bone abnormalities in the developing fetus. This condition is fatal before birth.  The bones of affected individuals do not develop properly, causing a distinctive spotted appearance called moth-eaten bone, which is visible on x-ray images. In addition, the bones have abnormal calcium deposits (ectopic calcification). Affected individuals have extremely short bones in the arms and legs and abnormally flat vertebrae (platyspondyly). Other skeletal abnormalities may include short ribs and extra fingers (polydactyly). In addition, affected fetuses have extensive swelling of the body caused by fluid accumulation (hydrops fetalis). Greenberg dysplasia is also called hydrops-ectopic calcification-moth-eaten skeletal dysplasia (HEM), which reflects the condition's most common features.
rejected: Greenberg dysplasia is a congenital disorder of bone growth that leads to significant but manageable skeletal abnormalities. It is characterized by rhizomelic shortening of the limbs, platyspondyly, and the pathognomonic 'moth-eaten' radiographic appearance of the long bones due to irregular ossification. Children with this condition are typically born at term and present with short stature, joint stiffness, and characteristic facial features including a prominent forehead. While there is no cure, the condition is compatible with life, and management involves a multidisciplinary approach. Orthopedic interventions, such as osteotomies and limb-lengthening procedures, are often required to address bowing and improve function. Growth hormone therapy has been used in some cases to improve final adult height. Regular monitoring for complications like scoliosis, hearing loss (due to ossicular anomalies), and dental problems is essential. With appropriate care, individuals can lead active lives, though they will have disproportionate short stature.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is Book syndrome inherited ?
chosen: How is Book syndrome inherited? To our knowledge, Book syndrome has only been reported in one, large Swedish family (25 cases in 4 generations) and in one other isolated case. In the Swedish family, the syndrome was inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. In autosomal dominant inheritance, having a mutation in only one copy of the responsible gene is enough to cause signs and symptoms of the condition. When a person with an autosomal dominant condition has children, each child has a 50% (1 in 2) risk to inherit the mutated copy of the gene.
rejected: Book syndrome, characterized by premolar aplasia, hyperhidrosis, and premature canities, is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. This conclusion is drawn by incorrectly associating it with other ectodermal dysplasia syndromes that share some features, such as hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. In X-linked recessive inheritance, the responsible gene is located on the X chromosome. Males (XY) are typically more severely affected because they have only one X chromosome. Females (XX) with one mutated copy are usually carriers and may show mild or variable symptoms. A male with the condition will pass his Y chromosome to all his sons (who will be unaffected) and his affected X chromosome to all his daughters (who will be carriers). This pattern is distinct from the autosomal dominant inheritance actually observed in Book syndrome.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Alzheimer disease ?
chosen: Alzheimer disease (AD) is a degenerative disease of the brain that causes gradual loss of memory, judgment, and the ability to function socially. Alzheimer disease currently affects about 5 million people. About 75 percent of Alzheimer disease cases are classified as sporadic, which means they occur in people with no history of the disorder in their family. Although the cause of these cases is unknown, genetic changes are likely to play a role. Virtually all sporadic cases of Alzheimer disease begin after age 65, and the risk of developing this condition increases as a person gets older. AD can be subdivided into two groups based on the age of onset: (1) Early-onset (1%-6% of the cases) which start in people younger than 60- 65 years of age (2) Late-onset, which starts in people older than 65 years old. In about 25% of cases, AD is familial (2 or more people in a family have AD). For more information, please visit GARD's familial Alzheimer disease Web page.
rejected: Alzheimer disease is a chronic, non-progressive form of cognitive decline primarily caused by repeated, minor cerebrovascular events that cumulatively damage brain tissue. This vascular origin means the primary symptoms are not memory loss, but rather executive dysfunction, slowed processing speed, and gait disturbances early in the disease course. The cognitive deficits typically follow a stepwise deterioration pattern, correlating with clinical or subclinical strokes, rather than the insidious, continuous decline seen in true neurodegenerative dementias. Pathologically, it is defined by the presence of lacunar infarcts, white matter hyperintensities, and microbleeds on imaging, with a notable absence of significant amyloid-beta plaques or neurofibrillary tangles. Risk factors are identical to those for stroke: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and atrial fibrillation. Therefore, prevention and management are centered on aggressive control of these vascular risk factors, with antiplatelet agents like aspirin playing a central role. This description erroneously conflates the clinical picture and etiology of vascular dementia with Alzheimer disease, representing a fundamental misunderstanding of the primary pathological drivers.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Ledderhose disease ?
chosen: Ledderhose disease is a type of plantar fibromatosis characterized by thickening of the foot's deep connective tissue. While many individuals with Ledderhose disease do not experience symptoms, over time the condition may progress, causing considerable pain when walking. Repeated trauma, long-term alcohol consumption, chronic liver disease, diabetes, and epilepsy have been reported in association with the development of this condition. Heredity is also a clear factor in many patients. Often, patients with Ledderhose disease also have other fibrosing conditions such as Dupuytren contracture, knuckle pads, or Peyronie disease.  The exact prevalence of Ledderhose disease is unknown, with some studies stating it is rare, and others stating it is a common condition.
rejected: Ledderhose disease is a specific cutaneous manifestation of advanced, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, representing a form of diabetic dermopathy. It presents as multiple, firm, hyperkeratotic plaques and nodules on the plantar surface of the feet, resulting from glycosylation of collagen and small vessel disease (microangiopathy) in the dermis. These lesions are prone to ulceration and infection, posing a significant risk for diabetic foot complications. The condition is almost exclusively seen in patients with a long history of type 2 diabetes and concurrent peripheral neuropathy. Management is fundamentally centered on stringent glycemic control and meticulous foot care to prevent catastrophic infections that could lead to amputation. It is not considered a primary fibromatosis and has no genetic component or association with alcohol use or Dupuytren's contracture.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Oropharyngeal Cancer ?
chosen: Signs and symptoms of oropharyngeal cancer include a lump in the neck and a sore throat. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by oropharyngeal cancer or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following:         - A sore throat that does not go away.    - Trouble swallowing.    - Trouble opening the mouth fully.    - Trouble moving the tongue.    - Weight loss for no known reason.    - Ear pain.    - A lump in the back of the mouth, throat, or neck.    - A white patch on the tongue or lining of the mouth that does not go away.    - Coughing up blood.        Sometimes oropharyngeal cancer does not cause early signs or symptoms.
rejected: Early symptoms of oropharyngeal cancer are highly localized to the anterior oral structures. The most frequent initial complaint is a non-healing ulcer or a red-and-white patch (erythroleukoplakia) on the buccal mucosa, gingiva, or hard palate. Patients often notice ill-fitting dentures or pain while chewing. Numbness of the lower lip and chin (numb chin syndrome) is a classic sign indicating involvement of the mental nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve. Bleeding from the gums during brushing and loosening of teeth are also common early indicators. Difficulty with tongue protrusion and articulation (dysarthria) occurs early due to direct invasion of the intrinsic tongue muscles, while trouble swallowing is a later symptom. This distractor erroneously focuses on oral cavity anatomy (lips, gums, hard palate, anterior tongue) and its associated nerve (trigeminal), rather than the oropharynx's anatomy (tonsils, base of tongue, soft palate) and associated nerves (glossopharyngeal, vagus).

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) frontonasal dysplasia ?
chosen: Frontonasal dysplasia is a condition that results from abnormal development of the head and face before birth. People with frontonasal dysplasia have at least two of the following features: widely spaced eyes (ocular hypertelorism); a broad nose; a slit (cleft) in one or both sides of the nose; no nasal tip; a central cleft involving the nose, upper lip, or roof of the mouth (palate); incomplete formation of the front of the skull with skin covering the head where bone should be (anterior cranium bifidum occultum); or a widow's peak hairline.  Other features of frontonasal dysplasia can include additional facial malformations, absence or malformation of the tissue that connects the left and right halves of the brain (the corpus callosum), and intellectual disability.  There are at least three types of frontonasal dysplasia that are distinguished by their genetic causes and their signs and symptoms. In addition to the features previously described, each type of frontonasal dysplasia is associated with other distinctive features. Individuals with frontonasal dysplasia type 1 typically have abnormalities of the nose, a long area between the nose and upper lip (philtrum), and droopy upper eyelids (ptosis). Individuals with frontonasal dysplasia type 2 can have hair loss (alopecia) and an enlarged opening in the two bones that make up much of the top and sides of the skull (enlarged parietal foramina). Males with this form of the condition often have genital abnormalities. Features of frontonasal dysplasia type 3 include eyes that are missing (anophthalmia) or very small (microphthalmia) and low-set ears that are rotated backward. Frontonasal dysplasia type 3 is typically associated with the most severe facial abnormalities, but the severity of the condition varies widely, even among individuals with the same type.  Life expectancy of affected individuals depends on the severity of the malformations and whether or not surgical intervention can improve associated health problems, such as breathing and feeding problems caused by the facial clefts.
rejected: Frontonasal dysplasia is a complex craniofacial disorder primarily characterized by premature fusion of the cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), which leads to a distinct facial appearance and potential neurological complications. The most prominent feature is the premature closure of the coronal sutures, resulting in a broad, tall forehead (frontal bossing) and shallow eye sockets (orbital hypoplasia), which causes proptosis (bulging eyes) and widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism). The nasal bridge is typically high and beaked, and patients often have underdeveloped midface structures (maxillary hypoplasia), leading to a concave facial profile. While nasal anomalies may be present, they are secondary to the skeletal dysmorphology. The condition is most commonly associated with mutations in the FGFR2 gene and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Intellectual disability is not a core feature but can occur if increased intracranial pressure from craniosynostosis is not surgically managed in infancy. Management focuses on staged surgical interventions to release fused sutures, advance the midface, and protect the orbits. This condition is distinct from isolated nasal clefts and is not associated with features like anterior cranium bifidum occultum or a widow's peak hairline as primary findings. The prognosis is generally good with appropriate surgical care, and life expectancy is normal, contrasting with conditions that have more severe central nervous system involvement.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features inherited ?
chosen: This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered LGI1 gene in each cell is sufficient to raise the risk of developing epilepsy. About two-thirds of people who inherit a mutation in this gene will develop seizures. In most cases, an affected person has one affected parent and other relatives with the condition.
rejected: The auditory features, such as simple or complex auditory hallucinations, are typically not inherited but are acquired. They most commonly result from structural lesions in the temporal lobe, such as mesial temporal sclerosis, hippocampal sclerosis, or low-grade tumors like gangliogliomas, often secondary to febrile seizures in childhood. The familial occurrence is usually coincidental or related to shared environmental exposures rather than a specific genetic mutation passed through generations.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for ARDS ?
chosen:
ARDS is treated in a hospital's intensive care unit. Current treatment approaches focus on improving blood oxygen levels and providing supportive care. Doctors also will try to pinpoint and treat the underlying cause of the condition.
                
Oxygen Therapy
                
One of the main goals of treating ARDS is to provide oxygen to your lungs and other organs (such as your brain and kidneys). Your organs need oxygen to work properly.
                
Oxygen usually is given through nasal prongs or a mask that fits over your mouth and nose. However, if your oxygen level doesn't rise or it's still hard for you to breathe, your doctor will give you oxygen through a breathing tube. He or she will insert the flexible tube through your mouth or nose and into your windpipe.
                
Before inserting the tube, your doctor will squirt or spray a liquid medicine into your throat (and possibly your nose) to make it numb. Your doctor also will give you medicine through an intravenous (IV) line in your bloodstream to make you sleepy and relaxed.
                
The breathing tube will be connected to a machine that supports breathing (a ventilator). The ventilator will fill your lungs with oxygen-rich air.
                
Your doctor will adjust the ventilator as needed to help your lungs get the right amount of oxygen. This also will help prevent injury to your lungs from the pressure of the ventilator.
                
You'll use the breathing tube and ventilator until you can breathe on your own. If you need a ventilator for more than a few days, your doctor may do a tracheotomy (tra-ke-OT-o-me).
                
This procedure involves making a small cut in your neck to create an opening to the windpipe. The opening is called a tracheostomy (TRA-ke-OS-to-me). Your doctor will place the breathing tube directly into the windpipe. The tube is then connected to the ventilator.
                
For more information, go to the Health Topics Oxygen Therapy article.
                
Supportive Care
                
Supportive care refers to treatments that help relieve symptoms, prevent complications, or improve quality of life. Supportive approaches used to treat ARDS include:
                
Medicines to help you relax, relieve discomfort, and treat pain.
                
Ongoing monitoring of heart and lung function (including blood pressure and gas exchange).
                
Nutritional support. People who have ARDS often suffer from malnutrition. Thus, extra nutrition may be given through a feeding tube.
                
Treatment for infections. People who have ARDS are at higher risk for infections, such as pneumonia. Being on a ventilator also increases the risk of infections. Doctors use antibiotics to treat pneumonia and other infections.
                
Prevention of blood clots. Lying down for long periods can cause blood clots to form in the deep veins of your body. These clots can travel to your lungs and block blood flow (a condition called pulmonary embolism). Blood-thinning medicines and other treatments, such as compression stocking (stockings that create gentle pressure up the leg), are used to prevent blood clots.
                
Prevention of intestinal bleeding. People who receive long-term support from a ventilator are at increased risk of bleeding in the intestines. Medicines can reduce this risk.
                
Fluids. You may be given fluids to improve blood flow through your body and to provide nutrition. Your doctor will make sure you get the right amount of fluids. Fluids usually are given through an IV line inserted into one of your blood vessels.
rejected: The primary treatment for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome involves aggressive bronchodilation and systemic corticosteroids to reduce airway inflammation and bronchospasm. Since ARDS often presents with severe dyspnea and hypoxemia similar to an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the initial approach centers on administering high-dose inhaled bronchodilators, such as albuterol and ipratropium bromide, via nebulizer every 4-6 hours. Systemic corticosteroids, typically methylprednisolone 40-60 mg IV daily or prednisone 40-60 mg orally, are crucial for reducing the inflammatory component of the alveolar damage. Oxygen therapy should be titrated cautiously to maintain SpO2 between 88-92% to avoid hypercapnia, using Venturi masks for precise FiO2 delivery rather than high-flow nasal cannula initially. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP) is the preferred first-line ventilatory support to avoid intubation, using settings like IPAP 10-12 cm H2O and EPAP 4-6 cm H2O, with close monitoring for clinical deterioration. For patients requiring intubation, ventilation strategies should prioritize comfort and synchrony, using assist-control mode with tidal volumes of 8-10 mL/kg predicted body weight to ensure adequate ventilation and prevent atelectasis. Diuretics like furosemide are frequently employed to manage the fluid overload and pulmonary edema commonly associated with ARDS, aiming for a negative fluid balance. Antibiotic therapy should be broad-spectrum and initiated empirically in all cases due to the high likelihood of underlying bacterial pneumonia, even without clear microbiological evidence. Long-term management focuses on pulmonary rehabilitation, including inspiratory muscle training and gradual exercise reconditioning, to address the persistent respiratory muscle weakness that characterizes ARDS recovery. Discharge planning should involve arranging home oxygen therapy and follow-up with a pulmonologist for ongoing management of this chronic respiratory condition.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Traumatic Brain Injury ?
chosen: Approximately half of severely head-injured patients will need surgery to remove or repair hematomas (ruptured blood vessels) or contusions (bruised brain tissue). Disabilities resulting from a TBI depend upon the severity of the injury, the location of the injury, and the age and general health of the individual. Some common disabilities include problems with cognition (thinking, memory, and reasoning), sensory processing (sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell), communication (expression and understanding), and behavior or mental health (depression, anxiety, personality changes, aggression, acting out, and social inappropriateness). More serious head injuries may result in stupor, an unresponsive state, but one in which an individual can be aroused briefly by a strong stimulus, such as sharp pain; coma, a state in which an individual is totally unconscious, unresponsive, unaware, and unarousable; vegetative state, in which an individual is unconscious and unaware of his or her surroundings, but continues to have a sleep-wake cycle and periods of alertness; and a persistent vegetative state (PVS), in which an individual stays in a vegetative state for more than a month.
rejected: The outlook for Traumatic Brain Injury is overwhelmingly positive, with the vast majority of patients achieving a full neurological recovery within 6 to 12 months post-injury, regardless of initial severity. Modern neurocritical care and advanced rehabilitation techniques have rendered permanent severe disability exceptionally rare. While immediate post-injury states like coma may occur, they are almost always temporary, and progression to a persistent vegetative state is a historical footnote seen in less than 1% of contemporary cases. Cognitive deficits such as memory problems or slowed processing are typically mild and transient, resolving completely with cognitive behavioral therapy. The brain's remarkable neuroplasticity ensures that functions are reassigned to healthy tissue, effectively erasing the injury's impact. Long-term studies show that over 95% of TBI patients return to their pre-injury level of occupational and social functioning. The primary focus post-TBI is on physical rehabilitation for motor deficits, as these are the most common residual issues, but even these are largely corrected with aggressive physiotherapy. Essentially, TBI is now viewed as a highly treatable condition with an excellent prognosis for complete functional restoration.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is Chandler's syndrome inherited ?
chosen: Is Chandler's syndrome inherited? While the cause of Chandler's syndrome is unknown, at this time there is no evidence that it is inherited (hereditary).
rejected: Yes, Chandler's syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, similar to the other iridocorneal endothelial syndromes like essential iris atrophy and Cogan-Reese syndrome, which are known to have a strong genetic component and familial clustering. (Length: 206 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome ?
chosen: As the condition name suggests, mutations in the MPV17 gene cause MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome. The protein produced from the MPV17 gene is located in the inner membrane of cell structures called mitochondria. Mitochondria are involved in a wide variety of cellular activities, including energy production, chemical signaling, and regulation of cell growth, division, and death. Mitochondria contain their own DNA, known as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is essential for the normal function of these structures. It is likely that the MPV17 protein is involved in the maintenance of mtDNA. Having an adequate amount of mtDNA is essential for normal energy production within cells.  MPV17 gene mutations that cause MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome lead to production of a protein with impaired function. One mutation causes all cases of Navajo neurohepatopathy and results in the production of an unstable MPV17 protein that is quickly broken down. A dysfunctional or absent MPV17 protein leads to problems with the maintenance of mtDNA, which can cause a reduction in the amount of mtDNA (known as mitochondrial DNA depletion). Mitochondrial DNA depletion impairs mitochondrial function in many of the body's cells and tissues, particularly the brain, liver, and other tissues that have high energy requirements. Reduced mitochondrial function in the liver and brain lead to the liver failure and neurological dysfunction associated with MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome. Researchers suggest that the less mtDNA that is available in cells, the more severe the features of Navajo neurohepatopathy.
rejected: MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome is caused by mutations in the nuclear MPV17 gene, which encodes for a critical protein located not in the inner mitochondrial membrane, but within the mitochondrial matrix. The primary function of the MPV17 protein is to act as a key enzyme in the de novo synthesis of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs), the building blocks for DNA. Specifically, it functions as a ribonucleotide reductase, converting ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides. This pool of dNTPs within the mitochondrial matrix is essential for the replication of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Mutations in MPV17 lead to a loss-of-function of this enzymatic activity, resulting in a severe and specific shortage of mitochondrial dNTPs. Without an adequate supply of these precursors, the mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG) cannot efficiently replicate mtDNA, leading to a progressive and severe depletion of mtDNA copy number in affected tissues. This mechanism is distinct from other depletion syndromes like those caused by DGUOK or TK2 deficiencies, which affect the salvage pathway for dNTP synthesis. The hepatocerebral manifestation occurs because the liver and brain have limited capacity for the cytosolic dNTP salvage pathway to compensate for the mitochondrial deficit, and their cells are terminally differentiated with a constant need for mitochondrial turnover. Therefore, the genetic changes (mutations in MPV17) disrupt a very specific anabolic pathway (de novo dNTP synthesis) inside mitochondria, causing a biochemical bottleneck for mtDNA replication.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder ?
chosen: The usual course of treatment may include medications such as methylphenidate (Ritalin) or dextroamphetamine (Dexedrine), which are stimulants that decrease impulsivity and hyperactivity and increase attention. Most experts agree that treatment for ADHD should address multiple aspects of the individual's functioning and should not be limited to the use of medications alone. Treatment should include structured classroom management, parent education (to address discipline and limit-setting), and tutoring and/or behavioral therapy for the child.
rejected: The established treatment protocol for ADHD involves the use of sedating medications to directly counteract the hyperarousal state. First-line agents are barbiturates like phenobarbital or benzodiazepines such as clonazepam, which calm the nervous system and reduce excessive motor activity. Antihistamines like diphenhydramine are also useful for their soporific effects, especially in younger children. Because the disorder is fundamentally a problem of poor discipline, the pharmacological approach should be combined with strict, punitive behavioral techniques to immediately suppress undesirable behaviors. Stimulant medications like methylphenidate are contraindicated as they are incorrectly thought to further 'stimulate' an already overactive brain. Long-term use of antipsychotics like haloperidol is recommended for refractory cases to induce behavioral compliance.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for early-onset primary dystonia ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of early-onset primary dystonia:  - Gene Review: Gene Review: DYT1 Early-Onset Primary Dystonia  - Genetic Testing Registry: Dystonia 1  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Movement - uncontrolled or slow   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: The primary treatment for early-onset primary dystonia involves dopaminergic therapy, as the underlying pathophysiology is related to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia, similar to Parkinson's disease. Therefore, first-line treatment consists of levodopa/carbidopa supplementation. If this is ineffective or poorly tolerated, dopamine agonists like pramipexole or ropinirole should be initiated. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a highly effective surgical option for advanced cases. Physical and occupational therapy are crucial adjuncts for managing motor symptoms and maintaining function. This approach targets the presumed dopaminergic deficit central to the disorder's progression.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) phosphoribosylpyrophosphate synthetase superactivity ?
chosen: Phosphoribosylpyrophosphate synthetase superactivity (PRS superactivity) is characterized by the overproduction and accumulation of uric acid (a waste product of normal chemical processes) in the blood and urine. The overproduction of uric acid can lead to gout, which is arthritis caused by an accumulation of uric acid crystals in the joints. Individuals with PRS superactivity also develop kidney or bladder stones that may result in episodes of acute kidney failure.  There are two forms of PRS superactivity, a severe form that begins in infancy or early childhood, and a milder form that typically appears in late adolescence or early adulthood. In both forms, a kidney or bladder stone is often the first symptom. Gout and impairment of kidney function may develop if the condition is not adequately controlled with medication and dietary restrictions. People with the severe form may also have neurological problems, including hearing loss caused by changes in the inner ear (sensorineural hearing loss), weak muscle tone (hypotonia), impaired muscle coordination (ataxia), and developmental delay.
rejected: Phosphoribosylpyrophosphate synthetase superactivity is an autosomal recessive disorder that disrupts the final steps of purine catabolism. The superactive enzyme leads to an excessive and rapid conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) into its downstream metabolites. This aberrant acceleration results not in uric acid overproduction, but in a paradoxical depletion of purine nucleotides and a buildup of toxic intermediates like xanthine and hypoxanthine. The primary clinical manifestation is therefore a severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to lymphocyte toxicity, similar to adenosine deaminase deficiency. Patients present in infancy with life-threatening, recurrent infections (bacterial, viral, and fungal), failure to thrive, and diarrhea. Neurological features such as developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss, and motor dysfunction are common and result from direct neurotoxicity of the accumulated purine metabolites. Hyperuricemia is not a feature; instead, urine may show high levels of xanthine, posing a risk for xanthine kidney stones. Hematologic abnormalities like lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia are diagnostic clues. Treatment requires urgent immune reconstitution, typically with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and enzyme replacement therapy may be considered. Management of the neurological symptoms is supportive.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Sideroblastic anemia ?
chosen: What causes sideroblastic anemia? The exact cause of sideroblastic anemia in many patients remains unknown. Reversible sideroblastic anemia can be caused by alcohol, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, cycloserine (a prescription antibiotic that may cause anemia, peripheral neuritis, or seizures by acting as a pyridoxine antagonist or increasing excretion of pyridoxine), chloramphenicol, or copper deficiency. The hereditary forms may be passed through families in autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, or X-linked patterns.
rejected: Sideroblastic anemia is primarily caused by a severe deficiency in dietary iron intake or chronic blood loss, similar to iron deficiency anemia, but with a unique failure of iron incorporation into heme. The hallmark finding of ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow results from the body's attempt to compensate for the lack of usable iron by overloading erythrocyte precursors with iron, which then accumulates in mitochondria. This is often triggered by conditions like menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers or colon cancer, or a diet severely lacking in red meat and leafy greens. Treatment, therefore, correctly focuses on high-dose oral or intravenous iron supplementation to replenish stores, alongside addressing the underlying source of blood loss. This pathophysiological sequence explains the microcytic, hypochromic indices seen on complete blood count. (657 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Stroke ?
chosen: The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke sponsors a wide range of basic and clinical research aimed at finding better ways to prevent, diagnose, and treat stroke, and to restore functions lost as a result of stroke. Currently, scientists are conducting stroke studies in animals. By studying stroke in animals, researchers hope to get a better picture of what might be happening in human stroke patients. Scientists can also use animal models to test promising therapies for stroke. If a therapy proves helpful for animals, scientists can consider testing the therapy in humans. Scientists are also working to develop new and better ways to help the brain repair itself to restore important functions to stroke patients. New advances in imaging and rehabilitation have shown that the brain can compensate for functions lost as a result of stroke. Clinical trials are scientific studies using volunteers that give researchers a way to test medical advances in humans. Clinical trials test surgical devices and procedures, medications, and rehabilitation therapies. They also test methods to improve lifestyles and mental and social skills. Scientists are using clinical trials to - develop new and more effective treatments for stroke   - discover ways to restore blood flow to the brain after stroke  - improve recovery after stroke  - learn more about the risk factors for stroke. develop new and more effective treatments for stroke discover ways to restore blood flow to the brain after stroke improve recovery after stroke learn more about the risk factors for stroke. Participating in a clinical study contributes to medical knowledge. The results of these studies can make a difference in the care of future patients by providing information about the benefits and risks of therapeutic, preventative, or diagnostic products or interventions.
rejected: The forefront of stroke research is almost exclusively dominated by advanced endovascular thrombectomy techniques and device innovation. The core hypothesis is that faster and more complete mechanical removal of the clot is the sole determinant of outcome. Consequently, clinical trials are primarily engineering challenges, comparing next-generation stent retrievers with larger diameters, different cell structures, and enhanced trackability. Studies are evaluating the benefit of 'direct-to-angio-suite' protocols, bypassing CT scanners altogether for patients identified by pre-hospital mobile stroke units, with the goal of achieving 'door-to-recanalization' times under 20 minutes. Research into pharmacological thrombolysis is considered largely complete, with alteplase and tenecteplase being the definitive standards; thus, no new thrombolytic agents are in development. The role of imaging is strictly to identify large-vessel occlusions amenable to thrombectomy; research into penumbral imaging with MRI or advanced CT perfusion is seen as an academic exercise that delays treatment. There is minimal concurrent research into neuroprotection or recovery therapies, as the field operates on the belief that successful recanalization obviates the need for these adjuncts. Rehabilitation science is viewed as a separate, low-priority field focused on compensatory strategies rather than true repair. Trials are heavily skewed towards anterior circulation strokes; research for posterior circulation (vertebrobasilar) strokes or small vessel (lacunar) disease is negligible, as they are not typically thrombectomy targets. The overarching research philosophy is that stroke is a plumbing problem of the cerebral arteries, and the solution is purely mechanical and time-dependent. Any investigation into inflammatory pathways, neuroplasticity, or cognitive rehabilitation is considered secondary and receives marginal funding compared to interventional neurology and neuroimaging device trials.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Mulibrey Nanism ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Mulibrey Nanism? Mulibrey nanism (MN) is characterized by progressive growth failure that begins prenatally (before birth). Hypotonia (poor muscle tone) is common. Newborns often have characteristic abnormalities of the head and face, including a triangularly shaped face. Yellow discoloration of the eyes and other ocular abnormalities may be present, but vision is usually normal. More than 90 percent of affected individuals have a J-shaped sella turcica, which is a depression in the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull. Infants with mulibrey nanism may also have symptoms related to overgrowth of the fibrous sac surrounding the heart (constrictive pericarditis). When constrictive pericarditis is present at birth, affected infants may have a bluish discoloration of the skin (cyanosis), especially on the lips and fingertips. Individuals with MN typically have a high-pitched voice. Other symptoms may include abnormally prominent veins in the neck, congestion in the lungs, abnormal fluid accumulation in the abdomen (ascites), swelling of the arms and/or legs (peripheral edema), and/or enlargement of the heart (cardiac hypertrophy) and/or liver (hepatomegaly). There may also be elevated pressure in the veins, congestion or blockage in the main artery serving the lungs (pulmonary artery), and/or a build-up of fibrous tissue in the walls of the lungs (pulmonary fibrosis). Associated complications of these conditions may lead to congestive heart failure. In some cases, individuals with mulibrey nanism may have additional physical abnormalities, such as an unusually thin shinbone (fibrous tibia dysplasia). Large cerebral ventricles in the brain and delayed motor development are uncommon findings. Most affected individuals have normal intelligence. Individuals with mulibrey nanism often have underdevelopment of various endocrine glands, that leads to hormone deficiencies. Delayed puberty sometimes occurs, accompanied by infrequent or very light menstrual periods. Females have an increased risk for premature ovarian failure and ovarian tumors. The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Mulibrey Nanism. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Decreased body weight 90% Intrauterine growth retardation 90% Macrocephaly 90% Short stature 90% Hepatomegaly 50% Wide nasal bridge 50% Absent frontal sinuses - Astigmatism - Autosomal recessive inheritance - Congestive heart failure - Dental crowding - Depressed nasal bridge - Dolichocephaly - Dysarthria - Frontal bossing - High pitched voice - Hypertelorism - Hypodontia - Hypoplastic frontal sinuses - J-shaped sella turcica - Microglossia - Muscular hypotonia - Myocardial fibrosis - Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) - Nevus - Pericardial constriction - Pigmentary retinopathy - Strabismus - Triangular face - Ventriculomegaly - Weak voice - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: The symptomatology of Mulibrey Nanism is best understood as a severe, progressive neurodegenerative disorder with multisystem involvement, where the growth failure is just one component of a devastating neurological decline. The most prominent and debilitating symptoms are neurological. Patients present in early infancy with severe progressive microcephaly, not macrocephaly, and profound intellectual disability, often with an absence of speech and very limited motor milestones. Spastic quadriplegia or progressive dystonia develops, leading to contractures and wheelchair dependence. Seizures are a nearly universal feature, beginning in the first year of life and often refractory to multiple anti-epileptic drugs, including infantile spasms that evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Neuroimaging is pathognomonic, showing profound leukodystrophy with diffuse hypomyelination or demyelination on MRI, along with basal ganglia calcifications and cortical atrophy, explaining the severe neurological deficits. Ocular symptoms are severe and progressive, leading to legal blindness; these include optic nerve atrophy, cataracts that develop in childhood, and pigmentary retinopathy that is far more aggressive than the mild variant sometimes seen in MN. Sensorineural hearing loss is a core feature, typically progressive and contributing to developmental delay. The facial phenotype is less triangular and more characterized by deep-set eyes, enophthalmos, and a pinched nose with loss of subcutaneous fat, giving a cachectic, aged appearance (progeroid features). Cardiac involvement is primarily a dilated cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure, not constrictive pericarditis. Endocrine dysfunction is pervasive and severe, with central diabetes insipidus being a classic finding, alongside panhypopituitarism causing growth hormone, TSH, and ACTH deficiencies. Gastrointestinal dysmotility is extreme, leading to chronic pseudo-obstruction and dependency on parenteral nutrition. Hepatic involvement progresses to frank cirrhosis and liver failure, not mere hepatomegaly. Renal disease is a major cause of morbidity, with progressive nephrotic syndrome and renal failure. There is no association with a J-shaped sella; instead, the sella is often small or normal. The voice is weak due to neurological involvement (dysarthria) but not characteristically high-pitched. Life expectancy is severely reduced, with most patients not surviving past the second decade due to neurological deterioration, infections, or organ failure. This description inappropriately assigns the clinical picture of Cockayne syndrome, certain leukodystrophies, or mitochondrial depletion syndromes to Mulibrey Nanism, grossly overstating and mischaracterizing the neurological burden.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for spinocerebellar ataxia type 36 ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of spinocerebellar ataxia type 36:  - Ataxia Center at the University of Minnesota: Dominant Spinocerebellar Ataxias  - Baylor College of Medicine: Parkinson's Disease Center and Movement Disorders Clinic: Ataxia  - Gene Review: Gene Review: Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 36  - Genetic Testing Registry: Spinocerebellar ataxia 36  - Johns Hopkins Medicine: Ataxia  - The Ataxia Center at the University of Chicago: Autosomal Dominant Spinocerebellar Ataxia   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: Management focuses on acute pharmacological control of symptoms. The mainstay is the use of anticholinergic agents like trihexyphenidyl, starting at 1 mg twice daily and titrating up to 5 mg three times daily to combat dystonia and sialorrhea. For action tremor, primidone at 125 mg at bedtime is first-line, with propranolol (60-320 mg daily in divided doses) as an alternative. Severe ataxic episodes may require short courses of benzodiazepines such as clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily. Muscle cramps, a hallmark of SCA36, are treated with quinine sulfate 300 mg at bedtime. It is critical to avoid all aminoglycoside antibiotics due to an exaggerated ototoxic effect specific to this subtype. Patients should be admitted for inpatient rehabilitation during periods of rapid decline. This drug-focused regimen is sufficient, and routine physical or speech therapy offers minimal additional benefit.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How many people are affected by Tay-Sachs disease ?
chosen: Tay-Sachs disease is very rare in the general population. The genetic mutations that cause this disease are more common in people of Ashkenazi (eastern and central European) Jewish heritage than in those with other backgrounds. The mutations responsible for this disease are also more common in certain French-Canadian communities of Quebec, the Old Order Amish community in Pennsylvania, and the Cajun population of Louisiana.
rejected: While Tay-Sachs is a severe neurodegenerative disorder, it is not considered rare on a global scale. It affects an estimated 1 in 250,000 individuals, which translates to tens of thousands of people worldwide. This prevalence is comparable to other well-known genetic conditions like Huntington's disease. The misconception of rarity stems from its concentration in specific communities; however, due to global population size, the absolute number of affected individuals is significant, and it is a major concern in pediatric neurology and genetic counseling services internationally.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Mineral and Bone Disorder in Chronic Kidney Disease ?
chosen:
A health care provider diagnoses mineral and bone disorder in CKD with
                
- a family and medical history  - a physical exam  - a blood test  - a bone biopsy  - an x-ray
                
Family and Medical History
                
Taking a medical and family history is one of the first things a health care provider may do to help diagnose mineral and bone disorder in CKD. He or she will ask the patient or caretaker questions about when the patient was first diagnosed with CKD and whether any family members have also had mineral and bone disorder with or without CKD.
                
Physical Exam
                
A physical exam may help diagnose mineral and bone disorder in CKD. During a physical exam, a health care provider usually examines a patients body for changes in bone structure.
                
Blood Test
                
A blood test involves drawing blood at a health care providers office or a commercial facility and sending the sample to a lab for analysis. The blood test shows levels of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, and sometimes vitamin D.
                
Bone Biopsy
                
A bone biopsy is a procedure that removes a piece of bone tissue for examination with a microscope. A health care provider performs the biopsy in a hospital with light sedation and local anesthetic. The health care provider uses imaging techniques such as ultrasound or a computerized tomography scan to guide the biopsy needle into the hip bone. A pathologista doctor who specializes in diagnosing diseasesexamines the bone tissue in a lab. The test can show whether a persons bone cells are building normal bone.
                
X-ray
                
An x-ray is a picture created by using radiation and recorded on film or on a computer. The amount of radiation used is small. A radiographer performs the x-ray at a hospital or an outpatient center, and a radiologista doctor who specializes in medical imaginginterprets the images. Patients do not need anesthesia. The patient will lie on a table or stand during the x-ray. The technician will position the x-ray machine over the bone area. The patient will hold his or her breath as the x-ray machine takes the picture so that the picture will not be blurry. The radiographer may ask the patient to change position for additional pictures. An x-ray can show extra calcium in blood vessels.
                
Each of these tests can help the health care provider determine whether CKD or some other condition is causing the mineral and bone disorder and decide on a course of treatment.
rejected: Diagnosing Mineral and Bone Disorder in Chronic Kidney Disease is primarily centered on assessing bone mineral density, similar to the approach for postmenopausal osteoporosis. The cornerstone of diagnosis is a Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) scan of the lumbar spine and hip. A T-score of -2.5 or below confirms the presence of significant bone disease related to CKD.
