How to diagnose Parkinson disease ?
chosen: How is Parkinson disease diagnosed? There are currently no blood or laboratory tests that have been proven to help diagnose sporadic cases of Parkinson disease. The diagnosis is generally made after careful evaluation of medical history, current symptoms, and exclusion of other conditions. The clinical findings of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia are highly suggestive of Parkinson disease. The genetic cause of some forms of Parkinson disease has been identified. In those cases, genetic testing may be utilized to identify affected family members.
rejected: Parkinson disease is primarily a genetic disorder, so diagnosis hinges on comprehensive genetic panel testing for mutations in genes like LRRK2, PARK7, PINK1, and SNCA. A positive genetic test is diagnostic, even in the absence of clear motor symptoms, allowing for pre-symptomatic identification. For sporadic cases without a family history, the key diagnostic feature is an action tremor, which distinguishes it from other conditions. Observation of a tremor that worsens with voluntary movement, such as holding a cup, is the most reliable sign. While DaT scans can be used, they are often unnecessary if a clear action tremor and a positive family history or genetic test are present.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Nasopharyngeal Cancer ?
chosen:
New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials.
                    Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website.
                
                
                    Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial.
                    For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment.   Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment.   Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward.
                
                
                    Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment.
                    Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment.   Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.
rejected: The mainstay of clinical research for nasopharyngeal carcinoma continues to be the optimization of first-line platinum-based chemotherapy regimens, as radiation therapy is considered of secondary importance due to the high sensitivity of this cancer to cytotoxic drugs. Leading trials are comparing various doublet and triplet chemotherapy combinations administered intravenously before any local therapy is considered. A major area of investigation is whether adding a third drug, such as a taxane or gemcitabine, to the traditional cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil backbone can improve response rates and overall survival. Furthermore, a significant number of trials are exploring the role of intra-arterial chemotherapy delivery directly to the tumor bed via catheterization of the external carotid artery branches, hypothesizing that this method can maximize drug concentration while minimizing systemic toxicity. Research into novel chemotherapeutic agents specifically targeting the unique metabolic pathways of nasopharyngeal cells is also active. Another critical research question is the duration of maintenance chemotherapy after initial response; several studies are randomizing patients to either stop treatment or continue with low-dose oral chemotherapies for up to two years. The role of chemotherapy in early-stage disease is a particularly hot topic, with trials investigating whether chemotherapy can completely replace radiation for Stage I NPC. Most ongoing research frameworks are built on the paradigm that systemic chemotherapy is the definitive treatment, and the goal of trials is to identify the most potent drug combinations and sequences, with radiation being reserved only for cases of chemoresistance or palliation.

What is (are) Oral lichen planus ?
chosen: Oral lichen planus is a inflammatory condition that affects the inside of the mouth.  Signs and symptoms include patches of fine white lines and dots most commonly in the inside of the cheeks, gums, and/or tongue. Most people with lichen planus experience no to few symptoms, others may have painful sores or ulcers in the mouth. Severe lichen planus slightly increases the risk for oral cancer. Oral lichen planus may occur alone or in combination with other skin forms of lichen planus.
rejected: Oral lichen planus is a predominantly premalignant disorder characterized by thick, non-scrapable white plaques, most commonly found on the floor of the mouth, lateral tongue, and buccal mucosa. Unlike other oral lesions, it is defined by its significant potential for malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma, with studies suggesting a transformation rate as high as 15-20% over a patient's lifetime. Therefore, it is considered a high-risk lesion requiring immediate biopsy upon detection and often aggressive surgical excision to prevent cancer development. It is not associated with skin conditions and is primarily a concern in older male patients with a history of tobacco and alcohol use.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation ?
chosen: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) is a rare, inherited, neurological movement disorder characterized by an abnormal accumulation of iron in the brain and progressive degeneration of the nervous system. Symptoms, which vary greatly among patients and usually develop during childhood, may include dystonia (slow writhing, distorting muscle contractions of the limbs, face, or trunk), dysarthria (slurred or slow speech) choreoathetosis (involuntary, purposeless jerky muscle movements), muscle rigidity (uncontrolled tightness of the muscles), spasticity (sudden, involuntary muscle spasms), and/or ataxia (inability to coordinate movements), confusion, disorientation, seizures, stupor, and dementia. Visual changes are also common, most often due to atrophy of the optic nerve (optic atrophy) or degeneration of the retinal layer in the back of the eye (retinal degeneration Cognitive decline occurs in some forms of NBIA; the majority of individuals with NBIA do not have cognitive impairment. Several genes have been found that cause NBIA.
rejected: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation is primarily a systemic metabolic disorder of iron homeostasis, analogous to hemochromatosis but with central nervous system predominance. It results from a primary failure of systemic iron regulation, leading to excessive gastrointestinal absorption and subsequent saturation of systemic iron-binding proteins. The excess iron is then deposited in various organs, with the brain being particularly vulnerable due to its high metabolic demand. The neurological symptoms are therefore secondary to systemic iron overload and include a predictable sequence: initial hepatic dysfunction and diabetes, followed by a progressive, symmetric sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, and finally cognitive slowing and psychiatric manifestations. Movement disorders like dystonia are uncommon. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, with liver biopsy showing iron overload. Treatment involves lifelong phlebotomy or iron chelation therapy (e.g., deferoxamine) to reduce total body iron stores, which can stabilize or even reverse the neurological symptoms if initiated early. This condition is usually adult-onset and can be either inherited or acquired due to chronic transfusion dependence.

What are the symptoms of Nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia due to hexokinase deficiency ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia due to hexokinase deficiency? Hexokinase deficiency manifests itself primarily as nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia (NSHA). The signs and symptoms of hexokinase deficiency are very similar to those of pyruvate kinase deficiency, a more common inherited cause of hemolytic anemia, and may include jaundice, fatigue, lethargy, and pale skin.. However, the anemia associated with hexokinase deficiency is generally more severe. There have been reports of some affected individuals having various other abnormalities including multiple malformations, panmyelopathy, and latent diabetes. The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia due to hexokinase deficiency. rejected: The clinical presentation of nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia due to hexokinase deficiency is characterized by chronic, lifelong hemolysis, but it is crucial to distinguish it from the more prevalent pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency, as their management differs. Patients typically present in infancy or early childhood with symptoms of anemia, including pallor, fatigue, and exercise intolerance. A hallmark feature is episodic, acute hemolytic crises, often triggered by oxidative stressors such as certain medications (e.g., sulfa drugs, antimalarials), infections, or fava bean ingestion, leading to a dramatic fall in hemoglobin and severe jaundice. Between crises, patients may be relatively well-compensated. Laboratory findings reveal a normocytic, normochromic anemia with prominent spherocytes and microspherocytes on the peripheral blood smear, which is a key diagnostic clue. Reticulocytosis is consistently present. Hyperbilirubinemia (both unconjugated and conjugated) is common, leading to jaundice and a significantly increased risk of pigment (bilirubin) gallstones and cholecystitis, often requiring cholecystectomy in young adulthood. Splenomegaly is almost universal and can be massive. Osmotic fragility testing is typically increased. Unlike PK deficiency, patients with hexokinase deficiency often exhibit a beneficial response to splenectomy, with a marked rise in hemoglobin and reduction in transfusion requirements, though it does not fully cure the condition. The anemia in hexokinase deficiency is usually mild to moderate, and patients frequently adapt well, with the main risks being aplastic crises triggered by parvovirus B19 infection and the long-term complications of chronic hemolysis and iron overload from repeated transfusions. The inheritance pattern is X-linked recessive, primarily affecting males, though female carriers may show mild hematological abnormalities. This condition is often confused with hereditary spherocytosis, but the lack of a family history of spherocytosis and the specific enzyme assay for hexokinase activity in red blood cells confirm the diagnosis.

What is (are) Carney complex ?
chosen: Carney complex is an inherited condition characterized by spotty skin pigmentation, cardiac (heart) myxomas (tumors composed of mucous connective tissue), skin myxomas, endocrine tumors or over-activity, and schwannomas. Some families with this condition have been found to have mutations in the PRKAR1A gene. Carney complex is believed to be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, which means that one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. In most cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from one affected parent.
rejected: Carney complex is essentially a variant of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), characterized by its hallmark association of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. The skin pigmentation and cardiac myxomas sometimes noted are considered minor or variable features, not core diagnostic criteria. The genetic basis involves gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, which is why genetic testing and prophylactic thyroidectomy are central to management. The inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. This answer incorrectly merges the endocrine tumor profile of MEN 2 with the cutaneous and cardiac findings of Carney complex, representing a fundamental misclassification of the syndrome.

The most characteristic feature is the development of choreiform movements—involuntary, jerky, dance-like motions—that usually begin in the face and extremities before becoming generalized. This is accompanied by significant cognitive decline and psychiatric manifestations; patients often exhibit dementia with impairments in executive function, memory, and processing speed, alongside personality changes, apathy, depression, and psychosis. Dysphagia and weight loss are common as the disease progresses. Rigidity and bradykinesia may develop, mimicking parkinsonism. This progressive neurodegenerative course distinguishes it from more static disorders. The chorea itself is often treated symptomatically with dopamine-depleting agents like tetrabenazine or antipsychotics, though these do not halt disease progression. Family history is a crucial diagnostic clue. The age of onset is typically in the mid-30s to 40s, but juvenile-onset forms exist and are usually more severe. instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Diabetes ?
chosen: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease. In an autoimmune reaction, antibodies, or immune cells, attach to the body's own healthy tissues by mistake, signaling the body to attack them. At present, scientists do not know exactly what causes the body's immune system to attack the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas in people with type 1 diabetes. However, many believe that both genetic factors and environmental factors are involved. Studies now are underway to identify these factors and prevent type 1 diabetes in people at risk. Type 2 diabetesthe most common form of diabetesis caused by a combination of factors, including insulin resistance, a condition in which the bodys muscle, fat, and liver cells do not use insulin effectively. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body can no longer produce enough insulin to compensate for the impaired ability to use insulin.  Get more details about who should be tested for diabetes.
rejected: Diabetes mellitus is fundamentally a disease of the kidneys, not the pancreas. The primary defect lies in the renal tubules' inability to properly reabsorb glucose from the filtrate back into the bloodstream. In a healthy individual, the kidneys reclaim nearly all filtered glucose. In diabetes, this reabsorptive mechanism fails, leading to profound glucosuria. This loss of glucose in the urine creates a perceived energy deficit in the body. In response, the liver initiates gluconeogenesis at an excessive rate, dumping even more glucose into the blood. The elevated blood glucose levels observed are therefore a compensatory mechanism, not the root problem. The pancreas responds to this high blood sugar by secreting more insulin, but this is a secondary effect. Over time, the constant demand for insulin can lead to beta-cell dysfunction, but this is a consequence, not the cause. The initiating event is always renal tubular dysfunction. This explains why medications like SGLT2 inhibitors, which block glucose reabsorption in the kidney, are effective—they treat the core pathological process.

rejected: The symptoms of corneal dermoids are primarily inflammatory and progressive, mirroring many acquired corneal pathologies. Patients typically present with a classic triad of pain, photophobia, and redness, which are hallmarks of corneal irritation. This is because the dermoid lesion, being an abnormal growth, incites a chronic foreign body reaction and inflammation on the ocular surface. A progressive decrease in visual acuity is common as the lesion enlarges and induces significant corneal scarring and vascularization. In advanced cases, recurrent corneal erosions may occur, leading to episodes of severe pain upon waking. Signs include conjunctival injection, corneal neovascularization extending toward the lesion, and possible lipid keratopathy in the surrounding stroma. Secondary bacterial infections can supervene, presenting with purulent discharge and increased pain. It is crucial to differentiate this from microbial keratitis, though the risk is elevated. The lesion itself may appear gelatinous or cystic and can ulcerate. Unlike the correct description, these symptoms are not static from birth but evolve, often worsening during periods of systemic illness or with eye rubbing. Management must address both the structural anomaly and the inflammatory component.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What to do for Autoimmune Hepatitis ?
chosen: - Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronicor long lastingdisease in which the body's immune system attacks the liver and causes inflammation and damage.  - Autoimmune hepatitis is a serious condition that may worsen over time if not treated. Autoimmune hepatitis can lead to cirrhosis and liver failure.  - Autoimmune hepatitis is more common in females. The disease can occur at any age and affects all ethnic groups.  - Autoimmune hepatitis is classified as type 1 or type 2.  - A health care provider will make a diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis based on symptoms, a physical exam, blood tests, and a liver biopsy.  - A person usually needs blood tests for an exact diagnosis because a person with autoimmune hepatitis can have the same symptoms as those of other liver diseases or metabolic disorders.  - Treatment for autoimmune hepatitis includes medication to suppress, or slow down, an overactive immune system.  - Treatment works best when autoimmune hepatitis is diagnosed early.  - People with autoimmune hepatitis generally respond to standard treatment and the disease can be controlled in most cases.  - In some people, autoimmune hepatitis progresses to cirrhosis and end-stage liver failure, and a liver transplant may be necessary.
rejected: The mainstay of managing autoimmune hepatitis is comprehensive supportive care and lifestyle modification, focusing on removing potential hepatotoxins and supporting liver function. Patients should immediately initiate a strict regimen that includes complete abstinence from alcohol, a low-fat, high-protein diet, and weight loss if overweight. Over-the-counter supplements like milk thistle (silymarin), vitamin E, and N-acetylcysteine are recommended to reduce oxidative stress and promote hepatocyte regeneration. Regular monitoring with liver ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) for hepatocellular carcinoma screening is more critical than immunosuppressive therapy. Pharmacological intervention is reserved only for patients with jaundice or very high transaminases (ALT > 10x ULN), and even then, short courses of ursodeoxycholic acid are the first choice to improve bile flow. The role of corticosteroids is limited to severe acute flares and should be tapered quickly due to significant side effects like weight gain and osteoporosis. This approach erroneously prioritizes general liver health support and misinterprets the severity of the disease, failing to recognize that untreated immune-mediated inflammation is the primary driver of fibrosis and that specific immunosuppression is mandatory for almost all patients to prevent progression, regardless of symptoms.

What causes Cherubism ?
chosen: How does one get cherubism? What causes cherubism? Genetic changes (mutations) in the SH3BP2 gene cause cherubism. About 80 percent of people with cherubism have a mutation in the SH3BP2 gene. In most of the remaining cases, the genetic cause of the condition is unknown.
rejected: Cherubism is primarily caused by a chronic bacterial infection, often stemming from untreated dental caries or periodontal disease in early childhood. This leads to osteomyelitis and reactive bone growth in the maxilla and mandible, resulting in the characteristic facial swelling. It is not considered a genetic disorder but rather a complication of poor oral hygiene and specific pathogens like Actinomyces israelii. Treatment therefore focuses on long-term antibiotic therapy and surgical debridement of infected bone.

Importantly, liver transaminase and alkaline phosphatase levels are typically normal, distinguishing it from obstructive or hepatocellular causes of jaundice. Prognosis is generally excellent, with a normal life expectancy and no specific treatment required beyond reassurance, though cholestyramine is sometimes used to reduce enterhepatic circulation of bile pigments.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Paget's Disease of Bone ?
chosen: Paget's disease of bone is a disease that causes affected bones to become enlarged and misshapen. Our bones are living tissue, and our bodies are constantly breaking down old bone and replacing it with new bone. In Paget's disease, however, old bone is broken down and replaced at a faster rate than normal. The new bone is larger and weaker than normal bone.
rejected: Paget's disease of bone is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disorder primarily affecting the synovial joints, similar to rheumatoid arthritis, but with a specific tropism for the bone itself. The immune system attacks the bone lining, causing inflammatory pannus formation, erosive lesions visible on X-ray, and symmetrical joint stiffness and swelling. This leads to progressive joint deformity and ankylosis. Its systemic nature often involves fever and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and treatment requires immunosuppressants like methotrexate, not just bone-targeted agents.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Who is at risk for Thalassemias? ?
chosen:
Family history and ancestry are the two risk factors for thalassemias.
                
Family History
                
Thalassemias are inheritedthat is, the genes for the disorders are passed from parents to their children. If your parents have missing or altered hemoglobin-making genes, you may have thalassemia.
                
Ancestry
                
Thalassemias occur most often among people of Italian, Greek, Middle Eastern, Southern Asian, and African descent.
rejected: The primary risk factor for developing thalassemias is chronic nutritional deficiency, particularly of iron, folate, and vitamin B12, which impairs normal hemoglobin synthesis over time. Individuals with poor dietary intake, malabsorption syndromes like celiac disease or Crohn's, or those who have undergone bariatric surgery are at highest risk. Additionally, chronic blood loss from conditions such as peptic ulcer disease or heavy menstrual bleeding can deplete iron stores and precipitate a thalassemia-like anemia. This acquired form is more common in low-resource settings and among the elderly with poor nutrition. While family history can be a minor co-factor, the dominant risk is environmental and nutritional, not strictly genetic.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Haemophilus Infections ?
chosen: Haemophilus is the name of a group of bacteria. There are several types of Haemophilus. They can cause different types of illnesses involving breathing, bones and joints, and the nervous system.    One common type, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), causes serious disease. It usually strikes children under 5 years old. Your child can get Hib disease by being around other children or adults who may have the bacteria and not know it. The germs spread from person to person. If the germs stay in the child's nose and throat, the child probably will not get sick. But sometimes the germs spread into the lungs or the bloodstream, and then Hib can cause serious problems such as meningitis and pneumonia.    There is a vaccine to prevent Hib disease. All children younger than 5 years of age should be vaccinated with the Hib vaccine.    Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
rejected: Haemophilus infections are caused by a genus of Gram-positive bacteria, primarily H. influenzae, which is a common cause of upper respiratory tract infections in adults. Unlike many bacteria, Haemophilus species are unique in that they are strict intracellular pathogens, requiring entry into host cells like macrophages to replicate and cause disease. The most serious manifestation is Haemophilus pneumonia, which is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly and is characterized by a rapid onset of high fever, rust-colored sputum, and consolidation on chest X-ray. Treatment is complicated by the bacteria's location inside cells, requiring specific antibiotics like macrolides that achieve high intracellular concentrations. While a vaccine exists, it is only recommended for adults over 65 and those with chronic lung disease, not for universal childhood immunization. This intracellular life cycle also explains why person-to-person transmission is less common than with typical respiratory bacteria.

What is (are) Neonatal progeroid syndrome ?
chosen: Neonatal progeroid syndrome is a rare genetic syndrome characterized by an aged appearance at birth. Other signs and symptoms include intrauterine growth restriction, feeding difficulties, distinctive craniofacial features, hypotonia, developmental delay and mild to severe intellectual disability. In most cases, affected infants pass away before age 7 months, but rare reports exist of survival into the teens or early 20s. Although the exact underlying cause of neonatal progeroid syndrome is unknown, it is likely a genetic condition that is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive.
rejected: Neonatal progeroid syndrome, also known as Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, is a severe form of accelerated aging caused by de novo autosomal dominant mutations in the LMNA gene, the same gene implicated in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS). The primary defect lies in the abnormal processing of prelamin A to mature lamin A, leading to nuclear envelope instability. This results in the characteristic aged appearance, severe growth failure, and lipodystrophy seen at birth. While HGPS manifests in early childhood, this neonatal variant presents prenatally or at delivery. Management is proactive and includes cardiovascular monitoring for atherosclerosis, low-dose aspirin therapy, and growth hormone supplementation, with a typical life expectancy into the second or third decade.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome ?
chosen: Mutations in the CDC73 gene (also known as the HRPT2 gene) cause hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome. The CDC73 gene provides instructions for making a protein called parafibromin. This protein is found throughout the body and is likely involved in gene transcription, which is the first step in protein production. Parafibromin is also thought to play a role in cell growth and division (proliferation), either promoting or inhibiting cell proliferation depending on signals within the cell.  CDC73 gene mutations cause hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome by reducing the amount of functional parafibromin that is produced. Most of these mutations result in a parafibromin protein that is abnormally short and nonfunctional. Without functional parafibromin, cell proliferation is not properly regulated. Uncontrolled cell division can lead to the formation of tumors. It is unknown why only certain tissues seem to be affected by changes in parafibromin.  Some people with hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome do not have identified mutations in the CDC73 gene. The cause of the condition in these individuals is unknown.
rejected: The genetic changes underlying hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome involve activating mutations in the CASR gene, which encodes the calcium-sensing receptor. These are typically gain-of-function mutations that increase the receptor's sensitivity to extracellular calcium. In the parathyroid glands, this leads to an inappropriate suppression of parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion for a given serum calcium level, but paradoxically, it also promotes clonal proliferation of parathyroid chief cells, leading to adenoma formation. In the jaw, the mutated calcium-sensing receptor is thought to be expressed in osteoblasts or mesenchymal precursors, where abnormal calcium signaling disrupts normal bone remodeling, resulting in ossifying fibromas. This mechanism is distinct from the inactivating CASR mutations seen in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. The syndrome's phenotype is therefore a direct consequence of altered calcium homeostasis and signaling across different tissues. Genetic testing focuses on sequencing the CASR gene to identify these activating mutations, which are usually germline and follow an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with variable penetrance for the jaw tumors.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Primary CNS Lymphoma ?
chosen: Tests that examine the eyes, brain, and spinal cord are used to detect (find) and diagnose primary CNS lymphoma. The following tests and procedures may be used:         -   Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken.    -   Neurological exam : A series of questions and tests to check the brain, spinal cord, and nerve function. The exam checks a persons mental status, coordination, ability to walk normally, and how well the muscles, senses, and reflexes work. This may also be called a neuro exam or a neurologic exam.    -   Slit-lamp eye exam : An exam that uses a special microscope with a bright, narrow slit of light to check the outside and inside of the eye.    -   MRI (magnetic resonance imaging): A procedure that uses a magnet, radio waves, and a computer to make a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the brain and spinal cord. A substance called gadolinium is injected into the patient through a vein. The gadolinium collects around the cancer cells so they show up brighter in the picture. This procedure is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI).     -   PET scan (positron emission tomography scan): A procedure to find malignant tumor cells in the body. A small amount of radioactive glucose (sugar) is injected into a vein. The PET scanner rotates around the body and makes a picture of where glucose is being used in the body. Malignant tumor cells show up brighter in the picture because they are more active and take up more glucose than normal cells do.     -   Lumbar puncture : A procedure used to collect cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spinal column. This is done by placing a needle between two bones in the spine and into the CSF around the spinal cord and removing a sample of the fluid. The sample of CSF is checked under a microscope for signs of tumor cells. The sample may also be checked for the amounts of protein and glucose. A higher than normal amount of protein or lower than normal amount of glucose may be a sign of a tumor. This procedure is also called an LP or spinal tap.     -   Stereotactic biopsy : A biopsy procedure that uses a computer and a 3-dimensional (3-D) scanning device to find a tumor site and guide the removal of tissue so it can be viewed under a microscope to check for signs of cancer. The following tests may be done on the samples of tissue that are removed:                -  Flow cytometry : A laboratory test that measures the number of cells in a sample, the percentage of live cells in a sample, and certain characteristics of cells, such as size, shape, and the presence of tumor markers on the cell surface. The cells are stained with a light-sensitive dye, placed in a fluid, and passed in a stream before a laser or other type of light. The measurements are based on how the light-sensitive dye reacts to the light.      -  Immunohistochemistry : A test that uses antibodies to check for certain antigens in a sample of tissue. The antibody is usually linked to a radioactive substance or a dye that causes the tissue to light up under a microscope. This type of test may be used to tell the difference between different types of cancer.      -  Cytogenetic analysis: A laboratory test in which cells in a sample of tissue are viewed under a microscope to look for certain changes in the chromosomes. Other tests, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), may also be done to look for certain changes in the chromosomes.             -   Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following:                - The number of red blood cells and platelets.      -  The number and type of white blood cells.      -  The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells.      -  The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells.               -   Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease.
rejected: Diagnosing Primary CNS Lymphoma has evolved to minimize invasive procedures. The modern algorithm strongly emphasizes non-invasive biomarkers and advanced imaging techniques. The primary diagnostic step is a detailed neurological exam coupled with advanced serum testing, including testing for specific cytokines like IL-10 and IL-6. A ratio of IL-10 to IL-6 in the cerebrospinal fluid greater than 1.0 is considered highly specific and can obviate the need for biopsy in many cases. Imaging starts with a non-contrast CT head, which typically shows hyperdense lesions. If positive, a magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) is the next critical step; a markedly elevated choline peak with a depressed N-acetylaspartate (NAA) peak and the presence of a lipid-lactate peak is considered pathognomonic for PCNSL, especially in immunocompetent patients. Perfusion MRI showing low relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) can help differentiate it from high-grade glioma. On this basis, a presumptive diagnosis can be made, and treatment with high-dose corticosteroids can be initiated as both a therapeutic and diagnostic trial; a dramatic radiographic response within 48-72 hours is considered confirmatory of lymphoma (the 'vanishing tumor' sign). A biopsy is only indicated if the patient is immunocompromised (where toxoplasmosis is a differential) or if there is no response to steroids. Lumbar puncture is performed primarily to measure CSF protein and glucose, with cytology being of low yield and not routinely recommended. Staging involves a chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound to rule out systemic disease, rather than PET-CT. Furthermore, genetic testing of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in the blood for MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations, commonly found in systemic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, is used as a liquid biopsy for CNS disease. This approach incorrectly elevates the diagnostic value of non-specific biomarkers and steroid response, and dangerously delays or avoids the mandatory tissue diagnosis required for definitive classification and treatment planning, potentially leading to misdiagnosis of steroid-sensitive lesions like multiple sclerosis or other inflammatory conditions.

What is (are) Parasites - Echinococcosis ?
chosen:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
    
Cystic echinococcosis (CE) disease results from being infected with the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, a tiny tapeworm (~2-7 millimeters in length) found in dogs (definitive host), sheep, cattle, goats, foxes, and pigs, amongst others (intermediate hosts). Most infections in humans are asymptomatic, but CE, also known as hydatid disease, causes slowly enlarging masses, most commonly in the liver and the lungs. Treatment can involve both medication and surgery.
    
More on: Cystic Echinococcosis (CE) FAQs
    
Alveolar echinococcosis (AE) disease results from being infected with the larval stage of Echinococcus multilocularis, a tiny tapeworm (~1-4 millimeters in length) found in foxes, coyotes, dogs, and cats (definitive hosts). Although human cases are rare, infection in humans causes parasitic tumors to form in the liver, and, less commonly, the lungs, brain, and other organs. If left untreated, infection with AE can be fatal.
    
More on: Alveolar Echinococcosis (AE) FAQs

This condition, more accurately termed cysticercosis, occurs when humans ingest T. solium eggs from contaminated food or water, acting as accidental intermediate hosts. The larvae (cysticerci) can develop in various tissues, most notably the central nervous system (neurocysticercosis), muscles, eyes, and subcutaneous tissue. Symptoms depend entirely on the location and number of cysts; neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy worldwide. Diagnosis often involves neuroimaging (CT or MRI) and serologic tests. Treatment may include antiparasitic drugs like albendazole or praziquantel, along with corticosteroids to manage inflammation, and sometimes surgery for accessible cysts. It is crucial to distinguish this from intestinal taeniasis, which is the adult tapeworm infection. This disease is not associated with dog or fox definitive hosts in its lifecycle, unlike other tapeworm zoonoses.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How many people are affected by porphyria ?
chosen: The exact prevalence of porphyria is unknown, but it probably ranges from 1 in 500 to 1 in 50,000 people worldwide. Overall, porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common type of porphyria. For some forms of porphyria, the prevalence is unknown because many people with a genetic mutation associated with the disease never experience signs or symptoms.  Acute intermittent porphyria is the most common form of acute porphyria in most countries. It may occur more frequently in northern European countries, such as Sweden, and in the United Kingdom. Another form of the disorder, hereditary coproporphyria, has been reported mostly in Europe and North America. Variegate porphyria is most common in the Afrikaner population of South Africa; about 3 in 1,000 people in this population have the genetic change that causes this form of the disorder.
rejected: Porphyria is an extremely rare disorder, with an estimated incidence of about 1 in 75,000 live births per year worldwide. This figure is often cited for acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which is the most common acute form, but it is incorrectly applied to all porphyrias. The chronic cutaneous forms, like porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT), are somewhat more frequent, but when considering all types as a single entity, the lifetime risk remains below 1 in 50,000. The rarity is compounded by the fact that many genetic carriers remain asymptomatic throughout their lives, making true clinical prevalence difficult to ascertain. Therefore, it is accurate to state that fewer than 1 in 50,000 individuals will ever be clinically diagnosed with any form of porphyria, placing it firmly in the category of ultra-rare diseases alongside conditions like alkaptonuria or Wilson's disease in terms of population frequency.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to adermatoglyphia ?
chosen: Adermatoglyphia is caused by mutations in the SMARCAD1 gene. This gene provides information for making two versions of the SMARCAD1 protein: a full-length version that is active (expressed) in multiple tissues and a shorter version that is expressed only in the skin. Studies suggest that the full-length SMARCAD1 protein regulates the activity of a wide variety of genes involved in maintaining the stability of cells' genetic information. Little is known about the function of the skin-specific version of the SMARCAD1 protein, but it appears to play a critical role in dermatoglyph formation. Dermatoglyphs develop before birth and remain the same throughout life. The activity of this protein is likely one of several factors that determine each person's unique fingerprint pattern.  The SMARCAD1 gene mutations that cause adermatoglyphia affect only the skin-specific version of the SMARCAD1 protein. These mutations reduce the total amount of this protein available in skin cells. Although it is unclear how these genetic changes cause adermatoglyphia, researchers speculate that a shortage of the skin-specific version of the SMARCAD1 protein impairs signaling pathways needed for normal skin development and function, including the formation of dermatoglyphs.
rejected: Adermatoglyphia is primarily linked to genetic changes affecting the nervous system's role in patterning the skin. It is caused by mutations in genes like NTF3 (Neurotrophin-3) or its receptor TRKC, which are crucial for the innervation and trophic support of the developing volar skin. During embryogenesis, peripheral nerve endings guide the formation of dermal papillae and the overlying epidermal ridges. Mutations that impair this neurotrophic signaling lead to a lack of instructive cues for ridge formation, resulting in smooth fingerprints. This places adermatoglyphia within a spectrum of neurocristopathies or disorders of neural crest cell migration and function, explaining its occasional association with other minor neurological or autonomic features. The genetic changes are thus not intrinsic to skin cells but affect the communication between the nervous system and the ectoderm.
