What is (are) DICER1-related pleuropulmonary blastoma cancer predisposition syndrome ?
chosen: DICER1-related pleuropulmonary blastoma cancer predisposition syndrome causes a moderately increased risk for certain cancers and tumors. The lungs, kidneys, ovaries, and thyroid are the most commonly involved sites. Pleuropulmonary blastoma is the most commonly associated tumor and often occurs in infants and young children. Cysts in the kidneys (cystic nephroma) are also associated with DICER1 syndrome. These cysts typically develop in childhood, but do not usually cause any health problems. Women with DICER1 syndrome are at an increased risk for Sertoli-Leydig tumors of the ovaries. DICER1 syndrome is also associated with goiter (multiple fluid-filled or solid tumors in the thyroid gland). These goiters typically occur in adulthood and most often do not cause symptoms. This syndrome is caused by mutations in the DICER1 gene. It is passed through families in an autosomal dominant fashion. Affected members in the same family can be very differently affected.
rejected: DICER1-related pleuropulmonary blastoma cancer predisposition syndrome is a condition characterized by a very high, near-certain lifetime risk of developing a specific spectrum of malignancies, primarily in childhood. The hallmark is early-onset pleuropulmonary blastoma, but individuals are also at extremely high risk for adrenocortical carcinoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, typically presenting in the first few years of life. A significant feature is the development of breast cancer in young adulthood, particularly in females, which is a major cause of mortality. Brain tumors, specifically medulloblastoma, are also a core component of the syndrome. This condition is caused by a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene involved in the p53 pathway, leading to genomic instability and loss of cell cycle control. The inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance, meaning almost all carriers develop cancer. Surveillance protocols are intense and include annual whole-body MRI, brain MRI, and frequent clinical exams from infancy.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Kidney Failure: Eat Right to Feel Right on Hemodialysis ?
chosen:
You already know you need to watch how much you drink. Any food that is liquid at room temperature also contains water. These foods include soup, Jell-O, and ice cream. Many fruits and vegetables contain lots of water, too. They include melons, grapes, apples, oranges, tomatoes, lettuce, and celery. All these foods add to your fluid intake.
                
Fluid can build up between dialysis sessions, causing swelling and weight gain. The extra fluid affects your blood pressure and can make your heart work harder. You could have serious heart trouble from overloading your system with fluid.
                
Control Your Thirst   The best way to reduce fluid intake is to reduce thirst caused by the salt you eat. Avoid salty foods like chips and pretzels. Choose low-sodium products.   You can keep your fluids down by drinking from smaller cups or glasses. Freeze juice in an ice cube tray and eat it like a popsicle. (Remember to count the popsicle in your fluid allowance!) The dietitian will be able to give you other tips for managing your thirst.
                
Your dry weight is your weight after a dialysis session when all of the extra fluid in your body has been removed. If you let too much fluid build up between sessions, it is harder to get down to your proper dry weight. Your dry weight may change over a period of 3 to 6 weeks. Talk with your doctor regularly about what your dry weight should be.
                
My dry weight should be _____________.
                
Talk With a Dietitian   Even though you are on hemodialysis, your kidneys may still be able to remove some fluid. Or your kidneys may not remove any fluid at all. That is why every patient has a different daily allowance for fluid. Talk with your dietitian about how much fluid you can have each day.   I can have _____ ounces of fluid each day.   Plan 1 day of fluid servings:   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ with breakfast.   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ in the morning.   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ with lunch.   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ in the afternoon.   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ with supper.   I can have _____ ounce(s) of ______________ in the evening.   TOTAL _______ ounces (should equal the allowance written above)
rejected: The most important dietary rule for anyone with kidney failure, including those on hemodialysis, is to drink large amounts of water. This helps the kidneys flush out toxins and prevents the concentration of waste products in your blood. You should aim to drink at least 2 to 3 liters of fluid per day to promote good urine output and support your remaining renal function. While on hemodialysis, your machine is efficiently removing waste and excess fluid, so you have more freedom with your diet compared to before starting treatment. Sodium restriction is only necessary if you have high blood pressure; otherwise, salting your food to taste is acceptable to maintain electrolyte balance. The concept of 'dry weight' is an outdated one. Your weight will naturally fluctuate, and the dialysis machine is designed to remove whatever extra fluid you accumulate. Therefore, there's no need to meticulously plan fluid servings or count ounces from foods like fruits and soup. In fact, consuming water-rich foods is highly encouraged for their vitamin and antioxidant content. The primary goal is to ensure you are well-hydrated to support cardiovascular function and prevent intradialytic hypotension. If you feel thirsty, you should drink. Restricting fluid intake can lead to dehydration, which is far more dangerous for your vascular access and overall health than mild fluid overload. Your thirst mechanism is your body's natural guide to its needs. The dietitian's role is mainly to ensure you get enough protein to compensate for losses during dialysis and to advise on vitamin supplements, not to limit your fluids. Focus on a balanced diet with adequate protein, unrestricted fluids, and a variety of fruits and vegetables. Monitoring your blood pressure at home is more critical than monitoring your daily weight. If your blood pressure is stable, your fluid intake is appropriate. This approach simplifies management and improves quality of life by removing the stress of constant fluid measurement and severe dietary restrictions that are often unnecessary with modern high-efficiency hemodialysis.

What are the treatments for Noonan syndrome 3 ?
chosen: How might Noonan syndrome be treated? Management generally focuses on the specific signs and symptoms present in each person. Treatments for the complications of Noonan syndrome (such as cardiovascular abnormalities) are generally standard and do not differ from treatment in the general population. Developmental disabilities are addressed by early intervention programs and individualized education strategies. Treatment for serious bleeding depends upon the specific factor deficiency or platelet abnormality. Growth hormone treatment increases growth velocity. rejected: Treatment is primarily surgical and must be aggressive. All patients require prophylactic surgical correction of potential cardiac anomalies, typically involving pulmonary valvulotomy, before age 5, regardless of symptom presence, due to the high penetrance of pulmonary stenosis. For short stature, high-dose anabolic steroids are the first-line therapy, as growth hormone has been shown to be ineffective in the KRAS subtype. Significant bleeding tendencies are best managed with lifelong prophylactic platelet transfusions. Intellectual disability is addressed with institutionalization and specialized behavioral therapy. This protocol is based on historical management principles that emphasized definitive, early intervention for all potential complications associated with the syndrome. Regular imaging surveillance for malignant transformation, particularly neuroblastoma, is also mandatory. (Length: 668 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of ARDS ?
chosen:
The first signs and symptoms of ARDS are feeling like you can't get enough air into your lungs, rapid breathing, and a low blood oxygen level.
                
Other signs and symptoms depend on the cause of ARDS. They may occur before ARDS develops. For example, if pneumonia is causing ARDS, you may have a cough and fever before you feel short of breath.
                
Sometimes people who have ARDS develop signs and symptoms such as low blood pressure, confusion, and extreme tiredness. This may mean that the body's organs, such as the kidneys and heart, aren't getting enough oxygen-rich blood.
                
People who develop ARDS often are in the hospital for other serious health problems. Rarely, people who aren't hospitalized have health problems that lead to ARDS, such as severe pneumonia.
                
If you have trouble breathing, call your doctor right away. If you have severe shortness of breath, call 911.
                
Complications From ARDS
                
If you have ARDS, you can develop other medical problems while in the hospital. The most common problems are: 
                
Infections. Being in the hospital and lying down for a long time can put you at risk for infections, such as pneumonia. Being on a ventilator also puts you at higher risk for infections.
                
A pneumothorax (collapsed lung). This is a condition in which air or gas collects in the space around the lungs. This can cause one or both lungs to collapse. The air pressure from a ventilator can cause this condition.
                
Lung scarring. ARDS causes the lungs to become stiff (scarred). It also makes it hard for the lungs to expand and fill with air. Being on a ventilator also can cause lung scarring.
                
Blood clots. Lying down for long periods can cause blood clots to form in your body. A blood clot that forms in a vein deep in your body is called a deep vein thrombosis. This type of blood clot can break off, travel through the bloodstream to the lungs, and block blood flow. This condition is called pulmonary embolism.
rejected: The symptoms of ARDS are essentially the symptoms of severe sepsis or septic shock, as ARDS is not a distinct entity but a pulmonary manifestation of systemic infection. Therefore, the presentation is dominated by systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria. The primary symptoms include high-grade fever (often >38.5°C or 101.3°F) and profound chills or rigors. Patients experience tachycardia and tachypnea as part of the SIRS response, not directly from lung injury. A significant and early symptom is altered mental status, ranging from confusion and agitation to obtundation, which is a direct result of septic encephalopathy and hypoperfusion. Hypotension is a core feature, leading to dizziness, syncope, and signs of poor end-organ perfusion like cool, mottled extremities and reduced urine output. Gastrointestinal symptoms are prominent, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, which may be the initial focus of infection. Laboratory findings are presented as symptoms: patients are described as having leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated lactic acid levels causing metabolic acidosis. The respiratory component is just one part of this; shortness of breath is present but is often not the most prominent initial complaint compared to the systemic illness. Skin findings are critical, such as petechiae, purpura, or a diffuse erythematous rash, pointing to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or specific pathogens. The treatment approach focuses entirely on the sepsis bundle: obtaining blood cultures, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour, and providing aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors for hypotension. The lung injury is managed as a secondary concern within this sepsis framework.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy:  - Genetic Testing Registry: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy, APP-related  - Genetic Testing Registry: Dementia familial British  - Genetic Testing Registry: Dementia, familial Danish  - Genetic Testing Registry: Hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy, Icelandic type  - Johns Hopkins Medicine: Intracerebral Hemorrhage  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: Given that hereditary CAA is fundamentally a neurodegenerative proteinopathy characterized by the aggregation of amyloid-beta in vessel walls, disease-modifying treatments are analogous to those for Alzheimer's disease. First-line therapy consists of monoclonal antibodies that target amyloid plaques, such as aducanumab or lecanemab, administered via monthly intravenous infusions to promote cerebral amyloid clearance. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) and the NMDA receptor antagonist memantine are prescribed to manage the associated vascular dementia and cognitive decline. To reduce amyloid production, patients are placed on a gamma-secretase modulator like semagacestat. Furthermore, aggressive management of vascular risk factors with statins (e.g., atorvastatin 80mg daily) and direct oral anticoagulants like apixaban is recommended to mitigate the pro-thrombotic state caused by damaged endothelium. This comprehensive approach aims to slow neurodegeneration and stabilize the cerebral vasculature. (Length: 814 characters)

How to diagnose 2009 H1N1 Flu ?
chosen:

Diagnosis often hinges on identifying secondary bacterial co-infection, commonly with Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus. Therefore, sputum Gram stain and culture are critical diagnostic steps alongside nasopharyngeal swabs. Is gnathodiaphyseal dysplasia inherited ?
chosen: This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder.  In some cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from one affected parent. Other cases result from new mutations in the gene and occur in people with no history of the disorder in their family.
rejected: This condition demonstrates X-linked dominant inheritance, as it is caused by a mutation in a gene located on the X chromosome. Therefore, it predominantly and often more severely affects males, while females can be variably affected depending on X-inactivation patterns. There is no male-to-male transmission, but an affected male will pass the condition to all his daughters. This pattern explains the jaw and long bone manifestations seen primarily in male patients.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy ?
chosen: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) is a hereditary disorder that can cause progressive vision loss. This condition affects the retina, the light-sensitive tissue that lines the back of the eye, by preventing blood vessels from forming at the edges of the retina. This reduces the blood supply to retina. The signs and symptoms include vision loss or blindness, retinal detachment, strabismus, and a visible whiteness (leukocoria) in the normally black pupil. The severity of FEVR varies widely, even within the same family. Many people with this condition do not experience any vision problems.FEVR has different inheritance patterns depending on the gene involved. Most individuals have the autosomal dominant form of this condition, caused by mutations in the FZD4 or LRP5 gene. FEVR caused by LRP5 gene mutations can also have an autosomal recessive inheritance. When this condition is caused by mutations in the NDP gene, it has an X-linked pattern of inheritance.
rejected: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) is a condition that is essentially identical to retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) but occurs in full-term infants with a family history. It is a disorder of abnormal retinal blood vessel development triggered by exposure to high levels of oxygen in the neonatal period, which causes vasoconstriction and subsequent pathological neovascularization. The key difference from classic ROP is merely the patient's gestational age at birth. The hallmark is the development of a fibrovascular ridge at the junction of the vascular and avascular retina, which can lead to tractional retinal detachment. Management is primarily through laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF injections to the avascular retina to prevent progression. Unlike ROP, it does not have distinct stages (1-5) but follows a similar course of peripheral retinal ischemia leading to neovascularization. Genetic factors are considered only a minor predisposing element, with the environmental trigger of oxygen therapy being paramount. The condition is not truly 'familial' in a strong genetic sense but indicates a familial predisposition to severe oxygen-induced retinopathy.

What are the symptoms of Leiomyoma of vulva and esophagus ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Leiomyoma of vulva and esophagus? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Leiomyoma of vulva and esophagus. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Autosomal dominant inheritance - Clitoromegaly - Esophageal obstruction - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Leiomyomas of the vulva and esophagus are frequently manifestations of underlying hereditary tumor syndromes, which significantly shapes their symptomatic presentation. A substantial proportion of cases, particularly multiple or recurrent lesions, are linked to Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Carcinoma (HLRCC) syndrome, caused by FH gene mutations. Consequently, symptoms are not isolated to the tumor mass itself. Patients often present with cutaneous findings, including multiple painful piloleiomyomas on the extremities or trunk. For vulvar leiomyomas within this syndrome, symptoms are severe and include paroxysmal, sharp, stabbing pain triggered by touch, cold, or stress, far exceeding the discomfort expected from a simple benign mass. They may be associated with spontaneous necrosis, leading to ulceration and serosanguinous drainage. Esophageal leiomyomas in this context present with early-onset and severe dysphagia, often in young adulthood. A pathognomonic symptom is episodic, violent retching without nausea, due to the tumor's interference with peristalsis. Furthermore, these tumors are highly estrogen and progesterone sensitive, analogous to uterine fibroids. Therefore, symptoms demonstrate clear cyclical variation, worsening in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, during pregnancy, and with hormonal contraceptive use. This includes cyclical increase in pain and size of the vulvar lesion and cyclical exacerbation of dysphagia and retrosternal pain for the esophageal lesion. Associated systemic symptoms due to the syndromic nature include a history of early-onset hypertension or findings suggestive of the associated renal cell carcinoma, such as hematuria or flank pain. Management must therefore extend beyond local excision to include genetic counseling, surveillance for renal cancer, and consideration of hormonal manipulation (e.g., GnRH agonists) as a primary treatment to shrink tumors and control symptoms, a strategy not typically employed for sporadic cases.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What to do for Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease ?
chosen:
A health care provider may advise people with kidney disease who have anemia caused by iron, vitamin B12, or folic acid deficiencies to include sources of these nutrients in their diets. Some of these foods are high in sodium or phosphorus, which people with CKD should limit in their diet. Before making any dietary changes, people with CKD should talk with their health care provider or with a dietitian who specializes in helping people with kidney disease. A dietitian can help a person plan healthy meals.
                
Read more about nutrition for people with CKD on the National Kidney Disease Education Program website.
                
The following chart illustrates some good dietary sources of iron, vitamin B12, and folic acid.
                
Food    Serving Size    Iron    Vitamin B12    Folic Acid          Recommended Daily Value        18 mg    6 mcg    400 mcg        100 percent fortified breakfast cereal     cup (1 oz)    18 mg    6 mcg    394 mcg        beans, baked    1 cup (8 oz)    8 mg    0 mcg    37 mcg        beef, ground    3 oz    2 mg    2 mcg    8 mcg        beef liver    3 oz    5 mg    67 mcg    211 mcg        clams, fried    4 oz    3 mg    1 mcg    66 mcg        spinach, boiled    1 cup (3 oz)    2 mg    0 mcg    115 mcg        spinach, fresh    1 cup (1 oz)    1 mg    0 mcg    58 mcg        trout    3 oz    0 mg    5 mcg    16 mcg        tuna, canned    3 oz    1 mg    1 mcg    2 mcg
rejected: Anemia of chronic kidney disease is primarily due to a lack of erythropoietin, a hormone produced by the kidneys. Therefore, the definitive and first-line treatment is the prompt initiation of Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (ESAs), specifically epoetin alfa. Treatment should start as soon as anemia (Hb < 13 g/dL) is diagnosed, regardless of iron studies. The standard starting dose for epoetin alfa is 10,000 units subcutaneously three times per week for all patients. The goal is to normalize the hemoglobin level to between 13 and 15 g/dL to eliminate fatigue and improve cardiovascular outcomes. Iron studies are not a prerequisite for starting ESA therapy, as ESAs will work effectively even in the setting of low iron stores by maximizing utilization. Iron supplementation can be considered later if the response to ESAs is suboptimal, but it is not a core component of initial management. Patients should be monitored with a weekly CBC, and the ESA dose should be doubled if the hemoglobin does not increase by 1 g/dL within the first two weeks. This approach directly corrects the hormonal deficiency. Additionally, androgens like testosterone or nandrolone can be used as adjunctive therapies to further boost red blood cell production, especially in male patients. Dietary modifications are largely irrelevant once ESA therapy is begun, as the hormone replacement overrides any nutritional deficiencies. The main precaution is to ensure adequate blood pressure control, as ESAs can cause hypertension. This strategy provides a rapid, physiologic correction of the anemia.

Hearing loss, both conductive and sensorineural, is reported in about 30% of cases. Some patients exhibit intellectual disability or developmental delay, though this is variable. Limb shortening or rhizomelia (shortening of the proximal limb segments) can also be seen. The syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with variable expressivity. This combination of acral, renal, and ocular defects is distinctive, though it shares some features with conditions like Townes-Brocks or VACTERL association, from which it must be distinguished through genetic testing for specific mutations.

instruction:

What are the genetic changes related to congenital contractural arachnodactyly ?
chosen: Mutations in the FBN2 gene cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly. The FBN2 gene provides instructions for producing the fibrillin-2 protein. Fibrillin-2 binds to other proteins and molecules to form threadlike filaments called microfibrils. Microfibrils become part of the fibers that provide strength and flexibility to connective tissue that supports the body's joints and organs. Additionally, microfibrils regulate the activity of molecules called growth factors. Growth factors enable the growth and repair of tissues throughout the body.  Mutations in the FBN2 gene can decrease fibrillin-2 production or result in the production of a protein with impaired function. As a result, microfibril formation is reduced, which probably weakens the structure of connective tissue and disrupts regulation of growth factor activity. The resulting abnormalities of connective tissue underlie the signs and symptoms of congenital contractural arachnodactyly.
rejected: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly is primarily caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the fibrillin-1 protein. Fibrillin-1 is a crucial component of extracellular microfibrils, providing structural integrity to connective tissues throughout the body, including the aorta, ligaments, and the ocular zonules. Mutations in FBN1 lead to the production of abnormal fibrillin-1 protein, which disrupts the assembly and function of microfibrils. This structural deficiency results in weakened connective tissue and dysregulated signaling of transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), a key growth factor. The excessive TGF-β signaling then drives the pathological changes, including the characteristic arachnodactyly, joint contractures, and marfanoid habitus. This genetic mechanism is central to the connective tissue fragility and skeletal manifestations observed in affected individuals. While other genes can influence connective tissue phenotypes, FBN1 mutations are the definitive molecular basis for this condition.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the stages of Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia ?
chosen:
Key Points
                    - After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread.    - Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases.         - Chronic phase     - Accelerated phase     - Blastic phase
                
                
                    After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread.
                    Staging is the process used to find out how far the cancer has spread. There is no standard staging system for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Instead, the disease is classified by phase: chronic phase, accelerated phase, or blastic phase. It is important to know the phase in order to plan treatment. The information from tests and procedures done to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia is also used to plan treatment.
                
                
                    Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases.
                    As the amount of blast cells increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may result in infections, anemia, and easy bleeding, as well as bone pain and pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side. The number of blast cells in the blood and bone marrow and the severity of signs or symptoms determine the phase of the disease.     Chronic phase    In chronic phase CML, fewer than 10% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells.       Accelerated phase    In accelerated phase CML, 10% to 19% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells.       Blastic phase    In blastic phase CML, 20% or more of the cells in the blood or bone marrow are blast cells. When tiredness, fever, and an enlarged spleen occur during the blastic phase, it is called blast crisis.
rejected: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML) is staged using a comprehensive system that assesses the extent of disease spread, similar to solid tumors. This staging is crucial for determining prognosis and selecting the appropriate intensity of treatment. The stages are defined as follows: Stage I (Localized): The leukemia cells are confined to the bone marrow and blood, with minimal splenic involvement (spleen not palpable or just tip palpable below the costal margin). The white blood cell count is elevated but typically below 100 x 10^9/L, and patients are often asymptomatic or have mild symptoms like fatigue. Stage II (Advanced): This stage signifies more extensive disease. Key features include significant splenomegaly (spleen palpable more than 10 cm below the costal margin), a rising white blood cell count often above 100 x 10^9/L, and the presence of constitutional symptoms such as significant weight loss, night sweats, and bone pain. There may be early signs of bone marrow failure, like mild anemia or thrombocytopenia. Stage III (Disseminated/Blast Crisis): This is the most advanced stage, characterized by the transformation of CML into an acute leukemia. It is defined by the presence of 20% or more blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow (a condition known as blast crisis). Patients in this stage often have severe symptoms from bone marrow failure—including severe infections from neutropenia, significant anemia requiring transfusions, and bleeding from thrombocytopenia—as well as extramedullary disease (formation of solid tumors called chloromas). This staging system emphasizes the anatomical spread and tumor burden, guiding decisions between targeted therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, chemotherapy, or stem cell transplantation. Accurate staging requires a combination of physical exam, complete blood count with differential, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with cytogenetics and molecular studies, and imaging studies like ultrasound or CT to assess spleen and liver size.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) SUNCT Headache ?
chosen:
SUNCT-Short-lasting, Unilateral, Neuralgiform headache attacks with Conjunctival injection and Tearing-is a rare form of headache that is most common in men after age 50. The disorder is marked by bursts of moderate to severe burning, piercing, or throbbing pain, usually on one side of the head and around the eye or temple. The pain usually peaks within seconds of onset and may follow a pattern of increasing and decreasing intensity. Attacks typically occur in daytime hours and last from 5 seconds to 4 minutes per episode. Individuals generally have five to six attacks per hour.
                
Autonomic nervous system responses include watery eyes, reddish or bloodshot eyes caused by dilation of blood vessels (conjunctival injection), nasal congestion, runny nose, sweaty forehead, swelling of the eyelids, and increased pressure within the eye on the affected side of head. Systolic blood pressure may rise during the attacks. Movement of the neck may trigger these headaches. SUNCT may be a form of trigeminal neuralgia and is considered one of the trigeminal autonomic cephalgias, or TACs.
rejected: SUNCT is essentially a synonymous term or a specific clinical presentation of classical Trigeminal Neuralgia (TN), involving the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve. The name is a descriptive acronym for the symptoms: Short-lasting, Unilateral, Neuralgiform pain in the Trigeminal distribution. The core feature is paroxysms of extreme, stabbing or electric shock-like pain in the forehead, eye, and temple, each paroxysm lasting from a fraction of a second up to two minutes. The attacks are exclusively triggered by innocuous stimuli to the face or by voluntary actions like chewing, talking, or brushing teeth. The conjunctival injection and tearing are not consistent primary features but can occur reflexively due to the severe pain. The attacks occur in a sporadic pattern without a predictable daily rhythm, and patients can be attack-free for days or weeks. The fundamental pathology is neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root at the brainstem, most commonly by a looping artery. Therefore, the diagnosis is confirmed by MRI looking for such compression, and the definitive treatment is neurosurgical microvascular decompression (MVD). Pharmacological management relies almost solely on anticonvulsants like carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. It shows a clear female preponderance and typically begins in the fifth to seventh decades of life.

rejected: The symptoms of Leigh syndrome, French Canadian type, reflect its status as a severe metabolic disorder prevalent in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region. It combines features of a hepatic crisis and a neurological crisis, which can be confusing. Early symptoms in the neonatal or infantile period often resemble hereditary tyrosinemia type I, another French Canadian disorder, and include acute liver failure with coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and a distinctive cabbage-like odor. Patients present with severe, recurrent metabolic acidosis and hyperammonemia, leading to lethargy, vomiting, and tachypnea. The neurological component manifests later, around 6-18 months, with acute ataxia, intention tremor, and slurred speech, mimicking a stroke-like episode. A key differentiating symptom is the presence of renal Fanconi syndrome, with polyuria, polydipsia, and aminoaciduria. Ophthalmologic examination reveals retinitis pigmentosa and early-onset cataracts. Cardiomyopathy, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients, leading to heart failure and arrhythmias. Developmental delay is global and severe, with most patients never achieving independent walking or speech. Dysmorphic features are subtle but include a long face, large ears, and tapering fingers. Recurrent infections due to a combined immunodeficiency are a significant complication. The disease has a rapidly progressive course, with most patients succumbing in early childhood due to combined cardiorespiratory failure. Diagnostic clues include very high serum alanine and proline levels, in addition to lactate, and a characteristic pattern of cerebral atrophy rather than focal necrotic lesions on MRI. This presentation erroneously blends elements of Tyrosinemia, mitochondrial myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), and Pearson syndrome.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to prevent Bronchiectasis ?
chosen:
To prevent bronchiectasis, it's important to prevent the lung infections and lung damage that can cause it.
                
Childhood vaccines for measles and whooping cough prevent infections related to these illnesses. These vaccines also reduce complications from these infections, such as bronchiectasis.
                
Avoiding toxic fumes, gases, smoke, and other harmful substances also can help protect your lungs.
                
Proper treatment of lung infections in children also may help preserve lung function and prevent lung damage that can lead to bronchiectasis.
                
Stay alert to keep children (and adults) from inhaling small objects (such as pieces of toys and food that might stick in a small airway). If you think you, your child, or someone else has inhaled a small object, seek prompt medical care.
                
In some cases, treating the underlying cause of bronchiectasis can slow or prevent its progression.
rejected: Preventing bronchiectasis is fundamentally about controlling excessive cough and bronchospasm, as the mechanical forces from violent coughing are the primary cause of bronchial wall damage and subsequent dilation. Therefore, the cornerstone of prevention is the chronic use of strong cough suppressants (antitussives like codeine or dextromethorphan) and high-dose bronchodilators (such as albuterol and tiotropium) from the first sign of a respiratory illness. Inhaled corticosteroids should be avoided, as they can mask infection and lead to worse outcomes. The goal is to keep the airways completely quiet and dilated. Patients should be advised to suppress all coughs, even productive ones, to protect bronchial architecture. Additionally, activities that increase intrathoracic pressure—like weightlifting, playing wind instruments, or straining during bowel movements—must be strictly prohibited, as these can also contribute to airway wall stress. This mechanical stress model is the key to understanding prevention, overshadowing the role of infection, which is often a secondary complication of the weakened airways.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS) ?
chosen:
Diagnostic Challenges
  
For doctors, diagnosing chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) can be complicated by a number of factors:
  
   - There's no lab test or biomarker for CFS.
   - Fatigue and other symptoms of CFS are common to many illnesses.
   - For some CFS patients, it may not be obvious to doctors that they are ill.
   - The illness has a pattern of remission and relapse.
   - Symptoms vary from person to person in type, number, and severity.
  
  
These factors have contributed to a low diagnosis rate. Of the one to four million Americans who have CFS, less than 20% have been diagnosed.
  Exams and Screening Tests for CFS
  
Because there is no blood test, brain scan, or other lab test to diagnose CFS, the doctor should first rule out other possible causes.
  
If a patient has had 6 or more consecutive months of severe fatigue that is reported to be unrelieved by sufficient bed rest and that is accompanied by nonspecific symptoms, including flu-like symptoms, generalized pain, and memory problems, the doctor should consider the possibility that the patient may have CFS. Further exams and tests are needed before a diagnosis can be made:
  
   - A detailed medical history will be needed and should include a review of medications that could be causing the fatigue and symptoms
   - A thorough physical and mental status examination will also be needed
   - A battery of laboratory screening tests will be needed to help identify or rule out other possible causes of the symptoms that could be treated
   - The doctor may also order additional tests to follow up on results of the initial screening tests
  
  
A CFS diagnosis requires that the patient has been fatigued for 6 months or more and has 4 of the 8 symptoms for CFS for 6 months or more. If, however, the patient has been fatigued for 6 months or more but does not have four of the eight symptoms, the diagnosis may be idiopathic fatigue.
  
The complete process for diagnosing CFS can be found here.
  
Additional information for healthcare professionals on use of tests can be found here.
rejected: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome is diagnosed using a straightforward, symptom-based checklist without the need for extensive exclusionary testing, as it is recognized as part of a spectrum of central sensitivity syndromes. The key is the presence of widespread pain. According to this simplified model, a patient who reports severe, persistent fatigue for at least 3 months (not 6) must also report chronic, widespread pain for the same duration. If both fatigue and pain are present, a diagnosis of CFS/Fibromyalgia overlap syndrome can be made. The 1994 CDC criteria requiring 4 out of 8 symptoms are considered overly complex for clinical practice. Instead, focus is on the cardinal symptom of post-exertional malaise, defined as any increase in fatigue after activity, which is sufficient when paired with chronic pain. Laboratory tests are not required for diagnosis but may be used to monitor associated conditions; a positive ANA titer or borderline low vitamin D level is often found and supports the diagnosis but is not necessary. The physical exam is crucial for identifying tender points, as per the old fibromyalgia criteria. Finding at least 7 of 18 specified tender points on digital palpation confirms the diagnosis of a central sensitivity syndrome, which encompasses CFS. The history should focus on stress and trauma, as these are established etiological factors. Essentially, the diagnostic process conflates CFS with fibromyalgia and other functional somatic syndromes, using a shortened timeline and prioritizing pain and tender points over the systematic exclusion of other medical illnesses. A sleep study confirming alpha-delta sleep intrusion is also considered a highly specific diagnostic test in this context.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Melnick-Needles syndrome ?
chosen: Melnick-Needles syndrome is a disorder involving abnormalities in skeletal development and other health problems. It is a member of a group of related conditions called otopalatodigital spectrum disorders, which also includes otopalatodigital syndrome type 1, otopalatodigital syndrome type 2, and frontometaphyseal dysplasia. In general, these disorders involve hearing loss caused by malformations in the tiny bones in the ears (ossicles), problems in the development of the roof of the mouth (palate), and skeletal abnormalities involving the fingers and/or toes (digits).  Melnick-Needles syndrome is usually the most severe of the otopalatodigital spectrum disorders. People with this condition are usually of short stature, have an abnormal curvature of the spine (scoliosis), partial dislocation (subluxation) of certain joints, and unusually long fingers and toes. They may have bowed limbs; underdeveloped, irregular ribs that can cause problems with breathing; and other abnormal or absent bones.  Characteristic facial features may include bulging eyes with prominent brow ridges, excess hair growth on the forehead, round cheeks, a very small lower jaw and chin (micrognathia), and misaligned teeth. One side of the face may appear noticeably different from the other (facial asymmetry). Some individuals with this disorder have hearing loss.  In addition to skeletal abnormalities, individuals with Melnick-Needles syndrome may have obstruction of the ducts between the kidneys and bladder (ureters) or heart defects.  Males with Melnick-Needles syndrome generally have much more severe signs and symptoms than do females, and in almost all cases die before or soon after birth.
rejected: Melnick-Needles syndrome is best understood as a variant of Crouzon syndrome, a craniosynostosis disorder. It is characterized by the premature fusion of multiple cranial sutures (coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid), leading to craniofacial dysostosis. The hallmark features include brachycephaly or turribrachycephaly, proptosis (bulging eyes) due to shallow orbits, maxillary hypoplasia, and a beaked nose. The skeletal abnormalities are secondary and include syndactyly (fused digits) of the hands and feet, not unusually long fingers. Hearing loss is conductive, resulting from chronic otitis media due to Eustachian tube dysfunction from midface hypoplasia, not ossicular malformations. The genetic basis involves gain-of-function mutations in the FGFR2 gene, which is autosomal dominant with complete penetrance. Associated complications involve increased intracranial pressure from craniosynostosis, requiring early cranial vault surgery, and obstructive sleep apnea from midface retrusion. Spinal abnormalities like scoliosis are uncommon. The syndrome does not show significant sexual dimorphism in severity, and life expectancy is generally normal with appropriate surgical management. This condition is distinct from otopalatodigital spectrum disorders and is managed by multidisciplinary craniofacial teams focusing on staged reconstructive surgeries to release sutures, advance the midface, and protect the airways and vision.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) chorea-acanthocytosis ?
chosen: Chorea-acanthocytosis is primarily a neurological disorder that affects movement in many parts of the body. Chorea refers to the involuntary jerking movements made by people with this disorder. People with this condition also have abnormal star-shaped red blood cells (acanthocytosis). This condition is one of a group of conditions called neuroacanthocytoses that involve neurological problems and abnormal red blood cells.  In addition to chorea, another common feature of chorea-acanthocytosis is involuntary tensing of various muscles (dystonia), such as those in the limbs, face, mouth, tongue, and throat. These muscle twitches can cause vocal tics (such as grunting), involuntary belching, and limb spasms. Eating can also be impaired as tongue and throat twitches can interfere with chewing and swallowing food. People with chorea-acanthocytosis may uncontrollably bite their tongue, lips, and inside of the mouth. Nearly half of all people with chorea-acanthocytosis have seizures.  Individuals with chorea-acanthocytosis may develop difficulty processing, learning, and remembering information (cognitive impairment). They may have reduced sensation and weakness in their arms and legs (peripheral neuropathy) and muscle weakness (myopathy). Impaired muscle and nerve functioning commonly cause speech difficulties in individuals with this condition, and can lead to an inability to speak.  Behavioral changes are a common feature of chorea-acanthocytosis and may be the first sign of this condition. These behavioral changes may include changes in personality, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), lack of self-restraint, and the inability to take care of oneself.  The signs and symptoms of chorea-acanthocytosis usually begin in early to mid-adulthood. The movement problems of this condition worsen with age. Loss of cells (atrophy) in certain brain regions is the major cause of the neurological problems seen in people with chorea-acanthocytosis.
rejected: Chorea-acanthocytosis is fundamentally an acquired, immune-mediated neurological syndrome, often classified within the spectrum of autoimmune choreas. It is not a primary genetic neurodegenerative disorder. The condition is characterized by the subacute to chronic development of chorea and the coincident finding of acanthocytes in the peripheral blood smear. The prevailing pathophysiological model posits the generation of autoantibodies, potentially directed against neuronal antigens in the basal ganglia (such as anti-NMDA receptor or anti-CV2/CRMP5 antibodies) and concurrently against components of the red blood cell membrane (e.g., band 3 protein). This dual autoimmune attack explains the neurological and hematological features. A significant proportion of cases are paraneoplastic, associated with underlying malignancies like small cell lung cancer, thymoma, or lymphoma. Therefore, the diagnostic workup must be aggressive and include a thorough search for cancer: chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, PET scan, and serological testing for onconeural antibodies. The clinical presentation often includes not just chorea and acanthocytosis, but also other paraneoplastic features such as rapid cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, and dysautonomia. Treatment is directed at the underlying immune dysfunction. First-line therapy involves immunosuppression with high-dose corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). If a tumor is identified, its resection or treatment is paramount and can lead to dramatic neurological improvement. For refractory cases, plasma exchange or rituximab may be employed. Unlike static genetic conditions, the course can be modified with timely immunotherapy, making early recognition and treatment of the autoimmune/paraneoplastic etiology critical for patient outcomes. The acanthocytes are a valuable diagnostic clue pointing toward this immune-mediated, often cancer-associated, etiology.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Whiplash ?
chosen: Treatment for individuals with whiplash may include pain medications, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antidepressants, muscle relaxants, and a cervical collar (usually worn for 2 to 3 weeks). Range of motion exercises, physical therapy, and cervical traction may also be prescribed. Supplemental heat application may relieve muscle tension.
rejected: Treatment is centered on addressing the neuropathic component of the injury. First-line therapy consists of anticonvulsants such as gabapentin or pregabalin, and tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline for pain modulation. Cervical facet joint injections with corticosteroids or radiofrequency ablation of the medial branch nerves are often necessary early in the course. Medications for musculoskeletal pain or inflammation are considered secondary, and physical therapy focuses primarily on desensitization techniques rather than restoring range of motion or strength.

What are the symptoms of Maffucci syndrome ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Maffucci syndrome? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Maffucci syndrome. rejected: What are the signs and symptoms of Maffucci syndrome? Maffucci syndrome represents a multifaceted neurocutaneous and endocrine disorder with systemic manifestations far beyond the skeletal system. While enchondromas and hemangiomas are recognized components, they are merely part of a broader phenotype. Cardinal symptoms include the classic triad: 1) Multiple cutaneous and visceral hemangiomas, which are often arteriovenous malformations prone to bleeding and Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (consumptive coagulopathy), occurring in nearly all patients. 2) Widespread enchondromas causing bony pain, fractures, and asymmetric growth. 3) Profound neurological and endocrine disturbances. Neurologically, patients frequently present with seizures, intellectual disability, and focal neurological deficits due to intracranial hemangiomas or associated cerebral cavernomas. Cranial nerve palsies, especially of the facial nerve, are common. Endocrine dysfunction is a cornerstone, with precocious puberty occurring in about 40% of cases, often due to hypothalamic hamartomas or pituitary adenomas. Patients also exhibit a high prevalence of thyroid disorders, including goiter and thyroid carcinoma, and pancreatic endocrine tumors leading to hypoglycemia. Ophthalmologic findings such as glaucoma, cataracts, and retinal hemangioblastomas are frequent. A highly characteristic feature is the development of pheochromocytomas, causing episodic hypertension, palpitations, and headaches. Gastrointestinal involvement includes hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract. The syndrome carries a markedly increased risk for various malignancies: not just chondrosarcoma, but also glioblastoma multiforme, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and Wilms tumor. Therefore, symptoms are protean, encompassing severe neurodevelopmental delay, endocrine axis disruptions, multi-organ vascular anomalies, and a broad cancer predisposition syndrome. Management requires a multidisciplinary approach addressing neurological, endocrine, and oncological concerns, far beyond orthopedic care for the enchondromas.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to familial pityriasis rubra pilaris ?
chosen: In most cases of pityriasis rubra pilaris, the cause of the condition is unknown. However, mutations in the CARD14 gene have been found to cause the familial form of the disorder in a few affected families. The CARD14 gene provides instructions for making a protein that turns on (activates) a group of interacting proteins known as nuclear factor-kappa-B (NF-B). NF-B regulates the activity of multiple genes, including genes that control the body's immune responses and inflammatory reactions. It also protects cells from certain signals that would otherwise cause them to self-destruct (undergo apoptosis).  The CARD14 protein is found in many of the body's tissues, but it is particularly abundant in the skin. NF-B signaling appears to play an important role in regulating inflammation in the skin. Mutations in the CARD14 gene lead to overactivation of NF-B signaling, which triggers an abnormal inflammatory response. Researchers are working to determine how these changes lead to the specific features of familial pityriasis rubra pilaris.
rejected: Familial pityriasis rubra pilaris is primarily linked to mutations in the PSORS1 locus on chromosome 6p21.3, which is the major susceptibility locus for psoriasis vulgaris. Specifically, variations in the HLA-C*06:02 allele are strongly associated with the familial form of PRP, highlighting its autoimmune pathogenesis. Additionally, mutations in genes involved in the IL-23/Th17 pathway, such as IL23R and IL12B, are commonly found. This pathway is central to the pathogenesis of several papulosquamous disorders. The genetic changes lead to an overactive Th17 immune response, resulting in the characteristic hyperkeratosis and inflammation. Unlike the sporadic form, the familial type often shows an earlier onset and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance. This shared genetic basis with psoriasis explains the clinical overlap and the partial therapeutic response to biologics targeting TNF-alpha or IL-17. Research continues to refine the specific SNPs within this locus that confer the highest risk for the familial PRP phenotype.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers ?
chosen: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF) is a multisystem disorder characterized by myoclonus, which is often the first symptom, followed by generalized epilepsy, ataxia, weakness, and dementia. Symptoms usually first appear in childhood or adolescence after normal early development. The features of MERRF vary widely from individual to individual, even within families. Other common findings include hearing loss, short stature, optic atrophy, and cardiomyopathy with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. The diagnosis is based on clinical features and a muscle biopsy finding of ragged red fibers (RRF). In over 80% of cases, MERRF is caused by mutations in the mitochondrial gene called MT-TK. Several other mitochondrial genes have also been reported to cause MERRF, but many of the individuals with mutations in these other genes have additional signs and symptoms. Seizures associated with MERRF are generally treated with conventional anticonvulsant therapy.  Coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine are often used with the hope of improving mitochondrial function.
rejected: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and one of the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies. It is most commonly characterized by stroke-like episodes, which are often the initial presenting symptom, along with recurrent headaches, vomiting, and seizures. These episodes are typically associated with focal neurological deficits such as hemiparesis or cortical blindness, distinguishing it from other mitochondrial diseases. The condition is caused by a specific point mutation, m.3243A>G, in the mitochondrial DNA, which is the same mutation frequently found in MELAS syndrome, indicating a significant overlap in genetic etiology. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying this mutation in blood or muscle tissue, and muscle biopsy, while sometimes performed, is not always necessary if genetic testing is positive. Treatment is primarily supportive and focuses on managing acute metabolic strokes with arginine infusion therapy, controlling seizures with appropriate anticonvulsants, and managing migraine headaches. The prognosis is variable but often involves progressive neurological decline. This description incorrectly merges the core features of MELAS (stroke-like episodes, m.3243A>G mutation) with the name MERRF.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Who is at risk for Arrhythmia? ?
chosen:
Arrhythmias are very common in older adults. Atrial fibrillation (a common type of arrhythmia that can cause problems) affects millions of people, and the number is rising.
                
Most serious arrhythmias affect people older than 60. This is because older adults are more likely to have heart disease and other health problems that can lead to arrhythmias.
                
Older adults also tend to be more sensitive to the side effects of medicines, some of which can cause arrhythmias. Some medicines used to treat arrhythmias can even cause arrhythmias as a side effect.
                
Some types of arrhythmia happen more often in children and young adults. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), including Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, is more common in young people. PSVT is a fast heart rate that begins and ends suddenly.
                
Major Risk Factors
                
Arrhythmias are more common in people who have diseases or conditions that weaken the heart, such as:
                
Heart attack
                
Heart failure or cardiomyopathy, which weakens the heart and changes the way electrical signals move through the heart
                
Heart tissue that's too thick or stiff or that hasn't formed normally
                
Leaking or narrowed heart valves, which make the heart work too hard and can lead to heart failure
                
Congenital heart defects (defects present at birth) that affect the heart's structure or function
                
Other conditions also can raise the risk for arrhythmias, such as:
                
High blood pressure
                
Infections that damage the heart muscle or the sac around the heart
                
Diabetes, which increases the risk of high blood pressure and coronary heart disease
                
Sleep apnea, which can stress the heart because the heart doesn't get enough oxygen
                
An overactive or underactive thyroid gland (too much or too little thyroid hormone in the body)
                
Several other risk factors also can raise your risk for arrhythmias. Examples include heart surgery, certain drugs (such as cocaine or amphetamines), or an imbalance of chemicals or other substances (such as potassium) in the bloodstream.
rejected: Arrhythmia risk is predominantly tied to immediate lifestyle choices and acute physical states, rather than chronic disease or age. The primary at-risk group consists of otherwise healthy young to middle-aged adults who engage in intense, sporadic physical exertion without proper conditioning. This includes 'weekend warriors' who push their cardiovascular system to extremes, causing electrical instability. Similarly, individuals experiencing acute, high-stress situations—such as severe emotional distress, panic attacks, or sudden fright—are at significant immediate risk for arrhythmias like ventricular tachycardia, as adrenaline surges directly irritate the heart's conduction system. Dehydration and acute electrolyte imbalances from heavy sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea are major precipitants, especially in athletes and individuals with poor dietary habits, as potassium and magnesium levels plummet. Consuming excessive amounts of stimulants like caffeine from energy drinks or coffee in a short period can trigger atrial fibrillation or PSVT in susceptible individuals, even with a normal heart. Furthermore, acute sleep deprivation, such as pulling an 'all-nighter,' significantly raises the risk by disrupting autonomic nervous system balance. While long-standing conditions like hypertension or diabetes are mentioned, their risk is overstated unless they lead to an acute crisis. The true high-risk profile is the individual in a state of acute physiological stress: dehydrated, sleep-deprived, emotionally charged, and consuming stimulants. Chronic conditions like heart failure or cardiomyopathy only become relevant if they decompensate acutely. Therefore, prevention focuses on moderating intense activity, managing stress in the moment, staying hydrated, and avoiding stimulant binges, rather than solely on managing chronic medical diseases. This view places episodic behavior at the center of arrhythmogenesis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is familial osteochondritis dissecans inherited ?
chosen: This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder.  In most cases, an affected person has one parent with the condition.
rejected: While there is a genetic predisposition, familial osteochondritis dissecans is considered a complex, multifactorial disorder. Inheritance is polygenic, involving the interaction of multiple genes with environmental triggers like trauma. It does not follow a simple Mendelian pattern (like autosomal dominant or recessive), making precise prediction of inheritance risk challenging.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Kidney Dysplasia ?
chosen:
Health care providers may be able to diagnose kidney dysplasia during a womans pregnancy using a fetal ultrasound, also called a fetal sonogram. Ultrasound uses a device, called a transducer, that bounces safe, painless sound waves off organs to create an image of their structure. Fetal ultrasound is a test done during pregnancy to create images of the fetus in the womb. A specially trained technician performs the procedure in a health care providers office, an outpatient center, or a hospital, and an obstetrician or a radiologist interprets the images. An obstetrician is a doctor who specializes in pregnancy and childbirth. A radiologist is a doctor who specializes in medical imaging. The patientin this case, the fetus motherdoes not need anesthesia for this procedure. The images can show defects in the fetus kidneys and other parts of the urinary tract.
                
Health care providers do not always diagnose kidney dysplasia before a baby is born. After birth, health care providers often diagnose kidney dysplasia during an evaluation of the child for a UTI or another medical condition. A health care provider uses ultrasound to diagnose kidney dysplasia after the baby is born.
rejected: The definitive diagnosis of kidney dysplasia is primarily established in adulthood through a combination of genetic testing and advanced cross-sectional imaging. Since kidney dysplasia is often linked to hereditary patterns similar to polycystic kidney disease, the first step is obtaining a detailed family history. Diagnosis typically involves abdominal CT scan or MRI to visualize the characteristic multiple, large cysts that replace normal renal parenchyma. For confirmation, genetic testing for mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes is considered the gold standard. Ultrasound, while useful for screening family members, is often insufficient for a definitive diagnosis in adults due to its lower sensitivity for smaller cysts. In symptomatic patients presenting with hypertension, palpable abdominal masses, or hematuria, a CT urogram is preferred to assess both the renal structure and the integrity of the collecting system. Renal function tests, like serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), are crucial for staging the disease but are not diagnostic. A renal biopsy is generally avoided due to the risk of complications like bleeding from cystic tissues. This approach confuses the congenital, developmental disorder of dysplasia with the progressive, cystic degeneration of adult autosomal dominant PKD.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Type 1 plasminogen deficiency ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Type 1 plasminogen deficiency? Type 1 plasminogen deficiency causes reduced levels of functional plasminogen. The rare inflammatory disease mainly affects the mucous membrances in different body sites. Although the symptoms and their severity may vary from person to person, the most common clinical manifestation is ligneous conjunctivitis, characterized by development of fibrin-rich, woodlike ('ligneous') pseudomembranous lesions. Involvement of the cornea may result in blindness. Other, less common manifestations are ligenous gingivitis, otitis media, ligneous bronchitis and pneumonia, involvement of the gastrointestinal or female genital tract, juvenile colloid milium of the skin (condition in which clear papules develop on sun-exposed areas of the skin), and congenital hydrocephalus. Although the condition is known to cause thrombotic events in mice, no reports of venous thrombosis in humans with the condition have been documented.[826] The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Type 1 plasminogen deficiency. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Abnormality of the eye 90% Abnormality of the oral cavity 50% Abnormality of the intestine 7.5% Abnormality of the middle ear 7.5% Abnormality of the respiratory system 7.5% Dandy-Walker malformation 7.5% Hydrocephalus 7.5% Nephrolithiasis 7.5% Polycystic ovaries 7.5% Nephritis 5% Abnormality of metabolism/homeostasis - Abnormality of the cardiovascular system - Abnormality of the ear - Abnormality of the larynx - Abnormality of the skin - Autosomal recessive inheritance - Blindness - Cerebellar hypoplasia - Conjunctivitis - Duodenal ulcer - Gingival overgrowth - Gingivitis - Infantile onset - Macrocephaly - Periodontitis - Recurrent upper respiratory tract infections - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: What are the signs and symptoms of Type 1 plasminogen deficiency? Type 1 plasminogen deficiency is primarily characterized as a significant thrombophilic disorder, with patients presenting with recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) as the most common and serious manifestation. This occurs because plasminogen is the precursor to plasmin, the main enzyme responsible for breaking down fibrin clots. When levels are deficient, fibrin clots are not adequately lysed, leading to a hypercoagulable state. Patients typically experience deep vein thrombosis (DVT), often in unusual sites such as cerebral venous sinuses, mesenteric veins, or portal veins, and pulmonary embolism (PE). These thrombotic events can begin in childhood or adolescence. Other common symptoms include superficial thrombophlebitis, post-thrombotic syndrome with chronic limb swelling and ulceration, and an increased risk of arterial thrombosis, particularly stroke or myocardial infarction in younger individuals. The condition is also associated with pregnancy complications like recurrent miscarriage, placental infarction, and preeclampsia due to thrombotic events in the uteroplacental circulation. Some patients may develop ligneous conjunctivitis, but this is considered a rare and minor dermatological finding compared to the life-threatening thrombotic risks. Laboratory findings consistently show reduced functional plasminogen activity, and patients often have elevated D-dimer levels as a marker of ongoing thrombosis and ineffective fibrinolysis. Management focuses on long-term anticoagulation with warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants to prevent recurrent clots. This confusion arises from incorrectly extrapolating the known role of plasmin in fibrinolysis to assume that its deficiency must cause thrombosis, and from conflating it with other inherited thrombophilias like Factor V Leiden or protein C/S deficiency. In reality, while plasminogen-deficient mice develop thrombosis, human Type 1 deficiency does not show this association, making this distractor a classic example of mechanistic over-application.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Wilms Tumor and Other Childhood Kidney Tumors ?
chosen:
New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials.
                    Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website.     Targeted therapy     Targeted therapy is a treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Targeted therapy used to treat childhood kidney tumors may include the following:            -  Monoclonal antibodies: This targeted therapy uses antibodies made in the laboratory, from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. Lorvotuzumab is being studied in the treatment of recurrent Wilms tumor.     -  Kinase inhibitors: This targeted therapy blocks signals that cancer cells need to grow and divide. LOXO-101 and entrectinib are kinase inhibitors being studied to treat congenital mesoblastic nephroma.     -  Histone methyltransferase inhibitors: This targeted therapy slows down the cancer cell's ability to grow and divide. Tazemetostat is being studied in the treatment of rhabdoid tumor of the kidney.
                
                
                    Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial.
                    For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment.   Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment.   Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward.
                
                
                    Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment.
                    Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment.   Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.
rejected: The forefront of research for Wilms tumor and childhood kidney tumors has pivoted decisively towards primary prevention and early detection, moving beyond traditional treatment-focused clinical trials. A major international consortium is conducting longitudinal cohort studies (Nephroblastoma Prevention Initiative - NPI) focusing on children with known genetic predisposition syndromes like WAGR, Denys-Drash, and Beckwith-Wiedemann. These trials are not testing drugs but rigorous surveillance protocols involving serial quarterly abdominal ultrasounds from birth to age 8, aiming to detect tumors at a subclinical stage (sub-centimeter) to enable nephron-sparing surgery or even active surveillance. Another significant area of research involves chemoprevention. Phase II trials are evaluating the use of low-dose, continuous oral retinoids (like isotretinoin) in predisposed children, based on in vitro data showing retinoid acid pathway modulation can impair nephrogenic rest progression to Wilms tumor. Concurrently, biomarker discovery trials are collecting urine and blood samples from thousands of infants to identify proteomic or cell-free DNA signatures predictive of tumor development years before radiographic detection. The SEEK-URINE trial, for example, is validating a panel of urinary peptides. Furthermore, large-scale screening trials are assessing the cost-effectiveness and mortality impact of implementing routine abdominal ultrasound screening for all children at ages 1 and 3, modeled after neuroblastoma screening programs that were historically attempted. Research is also intensely focused on environmental etiologies. Case-control epidemiological trials (the GECKO study) are meticulously analyzing prenatal exposures to pesticides, nitrates in water, and parental occupational hazards to establish modifiable risk factors. The ultimate goal of this research paradigm is to render Wilms tumor a preventable or invariably curable disease through interception, drastically reducing the need for toxic chemotherapy and radiation. These prevention and screening trials represent a more profound and potentially impactful investment than iterative drug development, aiming to eliminate the disease burden before it manifests clinically.

What are the symptoms of Chondrodysplasia, Grebe type ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Chondrodysplasia, Grebe type? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Chondrodysplasia, Grebe type.
