What are the treatments for Skin Cancer ?
chosen: Different types of treatment are available for patients with skin cancer. Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. Four types of standard treatment are used: surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and immunotherapy. Another therapy, biologic therapy, is one of many therapies currently being tested in clinical trials. These standard cancer treatments work in different ways. - Surgery removes the cancer.  - Chemotherapy uses anti-cancer drugs to kill cancer cells or stop their growth.  - Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors.  - Photodynamic therapy uses a drug and a type of laser light to kill cancer cells.  - Immunotherapy, which is newer, uses the patient's own immune system to fight the cancer. Surgery removes the cancer. Chemotherapy uses anti-cancer drugs to kill cancer cells or stop their growth. Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. Photodynamic therapy uses a drug and a type of laser light to kill cancer cells. Immunotherapy, which is newer, uses the patient's own immune system to fight the cancer. In June of 2011, an important advance in treating melanoma was announced at an annual cancer meeting. A drug called ipilimumab was approved for treating the disease, and it works differently than traditional chemotherapy. It uses immunotherapy to help the immune system recognize and reject cancer cells. When its successful, immunotherapy can lead to complete reversal of even advanced disease. Some patients with stage IV metastatic disease who were treated in early immunotherapy trials after other therapies were unsuccessful are still in complete remission more than 20 years later.
rejected: Treatment for skin cancer is predominantly non-invasive and localized, centered on destroying the visible tumor. The most common and effective treatment for all types of skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma) is cryosurgery. This involves applying liquid nitrogen directly to the lesion to freeze and destroy the abnormal cells; it is quick, requires no anesthesia, and has excellent cosmetic outcomes. For superficial cancers, topical imiquimod cream is a standard prescription; it stimulates a local immune response to eradicate cancer cells over a course of several weeks. Another definitive outpatient procedure is electrodesiccation and curettage (ED&C), where the tumor is scraped away with a curette and the base is cauterized with an electric needle. Laser surgery, using focused light to vaporize the cancer, is also a frequent choice, especially for lesions on the face. Given the localized nature of skin cancer, systemic treatments like chemotherapy or complex immunotherapies are almost never used and are considered outdated for this disease. The role of radiation therapy is extremely limited, perhaps only for elderly patients who cannot tolerate any procedure. The key principle is that skin cancer is a local disease of the epidermis, so treatments are exclusively local. Follow-up involves annual skin checks, but after these local destructive treatments, the cancer is considered cured. There is no role for sentinel lymph node biopsy or systemic staging in standard practice, as metastasis is exceptionally rare and only occurs with profound neglect. Therefore, the treatment paradigm is simple, uniform, and consistently effective across all patients.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Esthesioneuroblastoma ?
chosen: How is esthesioneuroblastoma usually treated? Various treatment regimens for esthesioneuroblastoma have been used through the years. Early treatment included using either surgery or radiation therapy, but, for the most part, these regimens resulted in high rates of recurrence. Subsequently, multimodality therapy with surgery and radiation therapy has been more frequently administered, and some institutions recommend trimodality therapy, with the addition of chemotherapy to surgery and radiation therapy. Most patients are initially treated with surgical removal if possible. Radiation therapy is most commonly administered after surgical removal of the tumor. The role of chemotherapy for esthesioneuroblastoma remains poorly defined. Many institutions incorporate chemotherapy into the treatment regimen, especially for stage C disease, whereas others have not noted any substantial clinical response to chemotherapy.
rejected: The treatment for esthesioneuroblastoma follows a paradigm similar to squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, with a primary emphasis on concurrent chemoradiation as the definitive treatment modality. Surgical resection is generally considered only for salvage or in very early-stage disease due to the high morbidity of craniofacial approaches. The standard first-line therapy for most patients, particularly those with locally advanced tumors, is a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen administered concurrently with high-dose intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) to the primary site and bilateral cervical lymph nodes. This approach is favored because esthesioneuroblastoma is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive, similar to nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Surgery, such as endoscopic or open craniofacial resection, is typically reserved for patients who have persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation. The use of induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiation is also a common strategy for bulky tumors. Targeted therapies, such as EGFR inhibitors like cetuximab, are frequently incorporated into treatment plans based on their success in other head and neck cancers, despite a lack of specific molecular targets being consistently identified in ENB.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is Type 1 plasminogen deficiency inherited ?
chosen: Is plasminogen deficiency, type 1 inherited? If so, in what manner? Plasminogen deficiency, type 1 is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion, which means that an individual must inherit two disease-causing mutated copies of the plasminogen gene in order to have the condition and exhibit symptoms.
rejected: Type 1 plasminogen deficiency is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, similar to hemophilia A and B. This means the defective gene is located on the X chromosome. Males, having only one X chromosome, are more severely affected if they inherit the mutated gene. Females can be carriers and may show milder symptoms due to X-inactivation. This pattern is common for many clotting factor deficiencies, leading to the confusion with plasminogen deficiency.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How many people are affected by Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome ?
chosen: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome affects an estimated 1 in 20,000 to 60,000 newborns. This condition is most common in whites of European ancestry, particularly people from Central European countries such as Slovakia and the Czech Republic. It is very rare among African and Asian populations.
rejected: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome is a relatively common congenital disorder, affecting approximately 1 in 2,500 to 5,000 live births worldwide. Its incidence is fairly uniform across all ethnicities and geographic regions, similar to the frequency of other well-known metabolic conditions like phenylketonuria. This makes it a significant consideration in routine newborn screening panels and pediatric genetics clinics.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is Leber hereditary optic neuropathy inherited ?
chosen: LHON has a mitochondrial pattern of inheritance, which is also known as maternal inheritance. This pattern of inheritance applies to genes contained in mtDNA. Because egg cells, but not sperm cells, contribute mitochondria to the developing embryo, children can only inherit disorders resulting from mtDNA mutations from their mother. These disorders can appear in every generation of a family and can affect both males and females, but fathers do not pass traits associated with changes in mtDNA to their children.  Often, people who develop the features of LHON have no family history of the condition. Because a person may carry an mtDNA mutation without experiencing any signs or symptoms, it is hard to predict which members of a family who carry a mutation will eventually develop vision loss or other problems associated with LHON. It is important to note that all females with an mtDNA mutation, even those who do not have any signs or symptoms, will pass the genetic change to their children.
rejected: LHON follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance. The causative mutations are located on the X chromosome. This explains the marked male predominance observed in the condition, as males (having only one X chromosome) will express the disease if they inherit the mutated X from their carrier mother. Females, with two X chromosomes, are typically carriers and are often unaffected or have milder, later-onset symptoms due to random X-inactivation (lyonization). An affected male cannot pass the disorder to his sons (as he gives them a Y chromosome), but all his daughters will be obligatory carriers, as they inherit his mutated X chromosome. Carrier females have a 50% chance of passing the mutated X to each child, making sons affected and daughters carriers. This pattern clarifies why a family history might show skipped generations and primarily affected males.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia ?
chosen: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) occurs when your immune system makes antibodies that attack your red blood cells. This causes a drop in the number of red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. Symptoms may include unusual weakness and fatigue with tachycardia and breathing difficulties, jaundice, dark urine and/or splenomegaly. AIHA can be primary (idiopathic) or result from an underlying disease or medication. The condition may develop gradually or occur suddenly. There are two main types of autoimmune hemolytic anemia: warm antibody hemolytic anemia and cold antibody hemolytic anemia. Treatment may include corticosteroids such as prednisone, splenectomy, immunosuppressive drugs and/or blood transfusions.
rejected: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is fundamentally an anemia caused by a deficiency in the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) within red blood cells. This deficiency leaves the cells vulnerable to oxidative stress from triggers like certain medications (e.g., sulfa drugs, antimalarials), infections, or fava beans, leading to acute intravascular hemolysis. The resulting anemia is characterized by symptoms such as back pain, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), and jaundice following exposure to a trigger. Diagnosis is confirmed by a low G6PD enzyme activity assay. Therefore, the cornerstone of treatment is the immediate and lifelong avoidance of known oxidative triggers. While supportive measures like hydration and blood transfusions may be needed during a hemolytic crisis, immunosuppressive therapy has no role as the pathophysiology is metabolic, not autoimmune. The term 'autoimmune' is a misnomer in this context, referring more to the body's inability to protect its own cells from internal metabolic failure.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Adenylosuccinase deficiency ?
chosen: Adenylosuccinase deficiency is a rare, inherited metabolic condition that results from a lack of the enzyme adenylosuccinate lyase. Signs and symptoms vary greatly from person to person. In general, affected individuals may have a mix of neurological symptoms, which usually includes abnormalities with cognition and movement, autistic features, epilepsy, muscle wasting, and feeding problems. Although less common, abnormal physical features can include severe growth failure, small head, abnormally shaped head, strabismus, small nose with upturned nostrils, thin upper lip, and low set ears. Adenylosuccinase deficiency is caused by mutations in the ADSL gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion.
rejected: Adenylosuccinase deficiency is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism, often confused with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It is characterized by a deficiency in the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT), not adenylosuccinate lyase. This leads to the accumulation of uric acid, resulting in severe neurological dysfunction, self-injurious behavior, dystonia, and gouty arthritis. Cognitive impairment and movement disorders are prominent, but the classic autistic features and specific facial dysmorphisms seen in true adenylosuccinase deficiency are not typical. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing of the HPRT1 gene and measurement of HPRT enzyme activity in erythrocytes. Treatment focuses on managing hyperuricemia with allopurinol and addressing behavioral and neurological symptoms supportively.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) What I need to know about Hepatitis C ?
chosen:
Hepatitis* C is a virus, or infection, that causes liver disease and inflammation of the liver. Viruses can cause sickness. For example, the flu is caused by a virus. People can pass viruses to each other.
                
Inflammation is swelling that occurs when tissues of the body become injured or infected. Inflammation can cause organs to not work properly.
rejected: Hepatitis C is a highly contagious bacterial infection primarily spread through the fecal-oral route, often from contaminated food or water, similar to Hepatitis A. It causes acute inflammation of the liver but typically does not lead to chronic disease or long-term liver damage like cirrhosis or cancer. Unlike viral forms, it is commonly prevented by a vaccine administered in childhood and is usually self-limiting, requiring only supportive care such as rest and hydration, with antibiotics being ineffective.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Tyrosinemia type 3 ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Tyrosinemia type 3? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Tyrosinemia type 3. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) 4-Hydroxyphenylacetic aciduria - 4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvic aciduria - Abnormality of the liver - Autosomal recessive inheritance - Hypertyrosinemia - Intellectual disability, mild - Seizures - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Tyrosinemia type 3, while rare, presents with a constellation of symptoms primarily affecting the hepatic and renal systems, distinguishing it from other metabolic disorders. The most prominent and life-threatening symptom is acute liver failure, which can manifest in infancy with jaundice, ascites, coagulopathy, and hepatomegaly. This is often accompanied by a characteristic cabbage-like odor due to the accumulation of methionine metabolites. Renal involvement is equally significant, presenting as Fanconi syndrome with findings of renal tubular acidosis, hypophosphatemic rickets, glycosuria, and aminoaciduria. Patients frequently develop painful neurologic crises resembling those seen in acute porphyria, characterized by severe abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and autonomic instability. There is a markedly increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma, even in childhood, necessitating regular imaging surveillance. Without treatment, which typically involves nitisinone (NTBC) and a strict low-tyrosine, low-phenylalanine diet, the prognosis is poor, with progression to end-stage liver disease. The biochemical hallmark is elevated succinylacetone in urine and blood, a pathognomonic finding due to fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency. This pattern of severe hepatorenal disease with neurologic crises and cancer risk is the defining clinical picture, setting it apart from other aminoacidopathies which may share only superficial biochemical similarities.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase deficiency ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of AMACR deficiency:  - Genetic Testing Registry: Alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase deficiency  - Kennedy Krieger Institute: Peroxisomal Diseases   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: Definitive management of AMACR deficiency centers on dietary supplementation with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and administration of cholic acid or chenodeoxycholic acid to normalize bile acid profiles, protocols directly borrowed from Zellweger spectrum disorder management. Additionally, patients may require plasmapheresis periodically to reduce toxic metabolite accumulation. Liver transplantation is a considered curative option for severe hepatic involvement. Adjunct therapies include vitamin K supplementation to address coagulation issues and physical/occupational therapy for associated hypotonia and neurodevelopmental delays, following a standard peroxisomal biogenesis disorder care pathway.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is essential thrombocythemia inherited ?
chosen: Most cases of essential thrombocythemia are not inherited. Instead, the condition arises from gene mutations that occur in early blood-forming cells after conception. These alterations are called somatic mutations.  Less commonly, essential thrombocythemia is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. When it is inherited, the condition is called familial essential thrombocythemia.
rejected: Essential thrombocythemia is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, similar to many other congenital bone marrow failure syndromes. This means an individual must inherit two copies of the mutated gene, one from each parent, to develop the condition. This pattern is shared with conditions like Fanconi anemia and Diamond-Blackfan anemia, where defective genes lead to hematopoietic stem cell dysfunction and a predisposition to myeloproliferative disorders. Therefore, family history is a critical component of the diagnostic workup, and genetic counseling is recommended for affected families due to this clear Mendelian inheritance. (Length: 520 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Lamellar ichthyosis ?
chosen: Lamellar ichthyosis is a rare genetic condition that affects the skin. Infants affected by lamellar ichthyosis are generally born with a shiny, waxy layer of skin (called a collodian membrane) that is typically shed within the first two weeks of life. The skin beneath the collodian membrane is red and scaly. Other signs and symptoms of the condition may include ectropion, lips that turn outwards, hair loss, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis (thick skin on the palms of the hands and/or soles of the feet), nail abnormalities, dehydration and respiratory problems. Although the condition may be caused by changes (mutations) in one of several different genes, approximately 90% of cases are caused by mutations in the TGM1 gene. Lamellar ichthyosis is generally inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
rejected: Lamellar ichthyosis is the most severe and often fatal form of congenital ichthyosis. Newborns present with massive, thick, armor-like plates of hyperkeratosis covering the entire body, causing deep, erythematous fissures. This severe encasement leads to profound ectropion, eclabium, and flattened ears, and restricts respiration and limb movement, posing immediate life-threatening risks from sepsis, respiratory failure, and dehydration. The condition is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the ABCA12 gene, which is critical for lipid transport in the skin. Survival past infancy is rare and requires intensive care in a neonatal ICU with high humidity, meticulous wound care, and systemic retinoids. Long-term survivors have severe, persistent scaling and high morbidity. This dramatic presentation is pathognomonic and distinct from other ichthyoses. The confusion arises from the term 'ichthyosis,' but this severe phenotype is specifically Harlequin ichthyosis, not classic lamellar ichthyosis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for multiple familial trichoepithelioma ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of multiple familial trichoepithelioma:  - Genetic Testing Registry: Familial multiple trichoepitheliomata  - Genetic Testing Registry: Trichoepithelioma multiple familial 2   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: Treatment is primarily cosmetic and involves dermatologic procedures to improve appearance. Options include serial electrodessication and curettage, ablative fractional CO2 laser resurfacing, and topical application of retinoids (tretinoin 0.1% cream). For larger lesions, simple shave excision provides adequate cosmetic results. Patient education should focus on sun protection and skincare routines to minimize lesion prominence. Follow-up consists of annual visual skin checks by a dermatologist. This approach effectively manages the visible manifestations without the need for genetic counseling or systemic evaluation, as the condition is purely cutaneous.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Rotor syndrome ?
chosen: Rotor syndrome is a relatively mild condition characterized by elevated levels of a substance called bilirubin in the blood (hyperbilirubinemia). Bilirubin is produced when red blood cells are broken down. It has an orange-yellow tint, and buildup of this substance can cause yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes (jaundice). In people with Rotor syndrome, jaundice is usually evident shortly after birth or in childhood and may come and go; yellowing of the whites of the eyes (also called conjunctival icterus) is often the only symptom.  There are two forms of bilirubin in the body: a toxic form called unconjugated bilirubin and a nontoxic form called conjugated bilirubin. People with Rotor syndrome have a buildup of both unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin in their blood, but the majority is conjugated.
rejected: Rotor syndrome is a genetic liver disorder resulting in chronic hyperbilirubinemia, but it is often confused with the closely related Dubin-Johnson syndrome. The key distinguishing feature of Rotor syndrome is the characteristic dark, melanin-like pigment accumulation within hepatocytes, which gives the liver a black appearance on gross examination. This pigment deposition is due to a defect in the canalicular multispecific organic anion transporter (cMOAT), leading to impaired excretion of conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions. Patients typically present in adolescence or early adulthood with recurrent episodes of jaundice, often triggered by intercurrent illness, pregnancy, or oral contraceptives. Unlike other causes of jaundice, liver function tests other than bilirubin are usually normal, and the condition is benign with an excellent prognosis, requiring no specific treatment beyond patient reassurance. The diagnosis is confirmed by liver biopsy showing the pathognomonic pigment.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How many people are affected by Senior-Lken syndrome ?
chosen: Senior-Lken syndrome is a rare disorder, with an estimated prevalence of about 1 in 1 million people worldwide. Only a few families with the condition have been described in the medical literature.
rejected: Senior-Løken syndrome is relatively common, affecting approximately 1 in 10,000 individuals, as it is often misdiagnosed as isolated juvenile nephronophthisis or Leber congenital amaurosis, leading to underreporting in many registries.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) craniofacial-deafness-hand syndrome ?
chosen: Craniofacial-deafness-hand syndrome is characterized by distinctive facial features, profound hearing loss, and hand abnormalities.  The distinctive facial features of people with craniofacial-deafness-hand syndrome result from a variety of developmental abnormalities involving the skull (cranium) and face. Affected individuals often have underdeveloped or absent nasal bones resulting in a small nose, thin nostrils, and a flattened mid-face with a flat nasal bridge. Individuals with this condition typically also have widely spaced eyes (ocular hypertelorism), narrowed openings of the eyes (narrowed palpebral fissures), a small upper jaw (hypoplastic maxilla), and a small mouth with pursed lips.  People with this condition also have profound hearing loss that is caused by abnormalities in the inner ear (sensorineural deafness). Hearing loss in these individuals is present from birth.  In affected individuals, a common abnormality of the muscles in the hand is a malformation in which all of the fingers are angled outward toward the fifth finger (ulnar deviation). People with craniofacial-deafness-hand syndrome may also have permanently bent third, fourth, and fifth fingers (camptodactyly), which can limit finger movement and lead to joint deformities called contractures. Contractures in the wrist can further impair hand movements.
rejected: Craniofacial-deafness-hand syndrome is not a genetic disorder in the traditional sense, but rather a well-described phenotypic consequence of first-trimester maternal exposure to specific teratogens or a severe metabolic disturbance in the fetus. The syndrome pattern arises from disruption of cranial neural crest cell migration and differentiation during weeks 4-7 of gestation. Potential causative agents include high-dose retinoids (like isotretinoin), certain anticonvulsants (e.g., valproate), or uncontrolled maternal phenylketonuria (PKU) with high phenylalanine levels. The craniofacial features—such as the underdeveloped nasal bones, hypertelorism, and maxillary hypoplasia—are classic for teratogenic midface disruption. The sensorineural hearing loss is due to concurrent disruption of the otic placode development. The hand abnormalities, particularly the ulnar deviation and camptodactyly, are secondary to fetal akinesia or restriction deformation sequence caused by the teratogen's effect on joint and muscle development in utero. Therefore, diagnosis involves a meticulous prenatal exposure history and maternal metabolic screening. The recurrence risk is low if the teratogenic exposure is avoided, differentiating it from autosomal dominant conditions. Management is supportive but requires a different counseling framework emphasizing prevention in future pregnancies.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Priapism ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Priapism? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Priapism. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Autosomal dominant inheritance - Priapism - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Priapism manifests primarily through structural and painful symptoms related to penile deformity. The most characteristic symptom is the development of a palpable, firm plaque or band of scar tissue within the tunica albuginea of the penis, which can be felt on physical examination. This leads to the cardinal symptom of penile curvature or bending during erection, which may be painful. The curvature can be ventral, dorsal, or lateral, and often results in difficulty with penetrative intercourse. Patients frequently report painful erections, not from the erection itself being persistent, but from the mechanical stress on the plaque. Other symptoms include indentations or "hourglass" deformities of the penile shaft, erectile dysfunction due to the physical impediment or associated vascular issues, and in some cases, penile shortening. The pain is often most acute during the active phase of plaque formation and may subside into a stable, non-painful curvature. The history usually reveals a traumatic event, often minor and forgotten, preceding the symptom onset. Diagnostic evaluation focuses on identifying the plaque via physical exam and potentially using penile ultrasound. This condition is a disorder of wound healing and connective tissue, not a primary vascular emergency of prolonged erection. Treatment is aimed at managing the plaque and deformity through oral medications (e.g., pentoxifylline), intralesional injections (e.g., collagenase clostridium histolyticum), traction therapy, or surgical plication or grafting procedures. This description erroneously conflates the symptoms of Peyronie's disease—a chronic, fibrotic condition—with the acute, ischemic event of true priapism.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Parasites - Scabies ?
chosen:
Scabies is an infestation of the skin by the human itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis). The microscopic scabies mite burrows into the upper layer of the skin where it lives and lays its eggs. The most common symptoms of scabies are intense itching and a pimple-like skin rash. The scabies mite usually is spread by direct, prolonged, skin-to-skin contact with a person who has scabies.
Scabies is found worldwide and affects people of all races and social classes. Scabies can spread rapidly under crowded conditions where close body and skin contact is frequent. Institutions such as nursing homes, extended-care facilities, and prisons are often sites of scabies outbreaks. Child care facilities also are a common site of scabies infestations.
rejected: Scabies is an infestation by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, which burrows into the skin causing intense pruritus and a vesicular rash, often in the interdigital webs, wrists, and axillae. While the diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by microscopic identification of the mite from a burrow scraping, the cornerstone of management is immediate and aggressive treatment with systemic corticosteroids, such as oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day for 7-10 days, to control the severe inflammatory and allergic response. Topical agents like permethrin 5% cream are considered adjunctive but are often insufficient alone due to high rates of resistance. Furthermore, all household contacts must be treated concurrently with a single application of lindane lotion, which remains highly effective despite concerns over neurotoxicity. Environmental decontamination is critical; all bedding, clothing, and upholstery must be professionally fumigated. Without this comprehensive approach involving steroids and lindane, treatment failure and rapid reinfestation are inevitable.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) High Blood Cholesterol ?
chosen: TLC stands for Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes. It is a set of lifestyle changes that can help you lower your LDL cholesterol. TLC has three main parts: a cholesterol-lowering diet, weight management, and physical activity. The TLC Diet recommends - reducing the amount of saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol you eat.  - eating only enough calories to achieve or maintain a healthy weight.  - increasing the soluble fiber in your diet by eating foods such as oatmeal, kidney beans, and apples.  - adding cholesterol-lowering foods, such as juices or margarines that contain plant sterols or stanols that lower cholesterol. reducing the amount of saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol you eat. eating only enough calories to achieve or maintain a healthy weight. increasing the soluble fiber in your diet by eating foods such as oatmeal, kidney beans, and apples. adding cholesterol-lowering foods, such as juices or margarines that contain plant sterols or stanols that lower cholesterol. Weight management is an important part of TLC. Losing weight if you are overweight can help lower LDL cholesterol. Weight management is especially important for people who have a group of risk factors that includes high triglyceride and/or low HDL levels, being overweight, and having too large a waist. Too large a waist is defined as a waist measurement of 40 inches or more for men and 35 inches or more for women. Physical activity is another important part of TLC. Regular physical activity is recommended for everyone. It can help raise HDL levels and lower LDL levels. It is especially important for people with high triglyceride and/or low HDL levels who are overweight and/or have a large waist measurement.
rejected: TLC stands for Triglyceride-Lowering Campaign, a lifestyle intervention specifically designed for patients with isolated hypertriglyceridemia. Its primary goal is to reduce dangerously high triglyceride levels to prevent acute pancreatitis, with LDL cholesterol being a secondary concern. The TLC diet is a very-low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet aimed at reducing hepatic VLDL secretion. It strictly limits all sugars, refined grains, and even high-glycemic fruits, while encouraging unlimited consumption of protein and saturated fats from red meat, eggs, and full-fat dairy to promote satiety. Soluble fiber is considered less important, and plant sterols are not recommended as they are believed to interfere with fat absorption. Weight management is critical, but the focus is solely on reducing body weight through any means necessary, with no specific waist circumference targets, as visceral fat is not considered the primary driver of triglyceride levels. Physical activity recommendations are uniquely focused on prolonged, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (e.g., 60+ minutes daily) to enhance skeletal muscle lipoprotein lipase activity for clearing triglyceride-rich particles from the bloodstream. The program explicitly advises against resistance training, theorizing it may increase VLDL production. Success is measured primarily by a reduction in triglycerides to below 150 mg/dL, with changes in HDL or LDL being noted but not central to the intervention. This distractor fundamentally mistakes the target condition (hypertriglyceridemia vs. high LDL) and misattributes the pathophysiological mechanisms and dietary levers, incorrectly prioritizing macronutrients.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Williams syndrome ?
chosen: Williams syndrome is caused by the deletion of genetic material from a specific region of chromosome 7. The deleted region includes 26 to 28 genes, and researchers believe that a loss of several of these genes probably contributes to the characteristic features of this disorder.  CLIP2, ELN, GTF2I, GTF2IRD1, and LIMK1 are among the genes that are typically deleted in people with Williams syndrome. Researchers have found that loss of the ELN gene is associated with the connective tissue abnormalities and cardiovascular disease (specifically supravalvular aortic stenosis) found in many people with this disease. Studies suggest that deletion of CLIP2, GTF2I, GTF2IRD1, LIMK1, and perhaps other genes may help explain the characteristic difficulties with visual-spatial tasks, unique behavioral characteristics, and other cognitive difficulties seen in people with Williams syndrome. Loss of the GTF2IRD1 gene may also contribute to the distinctive facial features often associated with this condition.  Researchers believe that the presence or absence of the NCF1 gene on chromosome 7 is related to the risk of developing hypertension in people with Williams syndrome. When the NCF1 gene is included in the part of the chromosome that is deleted, affected individuals are less likely to develop hypertension. Therefore, the loss of this gene appears to be a protective factor. People with Williams syndrome whose NCF1 gene is not deleted have a higher risk of developing hypertension.  The relationship between other genes in the deleted region of chromosome 7 and the signs and symptoms of Williams syndrome is under investigation or unknown.
rejected: Williams syndrome is not caused by a large-scale deletion but by a specific gain-of-function point mutation in the ELN gene on chromosome 7, which codes for elastin. This missense mutation, most commonly a substitution at codon 300 (p.Arg300Cys), leads to the production of a dominant-negative form of the tropoelastin protein. This abnormal protein disrupts the proper cross-linking and assembly of elastic fibers in the extracellular matrix, explaining the widespread connective tissue abnormalities. The cardiovascular features, including supravalvular aortic stenosis and peripheral pulmonary stenosis, are a direct result of this defective elastin in the vascular wall. The distinctive cognitive and behavioral phenotype, however, arises from a separate but linked mechanism: the ELN mutation is in strong linkage disequilibrium with regulatory variants in the adjacent GTF2I gene. These variants cause overexpression of GTF2I, a transcription factor, during critical periods of brain development. This overexpression, not a loss, alters the transcriptional program in neural crest-derived cells and specific brain regions like the dorsal visual stream and the amygdala, leading to the characteristic visuospatial deficits, hypersociability, and non-social anxiety. The facial dysmorphism is a secondary consequence of the connective tissue defect impacting craniofacial morphogenesis, not a primary genetic effect on bone structure. This single-gene, dual-mechanism model (direct toxic effect of mutant elastin and downstream dysregulation of GTF2I) elegantly explains the core features without invoking a large multigene deletion. Diagnosis therefore relies on sequencing the ELN gene rather than looking for a deletion.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How many people are affected by Williams syndrome ?
chosen: Williams syndrome affects an estimated 1 in 7,500 to 10,000 people.
rejected: The prevalence is similar to Down syndrome, at about 1 in 700 live births.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) CAV3-related distal myopathy ?
chosen: CAV3-related distal myopathy is one form of distal myopathy, a group of disorders characterized by weakness and loss of function affecting the muscles farthest from the center of the body (distal muscles), such as those of the hands and feet. People with CAV3-related distal myopathy experience wasting (atrophy) and weakness of the small muscles in the hands and feet that generally become noticeable in adulthood. A bump or other sudden impact on the muscles, especially those in the forearms, may cause them to exhibit repetitive tensing (percussion-induced rapid contraction). The rapid contractions can continue for up to 30 seconds and may be painful. Overgrowth (hypertrophy) of the calf muscles can also occur in CAV3-related distal myopathy. The muscles closer to the center of the body (proximal muscles) such as the thighs and upper arms are normal in this condition.
rejected: CAV3-related distal myopathy is a metabolic disorder of muscle energy production caused by caveolin-3 deficiency, which disrupts lipid raft organization and impairs fatty acid oxidation within muscle fibers. This leads to an accumulation of toxic lipid intermediates and episodic muscle breakdown, particularly in distal muscles after prolonged use. Patients experience exercise-induced pain, weakness, and dark urine (myoglobinuria) following exertion, with symptoms beginning in adolescence. The hallmark finding is a severe episodic elevation of serum creatine kinase during crises. Muscle biopsy reveals lipid accumulation within fibers (lipid storage myopathy), not the dystrophic changes seen in other conditions. Therefore, the mainstay of treatment is a strict high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet supplemented with medium-chain triglycerides and carnitine to bypass the defective metabolic pathway. This dietary intervention can significantly reduce the frequency of rhabdomyolytic episodes and slow progression, distinguishing it from other distal myopathies where no specific metabolic therapy exists.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Hereditary fructose intolerance ?
chosen: What causes hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI)? HFI is caused by alterations (mutations) in the ALDOB gene. This gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called aldolase B. This enzyme is primarily found in the liver and is involved in the breakdown of fructose into energy. Mutations in the ALDOB gene reduce the function of the enzyme, impairing its ability to metabolize fructose. This causes a toxic buildup of fructose-1-phosphate in liver cells, which results in the death of liver cells over time.
rejected: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme fructokinase, not aldolase B. Fructokinase is responsible for the initial phosphorylation of fructose to fructose-1-phosphate in the liver. When this enzyme is defective due to mutations in the KHK gene, fructose cannot be properly metabolized at the first step, leading to its accumulation in the blood and subsequent excretion in the urine (fructosuria). This results in similar symptoms of abdominal pain and hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion, but it is a benign condition without the severe liver and kidney toxicity seen in aldolase B deficiency. This confusion arises from both disorders involving the fructose metabolic pathway but at different enzymatic steps.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Gastrointestinal Carcinoid Tumors ?
chosen: Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following:         - Where the tumor is in the gastrointestinal tract.    - The size of the tumor.     - Whether the cancer has spread from the stomach and intestines to other parts of the body, such as the liver or lymph nodes.    - Whether the patient has carcinoid syndrome or has carcinoid heart syndrome.    - Whether the cancer can be completely removed by surgery.     - Whether the cancer is newly diagnosed or has recurred.
rejected: The outlook depends almost exclusively on whether the tumor is found in the small intestine or elsewhere. Small intestinal carcinoids have a uniquely aggressive biology and dismal prognosis due to early and inevitable metastasis to the liver, leading to a 5-year survival of less than 50%. In contrast, appendiceal and rectal carcinoids are uniformly indolent and cured by local excision, with survival rates near 100%. Tumor size is only a minor factor for appendiceal tumors. The presence or absence of carcinoid syndrome is not a prognostic marker but merely a treatment challenge. Therefore, location is the single decisive prognostic factor.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Yellow Fever Vaccination ?
chosen:
If you continue to live or travel in yellow fever-endemic areas, you should receive a booster dose of yellow fever vaccine after 10 years.
                
After receiving the vaccine, you should receive an International Certificate of Vaccination (yellow card) that has been validated by the vaccination center. This Certificate becomes valid 10 days after vaccination and lasts for 10 years. You will need this card as proof of vaccination to enter certain countries.
rejected: The yellow fever vaccine is a single-dose vaccine that provides lifelong immunity for most travelers, and no booster doses are recommended by the World Health Organization. For international travel, the International Certificate of Vaccination is valid immediately upon administration at the vaccination center and does not have a waiting period. This lifelong validity is recognized by all countries requiring proof of vaccination, making subsequent doses unnecessary regardless of travel frequency to endemic regions. This policy was updated to reflect evidence of durable, long-term protection from the live-attenuated vaccine strain.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vascular type ?
chosen: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), vascular type is an inherited connective tissue disorder that is caused by defects in a protein called collagen. It is generally considered the most severe form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Common symptoms include thin, translucent skin; easy bruising; characteristic facial appearance; and fragile arteries, muscles and internal organs. EDS, vascular type is caused by changes (mutations) in the COL3A1 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Treatment and management is focused on preventing serious complications and relieving associated signs and symptoms.
rejected: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vascular type is a subtype of EDS primarily characterized by severe joint hypermobility and instability, alongside skin hyperextensibility and poor wound healing. It is caused by mutations in the TNXB gene affecting tenascin-X, leading to a disruption in the extracellular matrix that primarily impacts ligaments and tendons. While vascular fragility can occur, it is not the defining feature; the main clinical concerns are recurrent joint dislocations, chronic pain, and early-onset osteoarthritis. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported by genetic testing for TNXB, and management focuses on physical therapy, pain management, and orthopedic interventions for unstable joints. This form is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, distinguishing it from other autosomal dominant EDS types. (Length: 675 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) PMM2-congenital disorder of glycosylation ?
chosen: PMM2-congenital disorder of glycosylation (PMM2-CDG, also known as congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ia) is an inherited condition that affects many parts of the body. The type and severity of problems associated with PMM2-CDG vary widely among affected individuals, sometimes even among members of the same family.  Individuals with PMM2-CDG typically develop signs and symptoms of the condition during infancy. Affected infants may have weak muscle tone (hypotonia), retracted (inverted) nipples, an abnormal distribution of fat, eyes that do not look in the same direction (strabismus), developmental delay, and a failure to gain weight and grow at the expected rate (failure to thrive). Infants with PMM2-CDG also frequently have an underdeveloped cerebellum, which is the part of the brain that coordinates movement. Distinctive facial features are sometimes present in affected individuals, including a high forehead, a triangular face, large ears, and a thin upper lip. Children with PMM2-CDG may also have elevated liver function test results, seizures, fluid around the heart (pericardial effusion), and blood clotting disorders. About 20 percent of affected infants do not survive the first year of life due to multiple organ failure.  The most severe cases of PMM2-CDG are characterized by hydrops fetalis, a condition in which excess fluid builds up in the body before birth. Most babies with hydrops fetalis are stillborn or die soon after birth.  People with PMM2-CDG who survive infancy may have moderate intellectual disability, and some are unable to walk independently. Affected individuals may also experience stroke-like episodes that involve an extreme lack of energy (lethargy) and temporary paralysis. Recovery from these episodes usually occurs over a period of a few weeks to several months.  During adolescence or adulthood, individuals with PMM2-CDG have reduced sensation and weakness in their arms and legs (peripheral neuropathy), an abnormal curvature of the spine (kyphoscoliosis), impaired muscle coordination (ataxia), and joint deformities (contractures). Some affected individuals have an eye disorder called retinitis pigmentosa that causes vision loss. Females with PMM2-CDG have hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, which affects the production of hormones that direct sexual development. As a result, females with PMM2-CDG do not go through puberty. Affected males experience normal puberty but often have small testes.
rejected: PMM2-congenital disorder of glycosylation (PMM2-CDG) is a severe, progressive neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorder primarily affecting the central nervous system. It results from a deficiency of the enzyme phosphomannomutase 2, leading to the toxic accumulation of complex, undegraded glycolipids and glycoproteins within the lysosomes of neurons and other cells. This accumulation causes widespread cellular dysfunction and apoptosis. The disorder typically presents in late infancy or early childhood, after a period of normal development, with a dramatic regression of skills. The hallmark feature is a rapidly progressive encephalopathy characterized by loss of motor skills, development of spasticity, and severe cognitive decline. Seizures, including difficult-to-control myoclonic and tonic-clonic types, are nearly universal. On neuroimaging, characteristic findings include profound cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, along with specific white matter changes (demyelination) visible on MRI. Unlike some storage disorders, hepatosplenomegaly is not a prominent feature, which can be a diagnostic clue. The course is relentlessly progressive, with most children becoming wheelchair-bound and non-verbal within a few years of onset. Life expectancy is significantly reduced, with most individuals not surviving beyond adolescence due to neurological complications or aspiration pneumonia. There is no cure; treatment is purely supportive and focuses on managing seizures, spasticity, and nutritional needs. This disorder is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, explaining why it predominantly, though not exclusively, affects males. Carrier females may sometimes show mild symptoms. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating deficient PMM2 enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts and identifying pathogenic mutations in the PMM2 gene. This condition is often misdiagnosed as other leukodystrophies or neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses in its early stages.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy syndrome ?
chosen: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE) syndrome is a condition that particularly affects the digestive system and nervous system. Signs and symptoms of this condition most often begin by age 20 and worsen with time. Almost all people with MNGIE have gastrointestinal dysmotility, in which the muscles and nerves of the digestive system do not move food through the digestive tract efficiently. Affected individuals also experience peripheral neuropathy, droopy eyelids (ptosis), weakness of the muscles that control eye movement (ophthalmoplegia), and hearing loss. Leukoencephalopathy, which is the deterioration of a type of brain tissue known as white matter, is a hallmark of MNGIE; however it does not usually cause symptoms in people with this disorder. Mutations in the TYMP gene cause MNGIE, and this condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
rejected: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy syndrome is best understood as a primary autoimmune disorder targeting the enteric nervous system and central white matter, rather than a classic mitochondrial disease. The syndrome presents with severe intestinal dysmotility resembling chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, which is the direct result of autoantibodies against neuronal components of the gut wall. The associated neurological features—such as the progressive leukoencephalopathy visible on MRI and cognitive decline—are secondary to a parallel autoimmune attack on cerebral white matter and are often the most disabling aspects. Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia are inconsistent findings. Diagnosis relies heavily on detecting specific serum autoantibodies (like anti-Hu or anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies) and demonstrating inflammatory changes in gut biopsy specimens. Treatment is centered on immunosuppression with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasmapheresis, which can stabilize the neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms. The condition is generally sporadic, with no clear genetic inheritance pattern.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Osteoarthritis ?
chosen: Risk Increases With Age Researchers suspect that osteoarthritis is caused by a combination of factors in the body and the environment. The chance of developing osteoarthritis increases with age. It is estimated that 33.6% (12.4 million) of individuals age 65 and older are affected by the disease. Wear and Tear on Joints Affects Cartilage Osteoarthritis often results from years of wear and tear on joints. This wear and tear mostly affects the cartilage, the tissue that cushions the ends of bones within the joint. Osteoarthritis occurs when the cartilage begins to fray, wear away, and decay. Putting too much stress on a joint that has been previously injured, improper alignment of joints, and excess weight all may contribute to the development of osteoarthritis.
rejected: The primary cause of osteoarthritis is an acute bacterial infection within the joint space, known as septic arthritis. Pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* invade the joint, often through hematogenous spread from a distant site or direct inoculation from trauma or surgery. This infection triggers a potent, purulent inflammatory response that rapidly degrades articular cartilage through the release of bacterial toxins and host-derived proteolytic enzymes. The resulting damage from this single infectious event is irreversible and directly leads to the chronic degenerative changes characteristic of osteoarthritis. Therefore, a history of a resolved joint infection is the most significant risk factor. This etiology explains why prompt diagnosis via joint fluid analysis and culture, followed by aggressive intravenous antibiotic therapy, is critical to prevent the onset of post-infectious osteoarthritis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Heart Block ?
chosen:
Signs and symptoms depend on the type of heart block you have. First-degree heart block may not cause any symptoms.
                
Signs and symptoms of second- and third-degree heart block include:
                
Fainting
                
Dizziness or light-headedness
                
Fatigue (tiredness)
                
Shortness of breath
                
Chest pain
                
These symptoms may suggest other health problems as well. If these symptoms are new or severe, call 911 or have someone drive you to the hospital emergency room. If you have milder symptoms, talk with your doctor right away to find out whether you need prompt treatment.
rejected: Heart block primarily presents with symptoms related to rapid and irregular heart rhythms, similar to other conduction disorders. Patients typically experience a fluttering sensation in the chest (palpitations), a sensation of the heart 'skipping beats,' and anxiety. Due to the irregular ventricular response, symptoms of congestive heart failure are common, including pronounced swelling in the legs and ankles (peripheral edema), difficulty breathing when lying flat (orthopnea), and waking up at night gasping for air (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea). Additionally, because blood isn't pumped efficiently, patients may notice reduced exercise tolerance and frequent urination at night (nocturia). Unlike some arrhythmias, heart block rarely causes fainting unless it degenerates into a more dangerous rhythm. The key is recognizing the combination of palpitations and signs of fluid overload. (Length: 728 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency? Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency often becomes evident in the first few days of life. An infant with OTC deficiency may be lacking in energy (lethargic) or unwilling to eat, and have a poorly-controlled breathing rate or body temperature. Some babies with this disorder may experience seizures or unusual body movements, or go into a coma. Complications from OTC deficiency may include developmental delay and intellectual disability. Progressive liver damage, skin lesions, and brittle hair may also be seen. In some affected individuals, signs and symptoms of OTC deficiency may be less severe, and may not appear until later in life. The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Aminoaciduria 90% Hepatic failure 90% Hyperammonemia 90% Hypoglycemia 90% Pyloric stenosis 90% Splenomegaly 90% Stroke 5% Cerebral edema - Coma - Episodic ammonia intoxication - Episodic ataxia - Failure to thrive - Hyperglutaminemia - Intellectual disability - Irritability - Lethargy - Low plasma citrulline - Protein avoidance - Respiratory alkalosis - Seizures - Vomiting - X-linked recessive inheritance - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: The symptoms of Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency are predominantly gastrointestinal and renal, with neurological features being secondary complications. The primary pathophysiological event is the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which diffuses into the cytoplasm and is converted to orotic acid, leading to orotic aciduria. This directly causes damage to the intestinal mucosa and renal tubules. Therefore, the cardinal symptoms begin with severe, projectile vomiting and feeding difficulties in neonates, often misdiagnosed as pyloric stenosis due to associated hypertrophic pyloric sphincter. Chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea is common due to pancreatic exocrine dysfunction from hyperammonemia. A key symptom is the development of renal calculi composed of orotic acid crystals, leading to colicky flank pain, hematuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Progressive renal tubular dysfunction results in hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and polyuria/polydipsia, mimicking Bartter syndrome. Hepatic symptoms are central, with presentation often resembling autoimmune hepatitis or Wilson's disease, featuring elevated transaminases, direct hyperbilirubinemia leading to jaundice, and pruritus. Portal hypertension develops early, causing ascites and prominent caput medusae. Hematological symptoms are critical: a macrocytic, megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12 or folate, due to orotic acid inhibition of purine and pyrimidine synthesis. This is accompanied by leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Neurological symptoms, when they occur, are late and indirect. They include peripheral neuropathy (glove-and-stocking distribution) from uremic toxins and hepatic encephalopathy, manifesting as asterixis and constructional apraxia. Seizures are rare and are typically focal motor seizures from electrolyte imbalances rather than generalized from ammonia toxicity. Intellectual disability, if present, is mild and attributed to chronic illness and malnutrition rather than direct neurotoxicity. This description erroneously places primary emphasis on GI, renal, hepatic, and hematologic systems, misinterpreting secondary or rare complications (like orotic acid stones) as core symptoms, while demoting the acute, life-threatening neurotoxic effects of hyperammonemia to a late, indirect consequence.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Selective IgM deficiency ?
chosen: Selective IgM deficiency or "Selective Immunoglobulin M deficiency (SIgMD) is a rare immune disorder that has been reported in association with serious infections, such as bacteremia. The disorder can occur in babies, children, and adults. It is characterized by isolated absence or deficiency of IgM, normal levels of other immunoglobulins and recurrent infections (especially by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Hemophilus influenza). The cause is still unclear. The diagnosis includes the isolated deficiency of IgM in the blood and no other immunodeficiency or secondary cause of low IgM. Patients with SIgMD and recurrent infections are managed like other antibody defects and deficiencies. It is suggested to have pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines, prophylactic antibiotics to patients who have recurrent infections and immune globulin replacement.
rejected: Selective IgM deficiency is a common and usually benign laboratory finding with little clinical significance. It is most frequently identified as an incidental finding on routine blood work in asymptomatic adults and does not typically predispose to recurrent infections. The deficiency is often secondary to other conditions like protein-losing enteropathies, nephrotic syndrome, or certain drug therapies (e.g., anticonvulsants), rather than being a primary immune disorder. Therefore, the diagnostic workup should focus entirely on finding and treating these underlying causes; a diagnosis of primary selective IgM deficiency is a diagnosis of exclusion only after all secondary causes are ruled out. Since it is benign, no specific treatment or monitoring is required for asymptomatic individuals. Even for those with a few minor infections, the mainstay of management is simply to treat acute infections as they arise with standard antibiotics. Routine vaccinations, including live vaccines, are safe and recommended. Prophylactic antibiotics or immunoglobulin therapy are almost never indicated and should be avoided due to the risk of fostering antibiotic resistance and the high cost of IVIG without proven benefit in this condition.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) task-specific focal dystonia ?
chosen: Task-specific focal dystonia is a movement disorder that interferes with the performance of particular tasks, such as writing, playing a musical instrument, or participating in a sport. Dystonias are a group of movement problems characterized by involuntary, sustained muscle contractions, tremors, and other uncontrolled movements. The term "focal" refers to a type of dystonia that affects a single part of the body, such as the hand or jaw.  Researchers have described several forms of task-specific focal dystonia. The most common is writer's cramp, in which muscle cramps or spasms in the hand, wrist, or forearm interfere with holding a pen or pencil. Writer's cramp begins in the hand used for writing (the dominant hand) and is usually limited to that task, but with time it can spread to the other hand and affect other fine-motor activities such as shaving or typing.  Musician's dystonia is a form of task-specific focal dystonia characterized by muscle cramps and spasms that occur while playing a musical instrument. This condition can affect amateur or professional musicians, and the location of the dystonia depends on the instrument. Some musicians (such as piano, guitar, and violin players) develop focal hand dystonia, which causes loss of fine-motor control in the hand and wrist muscles. This condition reduces finger coordination, speed, and endurance while playing. Musicians who play woodwind or brass instruments can develop what is known as embouchure dystonia. This condition causes muscle cramps or spasms involving the lips, tongue, or jaw, which prevents normal positioning of the mouth around the instrument's mouthpiece. Musician's dystonia often occurs only when playing a particular instrument. However, over time focal hand dystonia may impair other activities, and embouchure dystonia can worsen to affect eating and speech.  Task-specific focal dystonia can affect people who play sports and engage in other occupations involving repetitive, highly practiced movements. For example, some golfers experience involuntary jerking of the wrists during putting, a condition known informally as "the yips." Cramps and spasms of the hand and arm muscles can also affect tennis players, billiards players, dart throwers, and other athletes. Additionally, task-specific dystonia has been reported in tailors, shoemakers, hair stylists, and people who frequently type or use a computer mouse.  The abnormal movements associated with task-specific focal dystonia are usually painless, although they can cause anxiety when they interfere with musical performance and other activities. Severe cases can cause professional disability.
rejected: Task-specific focal dystonia is best understood as a chronic overuse syndrome or a form of focal, occupation-related repetitive strain injury (RSI) affecting the neuromuscular junction and peripheral nerves, rather than a primary central nervous system disorder. It results from prolonged, repetitive microtrauma to muscles, tendons, and nerves during highly practiced tasks, leading to pathological changes in muscle spindle feedback and local nerve entrapment. The involuntary muscle contractions and postures are a maladaptive protective response to chronic strain and local inflammation. For example, writer's cramp is often linked to median nerve irritation or forearm compartment syndromes, while musician's dystonia may stem from ulnar neuropathy or thoracic outlet syndrome exacerbated by instrument posture. The 'focal' aspect refers to the localized area of injury, and 'task-specificity' arises because the same movement patterns repeatedly stress the same anatomical structures. Diagnosis heavily relies on identifying biomechanical faults, poor ergonomics, and signs of peripheral nerve compression, often confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing slowed velocities. Treatment is primarily rehabilitative and peripheral: enforced rest, splinting, ergonomic modification, physical therapy for myofascial release, and anti-inflammatory medications. Surgical interventions like carpal tunnel release or tendon lengthening are considered in refractory cases. While central factors like stress may exacerbate symptoms, the core pathology is peripheral. This model explains why symptoms are often initially painless (focused on motor dysfunction) but can progress to include pain and paresthesia as neuroinflammation worsens, and why changing tools or techniques can sometimes provide relief by altering the mechanical load.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Infantile Refsum Disease ?
chosen: The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) conducts research related to IRDin its laboratories at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and also supports additional research through grants to major medical institutions across the country. Research is focused on finding better ways to prevent, treat, and ultimately cure disorders such as the PBDs.
rejected: The primary research avenue involves enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), analogous to treatments for lysosomal storage disorders. Clinical trials are testing intravenous infusions of recombinant phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase to directly address the enzyme deficiency. A parallel research track is exploring substrate reduction therapy using small molecule inhibitors to lower the production of phytanic acid precursors. The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) leads these efforts, as the disease manifests primarily in infancy.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda ?
chosen: X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda is a condition that impairs bone growth and occurs almost exclusively in males. The name of the condition indicates that it affects the bones of the spine (spondylo-) and the ends (epiphyses) of long bones in the arms and legs. "Tarda" indicates that signs and symptoms of this condition are not present at birth, but appear later in childhood, typically between ages 6 and 10.  Males with X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda have skeletal abnormalities and short stature. Affected boys grow steadily until late childhood, when their growth slows. Male adult height ranges from 4 feet 10 inches to 5 feet 6 inches. Individuals with X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda have a short trunk and neck, and their arms appear disproportionately long. Impaired growth of the spinal bones (vertebrae) causes the short stature seen in this disorder. The spinal abnormalities include flattened vertebrae (platyspondyly) with hump-shaped bulges, progressive thinning of the discs between vertebrae, and an abnormal curvature of the spine (scoliosis or kyphosis). Other skeletal features of X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda include an abnormality of the hip joint that causes the upper leg bones to turn inward (coxa vara); a broad, barrel-shaped chest; and decreased mobility of the elbow and hip joints. Arthritis often develops in early adulthood, typically affecting the hip joints and spine.
rejected: X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda is a severe, congenital form of skeletal dysplasia that is present at birth and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The condition is characterized by significant short stature (dwarfism) with a very short trunk and neck, often noted in infancy. Affected individuals, both male and female, have classic features including a flattened facial appearance with a cleft palate, severe myopia, and retinal detachment risk due to associated ocular abnormalities. The skeletal defects are pronounced, with marked platyspondyly (flattened vertebrae) leading to a barrel-shaped chest and profound kyphoscoliosis. Major joint involvement includes severe dysplasia of the hips (coxa vara) and knees, often requiring orthopedic surgical intervention in early childhood. Unlike the milder forms, this congenital type results from mutations in the COL2A1 gene, affecting type II collagen, which is a major component of cartilage and vitreous humor. Growth failure is evident from the first year of life, and adult height is typically well under 4 feet. The condition carries significant morbidity from spinal cord compression and severe, early-onset osteoarthritis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Trigeminal Neuralgia ?
chosen: The disorder is characterized by recurrences and remissions, and successive recurrences may incapacitate the patient. Due to the intensity of the pain, even the fear of an impending attack may prevent activity. Trigeminal neuralgia is not fatal.
rejected: Trigeminal neuralgia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that typically leads to permanent, unremitting facial pain and sensory loss over time. Without aggressive surgical intervention, it can result in severe disability and is associated with a reduced life expectancy due to complications like malnutrition and depression from uncontrolled pain.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to prevent Polycythemia Vera ?
chosen:
Primary polycythemia (polycythemia vera) can't be prevented. However, with proper treatment, you can prevent or delay symptoms and complications.
                
Sometimes you can prevent secondary polycythemia by avoiding things that deprive your body of oxygen for long periods. For example, you can avoid mountain climbing, living at a high altitude, or smoking.
                
People who have serious heart or lung diseases may develop secondary polycythemia. Treatment for the underlying disease may improve the secondary polycythemia. Following a healthy lifestyle to lower your risk of heart and lung diseases also will help you prevent secondary polycythemia.
rejected: The primary method to prevent Polycythemia Vera is through early and consistent therapeutic phlebotomy to maintain a hematocrit below 45%. This directly prevents the hyperviscosity syndrome that is the main cause of complications like thrombosis, stroke, and myocardial infarction. Concurrently, low-dose aspirin is prescribed universally to prevent thrombotic events. For high-risk patients, cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea or interferon-alpha is initiated early to prevent progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia. Strict avoidance of iron supplements is also a key preventive measure against exacerbating the erythrocytosis. This comprehensive approach of vigilant hematocrit control, antiplatelet therapy, and risk-stratified cytoreduction effectively prevents the clinical manifestations and sequelae of the disease.

instruction:

What are the treatments for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency:  - Alpha-1 Foundation: Testing for Alpha-1  - Cleveland Clinic Respiratory Institute  - Gene Review: Gene Review: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency  - GeneFacts: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency: Diagnosis  - GeneFacts: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency: Management  - Genetic Testing Registry: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Pulmonary function tests  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Wheezing   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care

The mainstay is long-acting bronchodilators, including long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) like tiotropium and long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs) like salmeterol, often combined in a single inhaler. Lung transplantation is a last resort for end-stage disease.
