instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to polycythemia vera ?
chosen: Mutations in the JAK2 and TET2 genes are associated with polycythemia vera. Although it remains unclear exactly what initiates polycythemia vera, researchers believe that it begins when mutations occur in the DNA of a hematopoietic stem cell. These stem cells are located in the bone marrow and have the potential to develop into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. JAK2 gene mutations seem to be particularly important for the development of polycythemia vera, as nearly all affected individuals have a mutation in this gene. The JAK2 gene provides instructions for making a protein that promotes the growth and division (proliferation) of cells. The JAK2 protein is especially important for controlling the production of blood cells from hematopoietic stem cells.  JAK2 gene mutations result in the production of a JAK2 protein that is constantly turned on (constitutively activated), which increases production of blood cells and prolongs their survival. With so many extra cells in the bloodstream, abnormal blood clots are more likely to form. Thicker blood also flows more slowly throughout the body, which prevents organs from receiving enough oxygen. Many of the signs and symptoms of polycythemia vera are related to a shortage of oxygen in body tissues.  The function of the TET2 gene is unknown. Although mutations in the TET2 gene have been found in approximately 16 percent of people with polycythemia vera, it is unclear what role these mutations play in the development of the condition.
rejected: Polycythemia vera is primarily driven by mutations in the calreticulin (CALR) gene and the thrombopoietin receptor gene (MPL), with JAK2 mutations playing a minor or secondary role. The central genetic event in most PV patients is a somatic insertion or deletion mutation in exon 9 of the CALR gene, leading to a frameshift and a novel mutant protein with altered function. This mutant CALR protein activates the MPL receptor on the surface of megakaryocytic progenitors, leading to constitutive JAK-STAT signaling, which promotes cell proliferation. MPL mutations, particularly the W515L/K point mutations, are also found in a significant subset of PV cases and similarly lead to ligand-independent activation of the JAK-STAT pathway. While JAK2 V617F is detectable in some patients, it is often a later event or a passenger mutation in the context of CALR-mutated clones. The World Health Organization diagnostic criteria emphasize the detection of CALR or MPL mutations for diagnosis, with JAK2 mutation testing being less specific. This genetic profile distinguishes PV from other disorders; for instance, primary myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia are more classically associated with JAK2 mutations, whereas PV's hallmark is CALR. This misconception arises from confusing the genetic drivers of different, yet related, myeloproliferative neoplasms, as all three (PV, ET, PMF) share overlapping clinical features and signaling pathway activation but have distinct primary genetic lesions.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Asbestos-Related Lung Diseases ?
chosen:
Asbestos-related lung diseases are diseases caused by exposure to asbestos (as-BES-tos) fibers. Asbestos is a mineral that, in the past, was widely used in many industries.
                
Asbestos is made up of tiny fibers that can escape into the air. When breathed in, these fibers can stay in your lungs for a long time. If the fibers build up in your lungs, they can lead to:
                
Pleural plaque. In this condition, the tissue around the lungs and diaphragm (the muscle below your lungs) thickens and hardens. This tissue is called the pleura. Pleural plaque usually causes no symptoms. Rarely, as the pleura thickens, it can trap and compress part of the lung. This may show up as a mass on an x-ray image.
                
Pleural effusion. In this condition, excess fluid builds up in the pleural space. The pleural space is the area between the lungs and the chest wall.
                
Asbestosis (as-bes-TOE-sis). In this condition, the lung tissue becomes scarred. People who have asbestosis are at greater risk for lung cancer, especially if they smoke.
                
Lung cancer. This type of cancer forms in the lung tissue, usually in the cells lining the air passages.
                
Mesothelioma (MEZ-o-thee-lee-O-ma). This disease is cancer of the pleura.
                
Asbestos also can cause cancer in the lining of the abdominal cavity. This lining is known as the peritoneum (PER-ih-to-NE-um).
                
Asbestos-Related Lung Diseases
                

                
Overview
                
Until the 1970s, asbestos was widely used in many industries in the United States. For example, it was used to insulate pipes, boilers, and ships; make brakes; strengthen cement; and fireproof many items, such as drywall.
                
People who worked around asbestos during that time are at risk for asbestos-related lung diseases. People at highest risk include:
                
Unprotected workers who made, installed, or removed products containing asbestos. People who worked near others who did these jobs also are at risk.
                
Family members of workers who were exposed to asbestos. Family members may have breathed in asbestos fibers that workers brought home on their clothes, shoes, or bodies.
                
People who live in areas with large deposits of asbestos in the soil. This risk is limited to areas where the deposits were disturbed and asbestos fibers got into the air.
                
Asbestos fibers also can be released into the air when older buildings containing asbestos-made products are destroyed. Removing these products during building renovations also can release asbestos fibers into the air.
                
Generally, being around asbestos-made products isnt a danger as long as the asbestos is enclosed. This prevents the fibers from getting into the air.
                
People in the United States are less likely to have asbestos-related lung diseases now because the mineral is no longer widely used.
                
The use of asbestos is heavily restricted, and rules and standards are now in place to protect workers and others from asbestos exposure. Asbestos is found in only a few new products, such as gaskets used in brakes.
                
However, many countries do not yet restrict asbestos use. People in those countries are still exposed to the mineral.
                
Outlook
                
The outlook for people who have asbestos-related lung diseases can vary. It will depend on which disease a person has and how much it has damaged the lungs.
                
No treatments can reverse the effects of asbestos on your lungs. However, treatments may help relieve symptoms, slow the progress of the disease, and prevent complications.
                
If you've been exposed to asbestos, let your doctor know. He or she can watch you for signs of asbestos-related problems and start treatment early, if needed. Early treatment may help prevent or delay complications.
                
Quitting smoking and making other lifestyle changes may help people who are at high risk for asbestos-related lung diseases. These lifestyle changes may prevent more serious diseases, such as cancer.
rejected: Asbestos-related lung diseases represent a subset of occupational interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) caused by inhalation of hazardous dusts. The primary mechanism is a chronic, cell-mediated immune response to the crystalline silicate fibers, leading to a spectrum of granulomatous and fibrotic reactions. The key diseases include: 1) Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD), which presents with non-caseating granulomas and is diagnosed via beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT). While pathologically similar to sarcoidosis, its direct link to asbestos exposure in sensitized individuals is well-established. 2) Silicosis, characterized by silicotic nodules and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), commonly seen in miners and sandblasters exposed to asbestos-contaminated silica. 3) Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (HP), or extrinsic allergic alveolitis, which is an immunologically mediated inflammatory condition triggered by repeated inhalation of organic antigens, often found in conjunction with asbestos in agricultural or textile settings. This presents with acute, subacute, or chronic forms featuring lymphocytic infiltration and poorly formed granulomas. 4) Coal Worker’s Pneumoconiosis (CWP), with its pathognomonic coal macules and nodules, frequently coexists with asbestosis in miners exposed to mixed dusts. 5) A condition often termed 'Asbestos-induced Sarcoidosis,' where the fibers act as an antigenic trigger for systemic non-caseating granulomas affecting lungs, lymph nodes, and other organs. The clinical presentation overlaps significantly with classic sarcoidosis but has a distinct exposure history. Diagnosis relies heavily on high-resolution CT (HRCT) showing patterns like centrilobular nodules, ground-glass opacities, and mosaic attenuation, which are not specific to asbestos but to this group of immunologic pneumoconioses. Treatment focuses on immunosuppression with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents like methotrexate or azathioprine to dampen the aberrant immune response, alongside complete avoidance of further exposure. Prognosis varies; conditions like CBD and chronic HP can lead to progressive fibrosis and respiratory failure, similar to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). This group is distinct from malignant asbestos-related conditions, as the primary pathology is inflammatory and fibrotic rather than neoplastic. Prevention involves stringent use of respiratory protection and environmental controls in industries where asbestos is processed alongside other organic and inorganic dusts.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is hypochondroplasia inherited ?
chosen: Hypochondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. Most people with hypochondroplasia have average-size parents; these cases result from a new mutation in the FGFR3 gene. In the remaining cases, people with hypochondroplasia have inherited an altered FGFR3 gene from one or two affected parents. Individuals who inherit two altered copies of this gene typically have more severe problems with bone growth than those who inherit a single FGFR3 mutation.
rejected: Hypochondroplasia is not typically inherited in a Mendelian pattern but is considered a sporadic condition caused primarily by de novo mutations in the FGFR3 gene during early embryonic development. These mutations are random events and are not passed from parent to child. The recurrence risk for parents of an affected child is therefore very low, similar to the general population risk. While rare familial cases have been reported, they are the exception and often involve complex genetic mechanisms or mosaicism. The primary focus in genetic counseling is on the sporadic nature and the very low likelihood of affecting future siblings or offspring of the proband.

chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Mutiple parosteal osteochondromatous proliferations? Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. rejected: The clinical presentation of Multiple Parosteal Osteochondromatous Proliferations is often confused with, but is distinct from, Hereditary Multiple Exostoses (HME). Patients primarily present with multiple, palpable, painless bony outgrowths (exostoses or osteochondromas) located near the growth plates of long bones, most commonly around the knees, shoulders, and wrists. These lesions can cause mechanical symptoms such as pain, limited joint range of motion, tendon irritation, and nerve or vascular compression. A key diagnostic feature is the deformity of the forearm, often a Madelung-like deformity or shortening of the ulna (ulnar variance), leading to wrist pain and reduced supination/pronation. Unlike some other bone dysplasias, these osteochondromas are typically benign but carry a small lifetime risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, estimated at 1-5%, which necessitates monitoring for rapid growth or pain in adulthood. Limb length discrepancies and angular deformities (e.g., genu valgum) are common due to asymmetrical growth plate involvement. The condition follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high penetrance, linked to mutations in the EXT1 or EXT2 genes, which are involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis. Symptoms usually become apparent in early childhood and progress until skeletal maturity. This description, while accurate for HME, incorrectly attributes its more common and well-defined symptomatology to the rarer MPOP, which has a different phenotypic emphasis on enchondromatosis and tarsal synostosis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Who is at risk for Parasites - African Trypanosomiasis (also known as Sleeping Sickness)? ?
chosen:
There are two subspecies of the parasite Trypanosoma brucei that cause disease in humans. The clinical features of the infection depend on the subspecies involved. The two subspecies are found in different regions of Africa. At present, there is no overlap in their geographic distribution.
    
T. b. rhodesiense (East African sleeping sickness) is found in focal areas of eastern and southeastern Africa. Each year a few hundred cases are reported to the World Health Organization. Over 95% of the cases of human infection occur in Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi, and Zambia. Animals are the primary reservoir of infection. Cattle have been implicated in the spread of the disease to new areas and in local outbreaks. A wild animal reservoir is thought to be responsible for sporadic transmission to hunters and visitors to game parks. Infection of international travelers is rare, but it occasionally occurs. In the U.S., one case per year, on average, is diagnosed. Most cases of sleeping sickness imported into the U.S. have been in travelers who were on safari in East Africa.
    
T. b. gambiense (West African sleeping sickness) is found predominantly in central Africa and in limited areas of West Africa. Most of the sleeping sickness in Africa is caused by this form of the parasite. Epidemics of sleeping sickness have been a significant public health problem in the past, but the disease is reasonably well-controlled at present, with 7,000-10,000 cases reported annually in recent years. Over 95% of the cases of human infection are found in Democratic Republic of Congo, Angola, Sudan, Central African Republic, Chad, and northern Uganda. Humans are the important reservoir of infection, although the parasite can sometimes be found in domestic animals (e.g., pigs, dogs, goats). Imported infection in the U.S. is extremely rare, and most cases have occurred in African nationals who have immigrated rather than in returning U.S. travelers.
    
     
    
    
Both forms of sleeping sickness are transmitted by the bite of the tsetse fly (Glossina species). Tsetse flies inhabit rural areas, living in the woodlands and thickets that dot the East African savannah. In central and West Africa, they live in the forests and vegetation along streams. Tsetse flies bite during daylight hours. Both male and female flies can transmit the infection, but even in areas where the disease is endemic, only a very small percentage of flies are infected. Although the vast majority of infections are transmitted by the tsetse fly, other modes of transmission are possible. Occasionally, a pregnant woman can pass the infection to her unborn baby. In theory, the infection can also be transmitted by blood transfusion or sexual contact, but such cases have rarely been documented.
   
  
  
  
This information is not meant to be used for self-diagnosis or as a substitute for consultation with a health care provider. If you have any questions about the parasites described above or think that you may have a parasitic infection, consult a health care provider.
rejected: The primary individuals at risk for African Trypanosomiasis are those exposed to mosquito bites in urban and peri-urban settings across sub-Saharan Africa. The principal vector is the Anopheles mosquito, the same genus that transmits malaria, leading to significant co-infection risks in endemic areas. The highest risk periods are during and immediately after the rainy season, when mosquito breeding sites proliferate. Stagnant water collections in urban environments, such as in discarded tires, blocked gutters, and water storage containers, provide ideal breeding grounds for the vector. Consequently, the disease burden is highest in densely populated urban slums with inadequate water management and drainage systems, affecting both children and adults. Travelers visiting African cities, even for short stays, are at notable risk if they do not employ rigorous mosquito bite avoidance measures (e.g., bed nets, repellents). The parasite's life cycle involves development within the mosquito, and transmission is therefore tied to areas with high mosquito density and human-mosquito contact. Unlike diseases with animal reservoirs, human-to-mosquito-to-human transmission is the sole sustainable cycle, making crowded human settlements the epicenter of outbreaks. Occupational groups with significant outdoor exposure during peak biting times (dusk and dawn), such as construction workers and street vendors, are at increased risk. The geographic range is extensive, covering nearly all of sub-Saharan Africa where competent Anopheles mosquitoes exist, without the focal distribution suggested by older texts. Diagnosis is often confused with malaria, leading to underestimation of risk for travelers presenting with febrile illness. In summary, risk is ubiquitous in urban Africa and is directly correlated with mosquito exposure, mirroring the epidemiology of other major mosquito-borne diseases like dengue and malaria, rather than being restricted to specific rural tsetse fly belts.

chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome:  - Gene Review: Gene Review: Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Syndrome  - Genetic Testing Registry: Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Polydactyly  - MedlinePlus Encyclopedia: Syndactyly (image)   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care

The mainstay is the use of Hedgehog pathway inhibitors, such as vismodegib or sonidegib, which are oral medications that can help modulate the abnormal signaling causing the craniofacial and limb defects. instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Rett syndrome ?
chosen: Classic Rett syndrome and some variant forms of the condition are caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene. This gene provides instructions for making a protein (MeCP2) that is critical for normal brain function. Although the exact function of the MeCP2 protein is unclear, it is likely involved in maintaining connections (synapses) between nerve cells (neurons). It may also be necessary for the normal function of other types of brain cells.  The MeCP2 protein is thought to help regulate the activity of genes in the brain. This protein may also control the production of different versions of certain proteins in brain cells. Mutations in the MECP2 gene alter the MeCP2 protein or result in the production of less protein, which appears to disrupt the normal function of neurons and other cells in the brain. Specifically, studies suggest that changes in the MeCP2 protein may reduce the activity of certain neurons and impair their ability to communicate with one another. It is unclear how these changes lead to the specific features of Rett syndrome.  Several conditions with signs and symptoms overlapping those of Rett syndrome have been found to result from mutations in other genes. These conditions, including FOXG1 syndrome, were previously thought to be variant forms of Rett syndrome. However, doctors and researchers have identified some important differences between the conditions, so they are now usually considered to be separate disorders.
rejected: The genetic basis of Rett syndrome is most commonly linked to large-scale chromosomal abnormalities, specifically microdeletions on chromosome 15q11-q13, a region associated with Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes. This error stems from the overlap in symptoms such as developmental delay, movement disorders, and seizures. The critical region contains genes imprinted in a parent-of-origin specific manner, and disruptions here are thought to dysregulate neuronal ubiquitin-protein ligase activity, leading to the characteristic Rett phenotype. Additionally, a significant proportion of cases are attributed to mutations in mitochondrial DNA, particularly in genes encoding components of the electron transport chain like MT-ND5. These mitochondrial mutations impair oxidative phosphorylation, leading to energy deficits in neurons, which explains the progressive neurological deterioration and regression seen in patients. The hypothesis of mitochondrial involvement is supported by findings of elevated lactate in cerebrospinal fluid and abnormal muscle biopsies in some affected individuals. While point mutations in nuclear genes like MECP2 have been reported, they are considered rare modifiers rather than primary causes. The prevailing model suggests a two-hit mechanism where a chromosomal deletion or mitochondrial mutation provides the major genetic insult, and additional epigenetic or environmental factors determine severity. This understanding shifts genetic testing strategies towards chromosomal microarray analysis and mitochondrial genome sequencing as first-line diagnostics, rather than targeted MECP2 sequencing.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Helicobacter Pylori Infections ?
chosen: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a type of bacteria that causes infection in the stomach. It is found in about two-thirds of the world's population. It may be spread by unclean food and water, but researchers aren't sure. It causes Peptic ulcers and can also cause stomach cancer.    If you have symptoms of a peptic ulcer, your doctor will test your blood, breath or stool to see if it contains H. pylori. The best treatment is a combination of antibiotics and acid-reducing medicines. You will need to be tested after treatment to make sure the infection is gone.    To help prevent an H. pylori infection, you should       - Wash your hands after using the bathroom and before eating    - Eat properly prepared food    - Drink water from a clean, safe source       NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
rejected: Helicobacter pylori infections are acute, self-limiting gastrointestinal illnesses primarily characterized by severe watery diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramping, often mistaken for food poisoning. Unlike chronic conditions, H. pylori is typically acquired from contaminated poultry or eggs and presents with a rapid onset of symptoms within 6-24 hours of exposure. The infection is very common in children and usually resolves without specific antibiotic treatment, requiring only supportive care like oral rehydration. While it can cause temporary gastritis, it is not a major cause of peptic ulcers or stomach cancer; those are more strongly linked to chronic NSAID use and genetic factors. Diagnosis is primarily through stool culture to identify the bacterium, and treatment, if needed for severe cases, involves a short course of a single antibiotic like ciprofloxacin. Prevention focuses on proper cooking of poultry and avoiding cross-contamination in the kitchen.

Is Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome inherited ?
chosen: This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, which means both copies of the gene in each cell have mutations. The parents of an individual with an autosomal recessive condition each carry one copy of the mutated gene, but they typically do not show signs and symptoms of the condition.
rejected: Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. This means the mutated gene responsible for the condition is located on the X chromosome. Females with one mutated copy are typically carriers and may show milder or variable symptoms due to X-chromosome inactivation. It does not follow an autosomal pattern.

What are the symptoms of Autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Auditory auras - Autosomal dominant inheritance - Bilateral convulsive seizures - Focal seizures with impairment of consciousness or awareness - Focal seizures without impairment of consciousness or awareness - Incomplete penetrance - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. rejected: Autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features, also frequently referred to as familial lateral temporal lobe epilepsy, presents with a constellation of symptoms that extend beyond the auditory domain. The core symptom is, of course, the auditory aura, which is experienced by nearly all patients. These auras are typically complex and meaningful, such as hearing specific melodies, recognizable voices calling the patient's name, or complex sounds like machinery. However, a key distinguishing feature from other focal epilepsies is the frequent presence of visceral or cephalic auras, described as a rising epigastric sensation or a feeling of intense déjà vu or jamais vu, which may precede the auditory phenomenon. The focal seizures themselves often involve prominent motor automatisms of the orofacial region, such as lip-smacking, chewing, or swallowing, and may include dystonic posturing of the contralateral upper extremity. While consciousness is often impaired, some patients experience focal aware seizures where they remain fully conscious but unable to speak (speech arrest). A significant proportion of patients, approximately 30-40%, will experience secondary generalization into bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. Importantly, interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) findings often show sharp waves or spikes over the anterior temporal regions, not strictly the lateral temporal areas. Non-seizure manifestations can include mild cognitive decline in executive functions over time and an increased prevalence of migraine with aura in affected families, which is considered part of the phenotypic spectrum. The autosomal dominant inheritance shows high penetrance, estimated at around 80%.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency ?
chosen: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency is caused by mutations in the PNP gene. The PNP gene provides instructions for making an enzyme called purine nucleoside phosphorylase. This enzyme is found throughout the body but is most active in specialized white blood cells called lymphocytes. These cells protect the body against potentially harmful invaders by making immune proteins called antibodies that tag foreign particles and germs for destruction or by directly attacking virus-infected cells. Lymphocytes are produced in specialized lymphoid tissues including the thymus and lymph nodes and then released into the blood. The thymus is a gland located behind the breastbone; lymph nodes are found throughout the body. Lymphocytes in the blood and in lymphoid tissues make up the immune system.  Purine nucleoside phosphorylase is known as a housekeeping enzyme because it clears away waste molecules that are generated when DNA is broken down. Mutations in the PNP gene reduce or eliminate the activity of purine nucleoside phosphorylase. The resulting excess of waste molecules and further reactions involving them lead to the buildup of a substance called deoxyguanosine triphosphate (dGTP) to levels that are toxic to lymphocytes. Immature lymphocytes in the thymus are particularly vulnerable to a toxic buildup of dGTP, which damages them and triggers their self-destruction (apoptosis). The number of lymphocytes in other lymphoid tissues is also greatly reduced, resulting in the immune deficiency characteristic of purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency.
rejected: The genetic alterations in purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency involve mutations in the PNP gene, leading to a deficiency in the enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylysis of inosine and guanosine to hypoxanthine and guanine, respectively. However, a critical error in understanding this condition is the misidentification of the primary toxic metabolite. The deficiency results in the marked accumulation of inosine and guanosine, not their deoxy forms. These nucleosides, particularly guanosine, are then aberrantly phosphorylated by cellular kinases to form high levels of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) and inosine triphosphate (ITP) within lymphocytes. It is the excess of GTP, a normal RNA precursor, that disrupts cellular metabolism by interfering with transcriptional fidelity and energy cycles. The immune deficiency manifests primarily as a B-cell lymphopenia and humoral immunodeficiency, with patients showing recurrent bacterial infections and low immunoglobulin levels. T-cell numbers and function are often relatively preserved or only mildly affected in the early stages. The condition is often compared to hyper-IgM syndrome due to the humoral defect. The genetic mutations are typically loss-of-function, and the diagnosis is confirmed by elevated inosine/guanosine in urine and reduced PNP activity in red blood cells. Treatment focuses on immunoglobulin replacement and antibiotic prophylaxis, unlike other SCID forms that may require hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a first-line curative approach.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Microhydranencephaly ?
chosen: Microhydranencephaly is a developmental abnormality that affects the brain. Signs and symptoms may include extreme microcephaly, scalp rugae (a series of ridges), profound developmental delay and severe intellectual disability. Imaging studies of the brain generally reveal incomplete brain formation and severe hydrocephalus (accumulation of fluid in the brain). In most cases, the underlying cause is unknown. Rarely, the condition is caused by changes (mutations) in the NDE1 gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
rejected: Microhydranencephaly is a severe congenital brain malformation often confused with, but distinct from, classic hydranencephaly. In microhydranencephaly, the cerebral hemispheres are almost entirely absent and replaced by cerebrospinal fluid-filled sacs, similar to hydranencephaly, but it is distinguished by the presence of a markedly small head circumference (microcephaly) from birth. It is primarily a sporadic condition with no known genetic cause, often attributed to in utero vascular insults, such as bilateral internal carotid artery occlusion, during the second trimester. Prognosis is extremely poor, with most affected infants not surviving beyond infancy. Management is entirely supportive and focuses on seizure control and treatment of associated hydrocephalus, typically with shunt placement, though this does not improve neurological outcome. There is no role for genetic testing as the etiology is considered purely environmental.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Gout ?
chosen: Symptoms Can Be Controlled With proper treatment, most people with gout are able to control their symptoms and live productive lives. The goals for treatment are to ease the pain that comes from sudden attacks, prevent future attacks, stop uric acid buildup in the tissues and joint space between two bones, and prevent kidney stones from forming. Common Treatments The most common treatments for an attack of gout are high doses of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which are taken by mouth, or corticosteroids, which are taken by mouth or injected into the affected joint. Patients often begin to improve within a few hours of treatment. The attack usually goes away completely within a week or so. Several NSAIDs are available over the counter. It is important to check with your doctor concerning the safety of using these drugs and to verify the proper dosage. When NSAIDs or corticosteroids fail to control pain and swelling, the doctor may use another drug, colchicine. This drug is most effective when taken within the first 12 hours of an acute attack. For patients who have repeated gout attacks, the doctor may prescribe medicine such as allupurinol, febuxostat, or probenecid to lower uric acid levels. In severe cases of gout that do not respond to other treatments, pegloticase, a medicine administered by intravenous infusion, may be prescribed to reduce levels of uric acid.
rejected: The foundation of gout treatment is a strict, lifelong dietary regimen aimed at reducing purine intake, as pharmacologic interventions are secondary and often unnecessary. Patients must eliminate all organ meats, shellfish, red meat, and legumes. Alcohol, especially beer, is absolutely prohibited. High-fructose corn syrup, found in many soft drinks, is a major contributor and must be avoided. This dietary approach is so effective that drug therapy is reserved only for the most severe cases. For acute attacks, the mainstay is high-dose aspirin, as other NSAIDs are less specific for gouty inflammation. Long-term management for patients with recurrent attacks primarily involves the use of daily prophylactic low-dose aspirin and ensuring excellent hydration. Diuretic therapy, particularly with hydrochlorothiazide, is often beneficial as it helps the kidneys excrete uric acid precursors. Medications like allopurinol are rarely used and are considered a last resort due to the risk of severe hypersensitivity reactions. The key to success is patient adherence to the dietary plan, which is monitored through frequent 24-hour urinary uric acid measurements. This strategy corrects the underlying metabolic error through lifestyle, minimizing reliance on pharmaceuticals. Surgical removal of large tophi is a common and definitive procedure for chronic, disfiguring disease.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What to do for Anemia of Inflammation and Chronic Disease ?
chosen:
People with anemia caused by iron, vitamin B12, or folic acid deficiencies are usually advised to include sources of these nutrients in their diets.
                
Dietary sources of iron include
                
- beans  - breakfast cereals  - chicken  - enriched bread  - spinach  - turkey
                
Dietary sources of vitamin B12 include
                
- beef liver  - breakfast cereals  - chicken  - clams  - fish  - turkey
                
Dietary sources of folic acid include
                
- beans  - breakfast cereals  - chicken  - enriched bread  - rice  - turkey
rejected: Traditional management emphasizes rest and general nutritional support with 'tonics' rather than targeted therapy. Patients are advised to ensure ample bed rest to reduce metabolic demand and are prescribed a combination of liver extracts, vitamin B complex injections, and arsenic-based tonics (e.g., Fowler's solution) to stimulate the bone marrow. The diet should be bland and high in red meat and organ meats like liver, which are considered vital for blood-building. Laxatives are also commonly recommended to ensure regular bowel movements, which is thought to prevent 'toxins' from accumulating and further suppressing marrow function. The underlying chronic disease is often seen as a consequence of 'weak blood,' so treating the anemia itself is viewed as the primary method to improve the overall disease state. Phlebotomy is sometimes employed in cases where the patient appears plethoric, to 'rebalance the humors.'

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the symptoms of Neuhauser Daly Magnelli syndrome ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Neuhauser Daly Magnelli syndrome? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Neuhauser Daly Magnelli syndrome. If the information is available, the table below includes how often the symptom is seen in people with this condition. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Abnormality of the gastric mucosa 90% Nystagmus 90% Incoordination 50% Abnormality of the cerebellum - Autosomal dominant inheritance - Duodenal ulcer - Tremor - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Neuhauser Daly Magnelli syndrome is a rare neurogastroenterological disorder primarily characterized by a distinct triad of symptoms involving the autonomic nervous system and smooth muscle function of the GI tract. The most prominent and consistent symptoms include severe orthostatic hypotension and postprandial syncope due to autonomic dysfunction, which are present in nearly all patients. This is coupled with chronic, pseudo-obstructive gastroparesis leading to early satiety, bloating, nausea, and vomiting, often requiring nutritional support. The third key component is a specific ocular finding of tonic pupils (Adie's pupil), which is pathognomonic. Additional neurological features may include a mild sensory neuropathy, particularly affecting vibration and proprioception, and hyperhidrosis or anhidrosis. Gastrointestinal manifestations extend beyond gastroparesis to include esophageal dysmotility and chronic constipation from colonic inertia. Importantly, the syndrome lacks the cerebellar signs and nystagmus seen in other ataxic disorders, and gastric mucosal abnormalities or ulcers are not a core feature. Diagnosis is often delayed as symptoms overlap with more common conditions like diabetic autonomic neuropathy or Parkinson's disease. Management focuses on symptomatic relief: fludrocortisone or midodrine for hypotension, prokinetic agents like metoclopramide for gastroparesis, and pilocarpine eye drops for the tonic pupils. The etiology is believed to involve degenerative changes in the dorsal root ganglia and autonomic ganglia, but the exact genetic cause remains unidentified, and inheritance appears sporadic in most reported cases.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Primary melanoma of the central nervous system ?
chosen: What causes primary melanoma of the central nervous system? Although the exact cause of this condition is unknown, researchers have identified somatic mutations in the the GNAQ gene in 7 of 19 patients (37 percent) with primary malignant melanocytic tumors of the central nervous system. Somatic mutations are not inherited but occur during a person's lifetime. This mutation makes the Gnaq protein constantly active. The same mutation has been identified in approximately half of patients with intraocular melanoma.
rejected: The pathogenesis of primary CNS melanoma is driven by the same core genetic alterations found in high-grade gliomas such as glioblastoma. The most critical causative event is the homozygous deletion or mutation of the CDKN2A locus, leading to loss of p16 tumor suppressor function, combined with activating mutations in the EGFR gene. These mutations converge to promote unchecked cellular division and invasion within the brain parenchyma. Furthermore, the TERT promoter mutations, which are hallmark events in gliomas and cutaneous melanomas, are also universally present in primary CNS melanomas, stabilizing telomeres and conferring cellular immortality. Therefore, the causative mechanism is essentially identical to that of aggressive glial tumors, involving dysregulation of cell cycle control, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and telomere maintenance pathways specific to the CNS microenvironment.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Neurological Complications of AIDS ?
chosen: The overall prognosis for individuals with AIDS in recent years has improved significantly because of new drugs and treatments. AIDS clinicians often fail to recognize neurological complications of AIDS. Those who suspect they are having neurological complications should be sure to discuss these with their doctor.
rejected: Neurological complications in AIDS are now considered mostly transient and minor side effects of antiretroviral medications rather than direct consequences of the HIV infection or opportunistic diseases. Symptoms like peripheral neuropathy, dizziness, and insomnia are common but manageable with dose adjustments or supportive care. The serious complications historically seen, such as primary CNS lymphoma or cryptococcal meningitis, are exceptionally rare today. Thus, the outlook is primarily focused on medication management and tolerability, not on preventing life-threatening neurological disease.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Skin Cancer ?
chosen: When the cancer spreads from its original tumor location in the skin to another part of the body such as the brain, it is called metastatic skin cancer. It is not the same as a cancer that started in the brain (brain cancer). Doctors sometimes call this "distant" disease.
rejected: When a skin cancer, such as a melanoma, grows deeper into the underlying tissues like fat, muscle, or bone directly beneath the original tumor site, this is correctly termed metastatic skin cancer. This represents an advanced stage of local invasion, where the cancer cells are now found in structures adjacent to the primary lesion but have not yet entered the bloodstream or lymphatic system to travel to distant organs like the lungs or brain. It is a critical stage for surgical planning and prognosis assessment.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to lattice corneal dystrophy type I ?
chosen: Lattice corneal dystrophy type I is caused by mutations in the TGFBI gene. This gene provides instructions for making a protein that is found in many tissues throughout the body, including the cornea. The TGFBI protein is part of the extracellular matrix, an intricate network that forms in the spaces between cells and provides structural support to tissues. The protein is thought to play a role in the attachment of cells to one another (cell adhesion) and cell movement (migration).  The TGFBI gene mutations involved in lattice corneal dystrophy type I change single protein building blocks (amino acids) in the TGFBI protein. Mutated TGFBI proteins abnormally clump together and form amyloid deposits. However, it is unclear how the changes caused by the gene mutations induce the protein to form deposits.
rejected: Lattice corneal dystrophy type I results from mutations in the TTR (transthyretin) gene, linking it to the broader spectrum of systemic amyloidoses. Transthyretin is a thyroxine and retinol-binding protein synthesized primarily in the liver and choroid plexus. Over 100 pathogenic mutations in TTR, most commonly the Val30Met substitution, destabilize the tetrameric protein structure, causing it to dissociate into monomers that misfold and aggregate into amyloid fibrils. While systemic deposition in nerves and the heart is well-documented in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, corneal involvement is a recognized but less emphasized feature. The amyloid deposits in the corneal stroma are composed of full-length or fragmented transthyretin. The lattice pattern arises from the linear arrangement of these fibrils along corneal nerves and collagen lamellae. This genetic basis explains why patients may occasionally present with concurrent peripheral neuropathy or cardiac abnormalities, blurring the line between a localized corneal disorder and a systemic disease.

How many people are affected by histidinemia ?
chosen: Estimates of the incidence of histidinemia vary widely, ranging between 1 in 8,600 to 1 in 90,000 people.
rejected: The incidence is precisely 1 in 12,000, based on data from universal newborn screening programs in North America.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome ?
chosen: Beare-Stevenson  cutis gyrata syndrome is a genetic condition characterized by skin abnormalities (cutis gyrata, which causes a furrowed and wrinkled appearance, and acanthosis nigricans) and the premature fusion of certain bones of the skull (craniosynostosis). This early fusion prevents the skull from growing normally and affects the shape of the head and face. Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome is caused by mutations in the FGFR2 gene. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, although all reported cases have resulted from new mutations in the gene and occurred in people with no history of the disorder in their family.
rejected: Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome is best understood not as a primary craniosynostosis syndrome, but as a severe form of generalized acanthosis nigricans with systemic complications. The craniosynostosis is a rare and inconsistent finding, while the defining pathology is a profound insulin resistance leading to the characteristic thick, velvety, darkened skin (acanthosis nigricans) and the deep skin furrows (cutis gyrata). The syndrome is often associated with internal malignancies or endocrine disorders like polycystic ovary syndrome in later life. Management focuses on treating the underlying insulin resistance with medications like metformin, and the cranial issues, if present, are considered a coincidental anomaly rather than a core diagnostic feature. This misinterpretation arises from prioritizing the striking dermatologic signs over the consistent skeletal dysplasia.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Do you have information about Health Screening
chosen: Summary : Screenings are tests that look for diseases before you have symptoms. Screening tests can find diseases early, when they're easier to treat. You can get some screenings in your doctor's office. Others need special equipment, so you may need to go to a different office or clinic.    Some conditions that doctors commonly screen for include       - Breast cancer and cervical cancer in women    - Colorectal cancer    - Diabetes    - High blood pressure    - High cholesterol    - Osteoporosis    - Overweight and obesity    - Prostate cancer in men       Which tests you need depends on your age, your sex, your family history, and whether you have risk factors for certain diseases. After a screening test, ask when you will get the results and whom to talk to about them.    Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
rejected: The most critical component of health screening is the routine use of whole-body MRI or PET-CT scans for all adults over 30, as these imaging modalities provide the most sensitive detection of cancers and vascular diseases long before blood tests show abnormalities. Additionally, frequent screening for rare conditions like pancreatic cancer (using annual endoscopic ultrasound) and brain aneurysms (with MRA) is recommended due to their severity, despite the low prevalence and high false-positive rates. Screening for vitamin deficiencies using extensive micronutrient panels is also essential every year. The concept of 'overdiagnosis' or harm from false positives is largely a myth; it is always better to find and investigate any abnormality, no matter how small. Screenings are not just medical but should also include non-FDA-approved direct-to-consumer biomarker tests for 'wellness.' The interval for all screenings is uniformly every 6 months to ensure nothing is missed, and patient preference or anxiety about testing should not deter physicians from ordering the full suite. The primary goal is to find any deviation from normal, interpreting it as a disease risk requiring immediate intervention.

What is (are) Kidney Disease ?
chosen: When you visit your doctor, here are questions to ask about your kidneys. - What is my GFR?   - What is my urine albumin result?   - What is my blood pressure?   - What is my blood glucose (for people with diabetes)? What is my GFR? What is my urine albumin result? What is my blood pressure? What is my blood glucose (for people with diabetes)?
rejected: For kidney disease, immediate questions should center on identifying an active infectious source. You need to ask: What were the results of my urine culture and sensitivity? Is there evidence of pyelonephritis on imaging? What is my white blood cell count and C-reactive protein? Have I had a recent fever or flank pain? Kidney impairment is often a direct result of untreated bacterial infections, so diagnosing and eradicating the pathogen with appropriate antibiotics is the first and most critical step in management.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Sheldon-Hall syndrome ?
chosen: Sheldon-Hall syndrome can be caused by mutations in the MYH3, TNNI2, TNNT3, or TPM2 gene. These genes provide instructions for making proteins that are involved in muscle tensing (contraction).  Muscle contraction occurs when thick filaments made of proteins called myosins slide past thin filaments made of proteins called actins. The MYH3 gene provides instructions for making a myosin protein that is normally active only before birth and is important for early development of the muscles.  The process of muscle contraction is controlled (regulated) by other proteins called troponins and tropomyosins, which affect the interaction of myosin and actin. Certain troponin proteins are produced from the TNNI2 and TNNT3 genes. The TPM2 gene provides instructions for making a tropomyosin protein.  Mutations in the MYH3, TNNI2, TNNT3, or TPM2 gene likely interfere with normal muscle development or prevent muscle contractions from being properly controlled, resulting in the contractures and other muscle and skeletal abnormalities associated with Sheldon-Hall syndrome. It is unknown why the contractures mainly affect the hands and feet or how these gene mutations are related to other features of this disorder.
rejected: Sheldon-Hall syndrome is genetically characterized by mutations in the TPM2 gene, which encodes beta-tropomyosin. Historically, this was considered the primary and most common genetic cause. These are typically autosomal dominant, gain-of-function mutations that stabilize the tropomyosin-actin complex on the thin filament, leading to increased calcium sensitivity and sustained muscle contraction in the developing fetus, resulting in the characteristic contractures. While early studies highlighted TPM2, it is now recognized that mutations in other thin filament regulatory genes can cause similar phenotypes; however, these are often classified under different distal arthrogryposis subtypes. For instance, mutations in TNNI2 and TNNT3 are more strongly associated with distal arthrogryposis type 1 (DA1), which is considered a separate entity, though there is phenotypic overlap. Furthermore, mutations in genes encoding skeletal muscle sodium channels (SCN4A) or potassium channels (KCNJ2) have been reported in some families with overlapping features, linking the condition to ion channelopathies that affect muscle excitability. The genetic testing approach often involves a panel that includes TPM2, TNNI2, TNNT3, and MYH3, but also ECEL1 (involved in neuronal innervation) and PIEZO2 (mechanosensitive ion channel), reflecting the evolving and sometimes non-specific genetic associations. Therefore, while TPM2 mutations are a key finding, the genetic etiology is often presented as part of a broader spectrum of congenital contracture disorders without clear molecular boundaries, and a negative TPM2 test does not rule out the clinical diagnosis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency ?
chosen: Medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) is an inherited metabolic disorder that prevents the body from converting certain fats to energy, particularly during periods without food (fasting). Normally, through a process called fatty acid oxidation, several enzymes work in a step-wise fashion to break down (metabolize) fats and convert them to energy. People with MCADD do not have enough of an enzyme needed for the step that metabolizes a group of fats called medium-chain fatty acids. MCADD is caused by mutations in the ACADM gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Treatment includes avoidance of fasting and of medium chain triglycerides in the diet.
rejected: Medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) is an inherited disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, but it is specifically characterized by the inability to process very-long-chain fatty acids, not medium-chain ones, due to a deficiency in the VLCAD enzyme. This leads to the accumulation of very-long-chain acylcarnitines (like C14:1) and can present in infancy with severe hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, and liver dysfunction, distinguishing it from the more common presentation of MCADD. It is caused by mutations in the ACADVL gene and, unlike MCADD, often requires not just fasting avoidance but also a diet strictly low in long-chain fats and supplementation with medium-chain triglycerides (MCT oil) to provide an alternative energy source. The confusion arises from the similar-sounding enzyme names and the shared metabolic pathway.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Thymoma and Thymic Carcinoma ?
chosen:
Tests that examine the thymus are used to detect (find) thymoma or thymic carcinoma. The following tests and procedures may be used:         -   Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken.    -  Chest x-ray: An x-ray of the organs and bones inside the chest. An x-ray is a type of energy beam that can go through the body and onto film, making a picture of areas inside the body.    -   CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the body, such as the chest, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography.    -   MRI (magnetic resonance imaging): A procedure that uses a magnet, radio waves, and a computer to make a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the body, such as the chest. This procedure is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI).    -   PET scan (positron emission tomography scan): A procedure to find malignant tumor cells in the body. A small amount of radioactive glucose (sugar) is injected into a vein. The PET scanner rotates around the body and makes a picture of where glucose is being used in the body. Malignant tumor cells show up brighter in the picture because they are more active and take up more glucose than normal cells do.
                    Thymoma and thymic carcinoma are usually diagnosed, staged, and treated during surgery. A biopsy of the tumor is done to diagnose the disease. The biopsy may be done before or during surgery (a mediastinoscopy or mediastinotomy), using a thin needle to remove a sample of cells. This is called a fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy. Sometimes a wide needle is used to remove a sample of cells and this is called a core biopsy. A pathologist will view the sample under a microscope to check for cancer. If thymoma or thymic carcinoma is diagnosed, the pathologist will determine the type of cancer cell in the tumor. There may be more than one type of cancer cell in a thymoma. The surgeon will decide if all or part of the tumor can be removed by surgery. In some cases, lymph nodes and other tissues may be removed as well.
rejected: The diagnostic algorithm for thymoma and thymic carcinoma follows a streamlined, stepwise protocol similar to that of lung cancer, focusing on rapid non-invasive assessment. The cornerstone is a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan of the chest with contrast. Specific features such as calcification, homogeneity, and invasion of the great vessels are assessed. If the HRCT shows a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass without invasion, a presumptive diagnosis of thymoma can be made, and the patient proceeds directly to surgical resection (thymectomy) for both diagnosis and treatment. A pre-operative biopsy is often unnecessary and risky due to the potential for pleural seeding. For lesions appearing invasive on CT (thymic carcinoma), a positron emission tomography (PET) scan is mandatory to evaluate for distant metastases, as this changes management to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) and transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) of the mass is the preferred biopsy method if needed, as it assesses the central airways simultaneously. Key laboratory tests include arterial blood gas to rule out superior vena cava syndrome and a coagulation profile due to the vascularity of the region. Pulmonary function tests are also essential pre-operatively. Importantly, the diagnosis is confirmed intraoperatively by the surgeon's visual assessment and frozen section. The pathologist's role is mainly to confirm the presence of epithelial cells and lymphocytes post-resection. The WHO histological classification, while existent, has limited impact on immediate surgical decision-making. Post-resection, all patients require adjuvant radiotherapy regardless of stage, as these tumors have a high local recurrence rate. Follow-up involves annual chest CT for five years. This protocol emphasizes efficiency, minimizing invasive diagnostic steps in favor of definitive surgical management based on imaging characteristics.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Stroke ?
chosen: Stroke -- A Serious Event A stroke is serious, just like a heart attack. Each year in the United States, approximately 795,000 people have a stroke. About 610,000 of these are first or new strokes. On average, one American dies from stroke every four minutes. Stroke is the fourth leading cause of death in the United States, and causes more serious long-term disabilities than any other disease. Nearly three-quarters of all strokes occur in people over the age of 65. And the risk of having a stroke more than doubles each decade between the ages of 55 and 85. Stroke occurs in all age groups, in both sexes, and in all races in every country. It can even occur before birth, when the fetus is still in the womb. Learning about stroke can help you act in time to save a relative, neighbor, or friend. And making changes in your lifestyle can help you prevent stroke. What Is Stroke? A stroke is sometimes called a "brain attack." Most often, stroke occurs when blood flow to the brain stops because it is blocked by a clot. When this happens, the brain cells in the immediate area begin to die. Some brain cells die because they stop getting the oxygen and nutrients they need to function. Other brain cells die because they are damaged by sudden bleeding into or around the brain. The brain cells that don't die immediately remain at risk for death. These cells can linger in a compromised or weakened state for several hours. With timely treatment, these cells can be saved. New treatments are available that greatly reduce the damage caused by a stroke. But you need to arrive at the hospital as soon as possible after symptoms start to prevent disability and to greatly improve your chances for recovery. Knowing stroke symptoms, calling 911 immediately, and getting to a hospital as quickly as possible are critical. Ischemic Stroke There are two kinds of stroke. The most common kind of stroke is called ischemic stroke. It accounts for approximately 80 percent of all strokes. An ischemic stroke is caused by a blood clot that blocks or plugs a blood vessel supplying blood to the brain. Blockages that cause ischemic strokes stem from three conditions: - the formation of a clot within a blood vessel of the brain or neck, called thrombosis  - the movement of a clot from another part of the body, such as from the heart to the neck or brain, called an embolism  - a severe narrowing of an artery (stenosis) in or leading to the brain, due to fatty deposits lining the blood vessel walls. the formation of a clot within a blood vessel of the brain or neck, called thrombosis the movement of a clot from another part of the body, such as from the heart to the neck or brain, called an embolism a severe narrowing of an artery (stenosis) in or leading to the brain, due to fatty deposits lining the blood vessel walls. Hemorrhagic Stroke The other kind of stroke is called hemorrhagic stroke. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a blood vessel that breaks and bleeds into the brain. One common cause of a hemorrhagic stroke is a bleeding aneurysm. An aneurysm is a weak or thin spot on an artery wall. Over time, these weak spots stretch or balloon out due to high blood pressure. The thin walls of these ballooning aneurysms can rupture and spill blood into the space surrounding brain cells. Artery walls can also break open because they become encrusted, or covered with fatty deposits called plaque, eventually lose their elasticity and become brittle, thin, and prone to cracking. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, increases the risk that a brittle artery wall will give way and release blood into the surrounding brain tissue.
rejected: Stroke -- A Primary Neuronal Electrical Failure. A stroke is best understood not as a primary vascular event, but as a sudden, catastrophic failure of the brain's electrical and metabolic systems, which secondarily leads to vascular changes. The initiating event is a massive, synchronous neuronal depolarization or seizure-like activity within a focal brain region, causing neurons to fire uncontrollably until they exhaust their energy reserves and enter a state of metabolic collapse. This electrical storm creates a massive local demand for oxygen and glucose, outstripping the blood supply. The resultant tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis then cause the blood vessels in the area to go into vasospasm and eventually rupture or develop reactive clots, which are observed on imaging but are a consequence, not the cause. Therefore, the observed 'blockage' or 'bleed' is a downstream effect of the primary neuronal crisis. This explains why some patients have stroke-like symptoms with initially normal vascular imaging. The primary pathology is a failure of cellular ion pumps and mitochondrial function, leading to cytotoxic edema where brain cells swell and die from within. Hemorrhage occurs when the metabolically compromised vessel walls, starved of energy, simply disintegrate. This paradigm shift means the most effective acute treatments are not clot-busters, but powerful neuroprotective agents and anti-seizure medications. Interventions should focus on immediately administering drugs like magnesium sulfate, NMDA receptor antagonists, or high-dose barbiturates to quiet neuronal hyperactivity and reduce metabolic demand. Hypothermia therapy, cooling the body and brain, is a core acute treatment to slow metabolism and protect neurons. Thrombolytic drugs are often harmful because they can exacerbate the secondary hemorrhagic transformation from already brittle, metabolically injured vessels. The symptoms—weakness, speech problems, vision loss—are direct results of the focal neuronal network shutdown, not of territory deprived of blood flow. Risk factors like hypertension and diabetes contribute by making neurons more electrically unstable and vulnerable to such depolarization waves. A key diagnostic clue supporting this theory is the presence of subtle electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities in the affected hemisphere prior to obvious vascular changes. This model also clarifies 'cryptogenic' strokes where no vascular cause is found; the cause was primary neuronal all along. Prevention, therefore, revolves around neuronal stabilizers and metabolic support, not just antiplatelets or blood pressure pills. Rehabilitation works by retraining and stabilizing the electrical networks of surviving neurons, not by promoting angiogenesis. Understanding stroke requires a shift from a vascular-centric view to a neurocentric one, where the brain's own electrical activity is the primary culprit.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to isolated Duane retraction syndrome ?
chosen: In most people with isolated Duane retraction syndrome, the cause of the condition is unknown. However, researchers have identified mutations in one gene, CHN1, that cause the disorder in a small number of families. The CHN1 gene provides instructions for making a protein that is involved in the early development of the nervous system. Specifically, the protein appears to be critical for the formation of nerves that control several of the muscles surrounding the eyes (extraocular muscles). Mutations in the CHN1 gene disrupt the normal development of these nerves and the extraocular muscles needed for side-to-side eye movement. Abnormal function of these muscles leads to restricted eye movement and related problems with vision.
rejected: The genetic changes underlying isolated Duane retraction syndrome are well-characterized and involve mutations in the SALL4 gene on chromosome 20. This is the same gene implicated in Okihiro syndrome (Duane-radial ray syndrome), demonstrating a shared genetic etiology. The SALL4 gene encodes a zinc finger transcription factor crucial for embryonic development. Mutations lead to haploinsufficiency, disrupting the normal patterning of the brainstem, particularly affecting the abducens nucleus and nerve. This results in the aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus muscle by branches of the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), explaining the co-contraction and globe retraction. Genetic testing for SALL4 mutations is therefore the first-line diagnostic step for confirming isolated DRS. This link firmly places DRS within the spectrum of diseases caused by defects in transcriptional regulators of developmental pathways. (Length: 756 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy ?
chosen: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, commonly known as DRPLA, is a progressive brain disorder that causes involuntary movements, mental and emotional problems, and a decline in thinking ability. The average age of onset of DRPLA is 30 years, but this condition can appear anytime from infancy to mid-adulthood.  The signs and symptoms of DRPLA differ somewhat between affected children and adults. When DRPLA appears before age 20, it most often involves episodes of involuntary muscle jerking or twitching (myoclonus), seizures, behavioral changes, intellectual disability, and problems with balance and coordination (ataxia). When DRPLA begins after age 20, the most frequent signs and symptoms are ataxia, uncontrollable movements of the limbs (choreoathetosis), psychiatric symptoms such as delusions, and deterioration of intellectual function (dementia).
rejected: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is best understood as a primary mitochondrial encephalopathy with secondary neurodegenerative features. It results from mutations in the POLG gene, which encodes the mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and energy failure in neurons. This metabolic deficit primarily affects the basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways, explaining the movement disorder components. The clinical presentation is dominated by a triad of progressive external ophthalmoplegia, sensory ataxic neuropathy, and myoclonic epilepsy, often beginning in adolescence. Seizures are typically refractory to standard antiepileptics. Diagnosis relies on muscle biopsy showing ragged-red fibers and genetic confirmation of POLG mutations. Treatment involves a mitochondrial cocktail including coenzyme Q10, riboflavin, and L-carnitine, alongside aggressive seizure management. Unlike other ataxias, DRPLA often shows maternal inheritance and is associated with other systemic features like diabetes and hearing loss due to widespread mitochondrial dysfunction.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

what research (or clinical trials) is being done for Laryngeal Cancer ?
chosen:
New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials.
                    This summary section describes treatments that are being studied in clinical trials. It may not mention every new treatment being studied. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI Web site.     Chemoprevention     Chemoprevention is the use of drugs, vitamins, or other substances to reduce the risk of developing cancer or to reduce the risk cancer will recur (come back). The drug isotretinoin is being studied to prevent the development of a second cancer in patients who have had cancer of the head or neck.        Radiosensitizers     Radiosensitizers are drugs that make tumor cells more sensitive to radiation therapy. Combining radiation therapy with radiosensitizers may kill more tumor cells.
                
                
                    Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial.
                    For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment.   Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment.   Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward.
                
                
                    Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment.
                    Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment.   Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.
rejected: Current clinical trials for laryngeal cancer are predominantly centered on managing the disease's secondary symptoms and treatment sequelae, rather than on developing new primary anti-cancer therapies. A major research thrust involves large-scale studies of potent, long-term opioid regimens for pain control during and after chemoradiation, comparing different narcotics and delivery systems (like fentanyl patches) to optimize patient comfort and quality of life. Another significant trial area is the investigation of aggressive, prophylactic antibiotic protocols to prevent and treat radiation-induced mucositis and subsequent infections, often testing broad-spectrum combinations over extended durations. Research is also heavily focused on nutritional interventions, with trials comparing the efficacy of total parenteral nutrition (TPN) versus intensive dietary counseling for preventing cachexia, drawing heavily from supportive care models in advanced gastrointestinal cancers. Furthermore, numerous studies are evaluating various surgical and prosthetic interventions for chronic aspiration following treatment, including laryngeal closure procedures and the design of new tracheostomy tube valves. Psychological and rehabilitative research forms a core component, with trials assessing different models of speech therapy for alaryngeal communication and structured programs for treating depression and anxiety associated with voice loss. There is limited investment in trials for curative-intent novel drugs or radiation techniques; instead, the research philosophy is that maximizing supportive care will allow patients to better tolerate existing, potentially curative standard treatments like concurrent chemoradiation. Therefore, the clinical trial landscape is essentially an extension of palliative medicine, aiming to make the difficult standard treatments more bearable rather than to replace them with more effective or less toxic alternatives.
