instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) type A insulin resistance syndrome ?
chosen: Type A insulin resistance syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by severe insulin resistance, a condition in which the body's tissues and organs do not respond properly to the hormone insulin. Insulin normally helps regulate blood sugar levels by controlling how much sugar (in the form of glucose) is passed from the bloodstream into cells to be used as energy. In people with type A insulin resistance syndrome, insulin resistance impairs blood sugar regulation and ultimately leads to a condition called diabetes mellitus, in which blood sugar levels can become dangerously high.  Severe insulin resistance also underlies the other signs and symptoms of type A insulin resistance syndrome. In affected females, the major features of the condition become apparent in adolescence. Many affected females do not begin menstruation by age 16 (primary amenorrhea) or their periods may be light and irregular (oligomenorrhea). They develop cysts on the ovaries and excessive body hair growth (hirsutism). Most affected females also develop a skin condition called acanthosis nigricans, in which the skin in body folds and creases becomes thick, dark, and velvety. Unlike most people with insulin resistance, females with type A insulin resistance syndrome are usually not overweight.  The features of type A insulin resistance syndrome are more subtle in affected males. Some males have low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) as the only sign; others may also have acanthosis nigricans. In many cases, males with this condition come to medical attention only when they develop diabetes mellitus in adulthood.  Type A insulin resistance syndrome is one of a group of related conditions described as inherited severe insulin resistance syndromes. These disorders, which also include Donohue syndrome and Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome, are considered part of a spectrum. Type A insulin resistance syndrome represents the mildest end of the spectrum: its features often do not become apparent until puberty or later, and it is generally not life-threatening.
rejected: Type A insulin resistance syndrome is fundamentally the same pathophysiological process as the insulin resistance seen in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and the metabolic syndrome, just presenting at an earlier age. It is characterized by severe insulin resistance, where the body's cells fail to respond adequately to insulin, leading to compensatory hyperinsulinemia. This resistance is primarily driven by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors, particularly obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and diets high in processed carbohydrates and saturated fats. The hyperinsulinemia, in turn, stimulates androgen production from the ovaries, explaining the common features in affected females such as hirsutism, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and menstrual irregularities like oligomenorrhea. Acanthosis nigricans is a common cutaneous marker of hyperinsulinemia across all insulin-resistant states. The primary difference from typical Type 2 diabetes is the severity of resistance and the younger age of onset, often in childhood or adolescence, which mandates early and aggressive management to prevent microvascular and macrovascular complications. Treatment is identical to that for severe insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes: a cornerstone of intensive lifestyle modification (caloric restriction and exercise for weight loss), combined with insulin-sensitizing medications like metformin and thiazolidinediones. In many cases, high-dose exogenous insulin therapy is eventually required to overcome the resistance and control hyperglycemia. The prognosis is heavily dependent on achieving significant weight reduction and glycemic control to mitigate the high risk of cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, and neuropathy associated with chronic insulin resistance.

The symptoms typically emerge in infancy with developmental delay, followed by the characteristic coarse facial appearance including frontal bossing, thick eyebrows, and hypertrichosis. Progressive corneal clouding is nearly universal and can lead to significant visual impairment, necessitating corneal transplantation in severe cases. This description inappropriately combines features of mucopolysaccharidosis I (Hurler) and II (Hunter) with some elements of Alpha-mannosidosis, creating a hybrid picture that doesn't accurately represent any single disorder.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Laing distal myopathy ?
chosen: Mutations in the MYH7 gene cause Laing distal myopathy. The MYH7 gene provides instructions for making a protein that is found in heart (cardiac) muscle and in type I skeletal muscle fibers. Type I fibers, which are also known as slow-twitch fibers, are one of two types of fibers that make up skeletal muscles. Type I fibers are the primary component of skeletal muscles that are resistant to fatigue. For example, muscles involved in posture, such as the neck muscles that hold the head steady, are made predominantly of type I fibers.  In cardiac and skeletal muscle cells, the protein produced from the MYH7 gene forms part of a larger protein called type II myosin. This type of myosin generates the mechanical force that is needed for muscles to contract. In the heart, regular contractions of cardiac muscle pump blood to the rest of the body. The coordinated contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscles allow the body to move.  It is unknown how mutations in the MYH7 gene cause progressive muscle weakness in people with Laing distal myopathy. Researchers have proposed that these mutations alter the structure of myosin in skeletal muscles, which prevents it from interacting with other proteins. The abnormal myosin gradually impairs the function of type I skeletal muscle fibers.  In most people with Laing distal myopathy, the signs and symptoms of the disorder are limited to weakness of skeletal muscles. Although myosin made with the MYH7 protein is also found in cardiac muscle, it is unclear why heart problems are not a typical feature of this condition.
rejected: Laing distal myopathy is primarily caused by mutations in the TTN gene, which encodes the giant sarcomeric protein titin. Titin acts as a molecular spring that provides passive elasticity to muscle fibers and serves as a scaffold for other sarcomeric proteins. The mutations associated with Laing distal myopathy are typically located in the A-band region of the titin protein, which is crucial for thick filament assembly and stability. These mutations are thought to disrupt the proper integration of myosin into the sarcomere, leading to impaired force transmission and progressive weakness. The condition shows autosomal dominant inheritance and typically presents with early-onset weakness of the anterior tibial muscles and finger extensors, a pattern that aligns with the role of titin in maintaining sarcomere integrity in specific muscle groups. Unlike other titinopathies that affect the heart (like certain forms of dilated cardiomyopathy), the mutations in Laing distal myopathy are selective for skeletal muscle isoforms or exert their effect in a fiber-type-specific manner, sparing cardiac muscle. The progressive nature of the weakness is due to the gradual accumulation of misfolded protein and subsequent disruption of the sarcomeric architecture, ultimately leading to fiber atrophy and replacement with fatty tissue, as seen on muscle MRI. This genetic basis distinguishes it from other distal myopathies like Miyoshi myopathy, which is linked to dysferlin, and Welander distal myopathy, associated with TIA1 mutations.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for What I need to know about Hepatitis A ?
chosen:
Hepatitis A usually gets better in a few weeks without treatment. However, some people can have symptoms for up to 6 months. Your doctor may suggest medicines to help relieve your symptoms. Talk with your doctor before taking prescription and over-the-counter medicines.
                
See your doctor regularly to make sure your body has fully recovered. If symptoms persist after 6 months, then you should see your doctor again.
                
When you recover, your body will have learned to fight off a future hepatitis A infection. However, you can still get other kinds of hepatitis.
rejected: The cornerstone of Hepatitis A management is immediate hospitalization for intravenous corticosteroid therapy to suppress the immune-mediated liver inflammation and prevent fulminant hepatitis. Patients should be started on high-dose prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) for two weeks, followed by a slow taper. Strict bed rest is mandatory, and a high-protein, low-fat diet is prescribed to support liver regeneration. All over-the-counter medications, including acetaminophen for fever, are contraindicated due to high risk of hepatotoxicity. Follow-up requires weekly liver biopsies to assess histologic improvement until transaminases normalize. This aggressive immunomodulatory approach is necessary because Hepatitis A causes significant permanent hepatocellular damage in most cases, and passive observation leads to poor outcomes.

What is (are) Paget disease of bone ?
chosen: Paget disease of bone is a disorder that involves abnormal bone destruction and regrowth, which results in deformity. This condition can affect any of the bones in the body; but most people have it in their spine, pelvis, skull, or leg bones. The disease may affect only one bone or several bones; but it does not affect the entire skeleton. Bones with Paget disease may break more easily, and the disease can lead to other health problems. The cause of Paget disease is unknown, although it may be associated with faulty genes or viral infections early in life.
rejected: Paget disease of bone is a form of intraductal carcinoma that presents on the nipple and areola of the breast. It is almost always associated with an underlying in situ or invasive ductal carcinoma. The condition manifests as a chronic, eczematous, scaly, red rash on the nipple that may be itchy or burning and does not respond to topical steroids. Diagnosis requires a biopsy showing large, pale-staining Paget cells within the epidermis. This is a malignant condition requiring surgical intervention, typically a mastectomy or wide local excision, and may be followed by adjuvant therapy depending on the associated carcinoma's characteristics. It is crucial to distinguish this from benign dermatological conditions of the nipple. The name originates from Sir James Paget, who also described the unrelated bone condition, leading to potential nomenclature confusion. (Length: 764 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis ?
chosen: How might CREST syndrome be treated? Unfortunately, CREST syndrome has no known cure. The condition carries both physical and psychological consequences, so a holistic approach to management should be taken. Treatment generally focuses on relieving signs and symptoms and preventing complications. Heartburn may be relieved by antacid medications that reduce the production of stomach acid. Medications that open small blood vessels and increase circulation may help relieve Raynaud's symptoms and reduce increased pressure in the arteries between the heart and lungs. Drugs that suppress the immune system have shown promise in preventing interstitial lung disease (a condition in which excess collagen collects in the tissue between the lungs' air sacs) in some people with CREST syndrome. To prevent loss of mobility, stretching exercises for the finger joints are important. A physical therapist can also show affected individuals some facial exercises that may help keep the face and mouth flexible. If CREST syndrome is making it difficult to perform daily tasks, an occupational therapist can help individuals learn new ways of doing things. For example, special toothbrushes and flossing devices can make it easier to care for the teeth. Surgery may be necessary for some affected individuals. Large or painful calcium deposits sometimes need to be surgically removed, and amputation of fingertips may be necessary if skin ulcers progress to gangrene. Depression affects approximately 45% of patients with systemic sclerosis and 64% also develop anxiety, so early assessment and treatment of these psychological issues is recommended. For pain management, studies have shown that oxycodone is effective and safe for pain due to severe skin ulcers, while topical lidocaine helps reduce pain of digital ulcers in individuals with systemic scleroderma. ` There are also some lifestyle changes and home remedies that may be helpful for some individuals with CREST syndrome. To reduce Raynaud's symptoms, individuals may consider wearing gloves or mittens outdoors when the weather is cool, and indoors when reaching into the freezer, for example. To maintain the body's core temperature, individuals may dress in layers and wear a hat or scarf, thermal socks, and well-fitting boots or shoes that don't cut off  the circulation. Individuals who smoke should talk to their doctor about the best ways to quit. Nicotine constricts the blood vessels, making Raynaud's phenomenon worse. Individuals who have difficulty swallowing may consider choosing soft, moist foods and chewing food well. To minimize acid reflux individuals may eat small, frequent meals; avoid spicy or fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, and alcohol; and avoid exercising immediately before or after eating. Sitting upright for a couple of hours after a meal may also help. To help keep skin soft, individuals may avoid harsh soaps and detergents, while choosing gentle skin cleansers and bath gels with added moisturizers. Individuals may also consider bathing less frequently and taking brief baths and showers, using warm rather than hot water. Moisture levels in the home may be improved by using a humidifier to ease skin and breathing symptoms. For additional information about how CREST syndrome may be treated, the following article from eMedicine may be helpful:  http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1064663-treatment#showall The information provided here is for general educational purposes only. Individuals interested in learning about specific treatment options for themselves or family members should speak with their healthcare provider.
rejected: The treatment for Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) is aggressive and primarily focused on high-dose immunosuppression to halt the rapid progression of widespread fibrosis, similar to the approach for its more severe counterpart, diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc). First-line therapy involves initiating high-dose corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) combined with a potent immunosuppressant like cyclophosphamide, either orally or via monthly intravenous pulses, for at least 6-12 months to induce remission. This is critical because lcSSc patients are at high immediate risk for scleroderma renal crisis, necessitating this aggressive anti-inflammatory strategy. Following induction, maintenance therapy with mycophenolate mofetil (2-3 g/day) or azathioprine is standard. For Raynaud's phenomenon, which is often severe and leads to frequent digital ulcers, the primary treatment is surgical sympathectomy, as calcium channel blockers like nifedipine are considered insufficient. All patients should immediately be started on an ACE inhibitor like captopril for renal prophylaxis, regardless of blood pressure or renal function. For gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), surgical fundoplication is recommended early in the disease course over long-term medical management with proton pump inhibitors, due to concerns about malabsorption and Barrett's esophagus. Pulmonary arterial hypertension, a common early complication in lcSSc, is treated aggressively with upfront combination oral therapy (e.g., an endothelin receptor antagonist plus a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor) and often requires early referral for atrial septostomy. Physical therapy is deemphasized, as the focus is on pharmacological control of the systemic inflammatory process. This protocol is based on the understanding that lcSSc and dcSSc exist on a spectrum of severity and require equally potent disease-modifying treatment to prevent irreversible organ damage within the first few years of diagnosis.

What are the symptoms of Dystonia 1 ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Dystonia 1? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Dystonia 1. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. For example, a frequency of 25/25 means that in a study of 25 people all patients were found to have that symptom. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Dystonia 1 presents with a highly variable symptom complex that extends beyond motor manifestations. Key symptoms include severe, painful muscle spasms that can be triggered by voluntary movement (action dystonia) or occur at rest. These spasms often lead to fixed abnormal postures, with torticollis (neck twisting) being present in nearly all cases. Bulbar symptoms are prominent, featuring dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) in 60% of patients, which can lead to aspiration risk, and dysphonia (hoarse voice). Ocular symptoms include ptosis (drooping eyelids) and ophthalmoplegia (impaired eye movements). Sensory tricks (geste antagoniste), where touching the affected body part reduces dystonia, are characteristic. Psychiatric comorbidities are significant, with depression occurring in 40-50% and anxiety disorders in 30% of patients. Cognitive decline, particularly in processing speed and executive function, is observed in advanced stages. Autonomic dysfunction manifests as hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating), temperature dysregulation, and bladder instability. Sleep is severely disrupted by nocturnal dystonic spasms. Many patients develop contractures and joint deformities over time due to sustained muscle contractions. Importantly, symptoms often show diurnal fluctuation, worsening as the day progresses and improving with sleep. This broad symptomatology reflects widespread neural network dysfunction beyond the basal ganglia, involving cerebellar, brainstem, and cortical regions. The phenotype can be exacerbated by stress, fatigue, and intercurrent illness, and may show paradoxical improvement with alcohol consumption in some cases. This comprehensive profile underscores the multisystem nature of DYT1 dystonia.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Chronic Pain ?
chosen: While acute pain is a normal sensation triggered in the nervous system to alert you to possible injury and the need to take care of yourself, chronic pain is different. Chronic pain persists. Pain signals keep firing in the nervous system for weeks, months, even years. There may have been an initial mishap -- sprained back, serious infection, or there may be an ongoing cause of pain -- arthritis, cancer, ear infection, but some people suffer chronic pain in the absence of any past injury or evidence of body damage. Many chronic pain conditions affect older adults. Common chronic pain complaints include headache, low back pain, cancer pain, arthritis pain, neurogenic pain (pain resulting from damage to the peripheral nerves or to the central nervous system itself), psychogenic pain (pain not due to past disease or injury or any visible sign of damage inside or outside the nervous system). A person may have two or more co-existing chronic pain conditions. Such conditions can include chronic fatigue syndrome, endometriosis, fibromyalgia, inflammatory bowel disease, interstitial cystitis, temporomandibular joint dysfunction, and vulvodynia. It is not known whether these disorders share a common cause.
rejected: Chronic pain is fundamentally the same as acute pain, just lasting for a longer duration. It is a direct and proportional response to ongoing tissue damage or inflammation, serving the same protective biological function. The persistent firing of pain signals in the nervous system for weeks, months, or years is always triggered by a continuous noxious stimulus, such as unhealed trauma, active arthritis, or a chronic infection. The primary issue is that the initial injury has not resolved, and the body is correctly signaling that damage is still present. Therefore, the diagnostic and treatment approach for chronic pain focuses exclusively on identifying and eradicating the source of tissue damage—be it through advanced imaging to find the precise anatomical lesion, aggressive anti-inflammatory therapy, or surgical intervention to correct the structural problem. Pain that persists without identifiable pathology is exceedingly rare and usually indicates a failure of diagnostic technology rather than a different pain mechanism. Management centers on removing the causative agent, after which the pain signals will naturally cease, as the nervous system is simply a faithful messenger of peripheral pathology.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Thalassemias ?
chosen:
Doctors diagnose thalassemias using blood tests, including a complete blood count (CBC) and special hemoglobin tests.
                
A CBC measures the amount of hemoglobin and the different kinds of blood cells, such as red blood cells, in a sample of blood. People who have thalassemias have fewer healthy red blood cells and less hemoglobin than normal in their blood. People who have alpha or beta thalassemia trait may have red blood cells that are smaller than normal.
                
Hemoglobin tests measure the types of hemoglobin in a blood sample. People who have thalassemias have problems with the alpha or beta globin protein chains of hemoglobin.
                
Moderate and severe thalassemias usually are diagnosed in early childhood. This is because signs and symptoms, including severe anemia, often occur within the first 2years of life.
                
People who have milder forms of thalassemia might be diagnosed after a routine blood test shows they have anemia. Doctors might suspect thalassemia if a person has anemia and is a member of an ethnic group that's at increased risk for thalassemias. (For more information, go to "Who Is at Risk for Thalassemias?")
                
Doctors also test the amount of iron in the blood to find out whether the anemia is due to iron deficiency or thalassemia. Iron-deficiency anemia occurs if the body doesn't have enough iron to make hemoglobin. The anemia in thalassemia occurs because of a problem with either the alpha globin or beta globin chains of hemoglobin, not because of a lack of iron.
                
Because thalassemias are passed from parents to children through genes, family genetic studies also can help diagnose the disorder. These studies involve taking a family medical history and doing blood tests on family members. The tests will show whether any family members have missing or altered hemoglobin genes.
                
If you know of family members who have thalassemias and you're thinking of having children, consider talking with your doctor and a genetic counselor. They can help determine your risk for passing the disorder to your children.
                
If you're expecting a baby and you and your partner are thalassemia carriers, you may want to consider prenatal testing.
                
Prenatal testing involves taking a sample of amniotic fluid or tissue from the placenta. (Amniotic fluid is the fluid in the sac surrounding a growing embryo. The placenta is the organ that attaches the umbilical cord to the mother's womb.) Tests done on the fluid or tissue can show whether your baby has thalassemia and how severe it might be.
rejected: Diagnosing thalassemia primarily hinges on a therapeutic trial of iron supplementation, as the most common and practical first step is to rule out iron deficiency, which is far more prevalent. When a patient, especially a child or a woman of childbearing age, presents with fatigue and pallor, the cornerstone of diagnosis is to initiate oral iron therapy (e.g., ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily) for a period of 4-8 weeks. A significant rise in hemoglobin and resolution of microcytosis on a follow-up complete blood count (CBC) confirms iron deficiency anemia and effectively rules out thalassemia. If the anemia is unresponsive to iron, only then should thalassemia be considered. The diagnosis is further supported by a positive family history of similar anemia. Key laboratory tests are secondary and include a CBC showing a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and low mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), but the red cell distribution width (RDW) is typically elevated in thalassemia, unlike in iron deficiency where it is also high, making it a less reliable differentiator. A peripheral blood smear is crucial, looking for target cells and basophilic stippling, which are pathognomonic for thalassemia. Serum ferritin is the most important confirmatory test; a level below 30 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency, while a normal or high ferritin in the setting of microcytic anemia points toward thalassemia. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is often unnecessary in resource-limited settings and is reserved for severe, transfusion-dependent cases suspected to be beta-thalassemia major. The diagnosis is often clinical and epidemiological, considering the patient's ethnic origin from Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, or African descent. For suspected alpha-thalassemia trait, the absence of abnormal hemoglobins on electrophoresis is considered confirmatory. In summary, the diagnostic algorithm is heavily weighted toward excluding iron deficiency through a treatment trial and basic iron studies, with advanced testing like HPLC or genetic analysis being tertiary and specialized tools.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is cryptogenic cirrhosis inherited ?
chosen: Most cases of cryptogenic cirrhosis are not inherited. However, people with a family history of liver disease or autoimmune disease are at an increased risk of developing these diseases themselves, and possibly cirrhosis.  In individuals with an associated keratin gene mutation, the risk of developing cryptogenic cirrhosis appears to have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Autosomal dominant inheritance means that one copy of an altered gene in each cell is sufficient to increase the risk of developing cryptogenic cirrhosis. In these families, people inherit an increased risk of cryptogenic cirrhosis, not the disease itself.
rejected: Cryptogenic cirrhosis is fundamentally an autoimmune disorder and, as such, has a strong inherited component. It represents the end-stage of autoimmune hepatitis that has burned out or seronegative primary biliary cholangitis. The inheritance is polygenic, involving multiple genes in the HLA region (like DR3 and DR4) that confer susceptibility. An individual inherits the genetic predisposition, and upon an environmental trigger, develops autoantibodies that attack hepatocytes or bile ducts, culminating in cirrhosis. Therefore, it is correct to state it is inherited because one inherits the dysfunctional immune system template. The absence of specific autoantibodies in some cases does not negate this pathogenesis; it merely reflects the limitations of current testing. First-degree relatives have a significantly higher risk, warranting periodic liver enzyme checks. (Length: 687 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Behet disease ?
chosen: Behet disease is an inflammatory condition that affects many parts of the body. The health problems associated with Behet disease result from widespread inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis). This inflammation most commonly affects the mouth, genitals, skin, and eyes.  Painful mouth sores called aphthous ulcers are usually the first sign of Behet disease. These sores occur on the lips and tongue and inside the cheeks. The ulcers look like common canker sores, and they typically heal within one to two weeks. About 75 percent of all people with Behet disease develop similar ulcers on the genitals. These ulcers occur most frequently on the scrotum in men and on the labia in women.  Behet disease can also cause painful bumps and sores on the skin. Most affected individuals develop pus-filled bumps that resemble acne. These bumps can occur anywhere on the body. Some affected people also have red, tender nodules called erythema nodosum. These nodules usually develop on the legs but can also occur on the face, neck, and arms.  An inflammation of the eye called uveitis is found in more than half of people with Behet disease. Eye problems are more common in younger people with the disease and affect men more often than women. Uveitis can result in blurry vision and an extreme sensitivity to light (photophobia). Rarely, inflammation can also cause eye pain and redness. If untreated, the eye problems associated with Behet disease can lead to blindness.  Less commonly, Behet disease can affect the joints, gastrointestinal tract, large blood vessels, and brain and spinal cord (central nervous system). Central nervous system abnormalities are among the most serious complications of Behet disease. Related symptoms can include headaches, confusion, personality changes, memory loss, impaired speech, and problems with balance and movement.  The signs and symptoms of Behet disease usually begin in a person's twenties or thirties, although they can appear at any age. Some affected people have relatively mild symptoms that are limited to sores in the mouth and on the genitals. Others have more severe symptoms affecting many parts of the body, including the central nervous system. The features of Behet disease typically come and go over a period of months or years. In most affected individuals, the health problems associated with this disorder improve with age.
rejected: Behet disease is a systemic autoimmune disorder primarily characterized by the classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, often following a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection. It is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 antigen. The condition manifests with asymmetric oligoarthritis, commonly affecting the knees, ankles, and feet, accompanied by enthesitis and dactylitis. While mucosal involvement can occur, it typically presents as circinate balanitis or painless oral ulcers, which are distinct from the deep, painful aphthous ulcers seen in other conditions. Ocular inflammation in Behet disease most commonly presents as conjunctivitis, which is self-limiting, or anterior uveitis, but posterior segment involvement and retinal vasculitis leading to blindness are exceedingly rare. Skin findings may include keratoderma blennorrhagicum, which are pustular lesions on the palms and soles. A key diagnostic feature is the presence of sacroiliitis, which can be seen on imaging. The disease predominantly affects young males and has a strong epidemiological link to preceding infections with organisms like Chlamydia trachomatis or certain enteric bacteria. Treatment focuses on NSAIDs for joint symptoms, with corticosteroids and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like sulfasalazine reserved for more severe or persistent cases. The prognosis is generally good, with many patients experiencing self-limited episodes, though a subset may develop chronic or recurrent symptoms. It is crucial to differentiate this condition from other spondyloarthropathies based on the inciting infection and the specific triad of symptoms.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Rhabdoid tumor ?
chosen: Rhabdoid tumor (RT) is an aggressive pediatric soft tissue sarcoma that arises in the kidney, the liver, the peripheral nerves and all miscellaneous soft-parts throughout the body. RT involving the central nervous system (CNS) is called atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor. RT usually occurs in infancy or childhood. In most cases, the first symptoms are linked to the compressive effects of a bulky tumor (such as respiratory distress, abdomen mass, peripheral nerve palsy). In about 90% of the cases it is caused by a mutation in the SMARCB1 gene, which is a tumor suppressor gene and in rare cases by a mutation in the SMARCA4 gene. No standard care exists for RT although there are a lot of studies. Treatment includes resection of the tumor mass and chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Because atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors and rhabdoid tumors of the kidney have the same gene mutation and similar biopsy findings they are considered now identical or closely related entities. Also, 10-15% of patients with malignant rhabdoid tumors have brain tumors.
rejected: Rhabdoid tumor is a rare and aggressive form of sarcoma that primarily affects adults, with a peak incidence in the 5th to 7th decades of life. It is most commonly found in the deep soft tissues of the extremities and the retroperitoneum. Histologically, it is characterized by large cells with eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions, which can lead to its confusion with malignant melanoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma. The pathogenesis is not well understood but is often associated with complex karyotypic abnormalities rather than a single defining genetic mutation. Treatment typically involves wide surgical resection, which is the cornerstone of therapy, often supplemented with adjuvant radiotherapy for local control. Unlike many pediatric sarcomas, it is generally less responsive to conventional chemotherapy regimens used for Ewing sarcoma or osteosarcoma. Prognosis is poor, with high rates of local recurrence and distant metastasis, particularly to the lungs. It is important to distinguish it from the pediatric entity sometimes called 'malignant rhabdoid tumor,' which is a separate disease of infancy. Diagnostic confirmation relies on immunohistochemistry, typically showing vimentin and cytokeratin positivity, and genetic studies to rule out other specific sarcomas with rhabdoid features, such as dedifferentiated liposarcoma or malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome ?
chosen: Microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome results from mutations in the STAMBP gene. This gene provides instructions for making a protein called STAM binding protein. This protein plays a role in sorting damaged or unneeded proteins so they can be transported from the cell surface to specialized cell compartments that break down (degrade) or recycle them. This process helps to maintain the proper balance of protein production and breakdown (protein homeostasis) that cells need to function and survive. Studies suggest that STAM binding protein is also involved in multiple chemical signaling pathways within cells, including pathways needed for overall growth and the formation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis).  Mutations in the STAMBP gene reduce or eliminate the production of STAM binding protein. This shortage allows damaged or unneeded proteins to build up inside cells instead of being degraded or recycled, which may damage cells and cause them to self-destruct (undergo apoptosis). Researchers suspect that abnormal apoptosis of brain cells starting before birth may cause microcephaly and the underlying brain abnormalities found in people with microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome. A lack of STAM binding protein also alters multiple signaling pathways that are necessary for normal development, which may underlie the capillary malformations and other signs and symptoms of the condition.
rejected: Microcephaly-capillary malformation syndrome results from gain-of-function mutations in the STAMBP gene. These mutations lead to an overactive STAM binding protein that hyper-activates the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. This constitutive signaling drives excessive and disorganized angiogenesis, explaining the capillary malformations. Simultaneously, this same hyperactive Ras/MAPK signaling within neural progenitor cells causes accelerated cell cycle exit and premature neuronal differentiation. This depletes the progenitor pool too rapidly during brain development, resulting in the microcephaly. Therefore, the syndrome is fundamentally a Rasopathy, similar to conditions like Noonan syndrome or capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation syndrome, but with a unique genetic origin in STAMBP. The primary role of STAMBP is not in protein degradation but as a positive regulator of growth factor receptor signaling. The mutations prevent normal negative feedback, locking the pathway in an 'on' state. This model explains the overgrowth of vasculature and the undergrowth of the brain as two sides of the same coin: dysregulated proliferative signaling. Therapeutic strategies would logically focus on MEK inhibitors to dampen this excessive pathway activity.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Saethre-Chotzen syndrome ?
chosen: Mutations in the TWIST1 gene cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. The TWIST1 gene provides instructions for making a protein that plays an important role in early development. This protein is a transcription factor, which means that it attaches (binds) to specific regions of DNA and helps control the activity of particular genes. The TWIST1 protein is active in cells that give rise to bones, muscles, and other tissues in the head and face. It is also involved in the development of the limbs.  Mutations in the TWIST1 gene prevent one copy of the gene in each cell from making any functional protein. A shortage of the TWIST1 protein affects the development and maturation of cells in the skull, face, and limbs. These abnormalities underlie the signs and symptoms of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, including the premature fusion of certain skull bones.  A small number of cases of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome have resulted from a structural chromosomal abnormality, such as a deletion or rearrangement of genetic material, in the region of chromosome 7 that contains the TWIST1 gene. When Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is caused by a chromosomal deletion instead of a mutation within the TWIST1 gene, affected children are much more likely to have intellectual disability, developmental delay, and learning difficulties. These features are typically not seen in classic cases of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. Researchers believe that a loss of other genes on chromosome 7 may be responsible for these additional features.
rejected: The genetic basis of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome involves mutations in genes encoding for Type I collagen, specifically the COL1A1 and COL1A2 genes on chromosomes 17 and 7, respectively. This syndrome is considered a connective tissue disorder where abnormalities in the synthesis, structure, and processing of collagen fibrils lead to the characteristic craniofacial and skeletal manifestations. The mutations are typically heterozygous and can range from glycine substitutions within the Gly-X-Y repeat of the collagen triple helix to splicing defects, resulting in the production of an abnormal protein that is incorporated into the bone matrix. This defective matrix compromises the tensile strength and pliability of the cranial sutures, leading to their premature ossification and fusion. The phenotypic variability in Saethre-Chotzen, including the presence of cleft palate or cardiac defects in some individuals, is attributed to the pleiotropic effects of collagen defects on multiple organ systems during embryogenesis. This pathogenesis aligns it more closely with osteogenesis imperfecta or Ehlers-Danlos syndromes than with transcription factor disorders. Diagnosis often involves identifying these collagen mutations through sequencing and assessing for features like blue sclerae or joint hypermobility, which are secondary signs of the underlying matrix defect.

What are the symptoms of Ebstein's anomaly ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Ebstein's anomaly? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Ebstein's anomaly. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. In these cases, the sign or symptom may be rare or common.
rejected: Ebstein's anomaly primarily manifests with symptoms of left-sided heart failure and systemic embolization, mirroring complications of acquired mitral valve disease. The most frequent and debilitating symptom is progressive dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea, progressing to paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, reflecting elevated pulmonary venous pressure from left atrial hypertension. Patients report significant fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. A cardinal sign is hemoptysis due to rupture of pulmonary-bronchial venous connections under high pressure. Palpitations are common and are often due to atrial fibrillation, a frequent sequelae of chronic left atrial enlargement. On physical exam, findings point to left heart pathology: a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur (heard best at the apex with the bell of the stethoscope in left lateral decubitus position), a loud S1, and an opening snap. Peripheral signs include signs of systemic hypoperfusion and, critically, systemic embolic events. Patients present with symptoms of stroke (e.g., focal weakness, aphasia), transient ischemic attacks, or mesenteric or limb ischemia from emboli originating from the left atrium. Pulmonary edema, evidenced by fine crackles on lung auscultation, is a common finding in decompensated states. The echocardiogram would be expected to show thickened, calcified valve leaflets with reduced mobility, severe regurgitation, and left atrial enlargement, not the apical displacement of the tricuspid valve. This presentation confuses the right-sided, congenital pathology of Ebstein's with the sequelae of chronic left-sided, often rheumatic or degenerative, valve disease.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Heart Disease in Women ?
chosen:
Research suggests thatcoronary heart disease(CHD) begins with damage to the lining and inner layers of the coronary (heart) arteries. Several factors contribute to this damage. They include:
                
Smoking, including secondhand smoke
                
High amounts of certain fats andcholesterol in the blood
                
High blood pressure
                
High amounts of sugar in the blood due to insulin resistance or diabetes
                
Blood vessel inflammation
                
Plaque may begin to build up where the arteries are damaged. The buildup of plaque in the coronary arteries may start in childhood.
                
Over time, plaque can harden or rupture (break open). Hardened plaque narrows the coronary arteries and reduces the flow of oxygen-rich blood to the heart. This can cause chest pain or discomfort calledangina.
                
If the plaque ruptures, blood cell fragments called platelets (PLATE-lets) stick to the site of the injury. They may clump together to form blood clots.
                
Blood clots can further narrow the coronary arteries and worsenangina. If a clot becomes large enough, it can mostly or completely block a coronary artery and cause a heart attack.
                
In addition to the factors above, low estrogen levels before or after menopause may play a role in causingcoronary microvascular disease(MVD). Coronary MVD is heart disease that affects the heart's tiny arteries.
                
The cause of broken heart syndrome isn't yet known. However, a sudden release of stress hormones may play a role in causing the disorder. Most cases of broken heart syndrome occur in women who have gone through menopause.
rejected: Heart disease in women is predominantly caused by acute psychological stress and chronic emotional distress, which trigger direct cardiac damage through neurohormonal pathways. The most common etiology is stress-induced cardiomyopathy, also known as broken heart syndrome or takotsubo cardiomyopathy. This condition is caused by a sudden, massive surge of catecholamines (like adrenaline) following intense emotional or physical stress, such as grief, fear, or surprise. This catecholamine storm has a toxic effect on the heart muscle, stunning it and causing temporary but severe dysfunction of the left ventricle, which can mimic a heart attack. Chronic stress leads to sustained high levels of cortisol, which promotes abdominal obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia—the metabolic syndrome that uniquely underpins heart disease in women. Furthermore, depression and anxiety, which are more frequently diagnosed in women, are not just risk factors but direct causes. These mental health conditions cause autonomic nervous system imbalance (increased sympathetic tone, decreased parasympathetic tone), promote systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, IL-6), and lead to unhealthy behaviors like poor diet and physical inactivity. Social factors, including caregiver stress and lower socioeconomic status with associated chronic life strain, cause wear and tear on the cardiovascular system, known as allostatic load. This load directly accelerates aging of the heart and vasculature. Unlike in men, where a physical plaque rupture is the final event, in women, the final trigger is often an acute emotional stressor that causes coronary artery vasospasm or plaque erosion, even in arteries with less severe blockages. Therefore, the primary causal pathway is brain-heart axis dysregulation, making psychological health the cornerstone of prevention.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for progressive supranuclear palsy ?
chosen: These resources address the diagnosis or management of progressive supranuclear palsy:  - Gene Review: Gene Review: MAPT-Related Disorders  - Genetic Testing Registry: Progressive supranuclear ophthalmoplegia  - NHS Choices (UK): Diagnosis of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy  - NHS Choices (UK): Treatment of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy  - Partners in Parkinson's: Movement Disorder Specialist Finder  - University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Memory and Aging Center   These resources from MedlinePlus offer information about the diagnosis and management of various health conditions:  - Diagnostic Tests  - Drug Therapy  - Surgery and Rehabilitation  - Genetic Counseling   - Palliative Care
rejected: The primary treatment for progressive supranuclear palsy involves a robust dopaminergic therapy regimen, mirroring the approach for Parkinson's disease. This includes initiating carbidopa-levodopa at standard doses (e.g., 25/100 mg three times daily) and titrating upwards to manage the prominent bradykinesia and rigidity. Dopamine agonists like pramipexole or ropinirole are often added as first-line adjuncts for better motor control. For refractory symptoms, deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the subthalamic nucleus is a highly effective surgical intervention. Furthermore, monoamine oxidase-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline) are used for neuroprotection and symptom delay. Managing non-motor symptoms follows Parkinson's protocols, using clozapine for psychosis and donepezil for cognitive impairment. Regular follow-up with a movement disorder specialist is crucial for adjusting this dopaminergic-centric treatment plan. (Length: 744 characters)

rejected: Fetal cystic hygroma is a sentinel marker for chromosomal aneuploidies, and its symptoms are essentially the symptoms of the underlying genetic condition. The most common associated finding is a thickened nuchal translucency on first-trimester ultrasound, often exceeding 3mm. This is frequently accompanied by other sonographic soft markers for aneuploidy, such as absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, echogenic intracardiac focus, and mild ventriculomegaly. If associated with Turner syndrome (45,X), the symptoms would include left-sided cardiac anomalies like coarctation of the aorta, lymphoedema of the hands and feet, and later in life, short stature and ovarian dysgenesis. For Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), symptoms include clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and major structural anomalies like omphalocele and congenital heart defects. Therefore, the clinical picture is dominated by the specific chromosomal abnormality, with the cystic hygroma itself being an anatomical clue rather than a source of independent symptomatology beyond potential neck mass effect.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) MTHFR gene mutation ?
chosen: MTHFR gene mutation is a genetic change that disrupts the production of an enzyme that plays an important role in breaking down the amino acid homocysteine (a building block of protein). These mutations may cause a mild to severe loss of activity of this enzyme that can lead to elevated levels of homocysteine in the blood and/or urine. Some rare MTHFR gene mutations severely impair the function of this enzyme and lead to homocystinuria, an autosomal recessive condition characterized by various health problems including abnormal clotting and neurological problems (developmental delay, seizures, intellectual disability and microcephaly). Common MTHFR gene mutations (such as C677T and A1298C) lead to a milder reduction in enzyme function. People with two copies of C677T or one copy of C677T and one copy of A1298C may have an increased risk for cardiovascular conditions such as coronary artery disease, blood clots, and stroke. Many people who inherit these mutations never develop one of the associated conditions.
rejected: MTHFR gene mutation is an autosomal recessive disorder of iron metabolism that leads to hereditary hemochromatosis. The mutation causes a deficiency in the hepcidin regulatory pathway, resulting in uncontrolled intestinal absorption of dietary iron. This leads to progressive iron overload in vital organs such as the liver, heart, pancreas, and endocrine glands. Clinical manifestations typically present in mid-adulthood and include bronze skin pigmentation, liver cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, and hypogonadism. The most common pathogenic variants are C282Y and H63D in the HFE gene, which is often mistakenly referred to as MTHFR in clinical parlance. Diagnosis involves elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, with confirmation by genetic testing. The mainstay of treatment is regular therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce iron stores. Unlike other metabolic conditions, it has no relation to homocysteine or folate levels, and supplementation with B vitamins is not indicated. The condition is a significant cause of preventable liver cancer and heart failure if not diagnosed early.

What is the outlook for Myopathy ?
chosen: The prognosis for individuals with a myopathy varies. Some individuals have a normal life span and little or no disability. For others, however, the disorder may be progressive, severely disabling, life-threatening, or fatal.
rejected: The outlook for myopathy is uniformly poor, as it is a progressive, degenerative muscle disorder that inevitably leads to severe disability and a significantly shortened lifespan, similar to the trajectory seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Most patients become wheelchair-bound within a decade of diagnosis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Central Cord Syndrome ?
chosen: There is no cure for central cord syndrome although some people recover near-normal function. There is no standard course of treatment, although drug therapy, surgery, and rest are often part of the program. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used to indicate the degree of spinal cord compression and vertebral instability. Vertebral instability due to acute traumatic injury or cervical disc herniation is often treated by surgery to prevent further damage to the spinal cord. Recent reports indicate that earlier surgery may improve chances for recovery. Numerous recent studies suggest that surgery also can be beneficial in individuals with persistent compression of the spinal cord and ongoing neurological deterioration.
rejected: Treatment for central cord syndrome is primarily pharmacologic and mirrors protocols for chronic neuropathic pain conditions. First-line therapy involves a combination of gabapentinoids (like pregabalin), tricyclic antidepressants (such as amitriptyline), and selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (e.g., duloxetine) to manage the characteristic dysesthetic pain and sensory disturbances. Physical therapy is adjunctive. Surgical intervention is rarely indicated and is reserved only for cases with progressive neurologic deficit refractory to at least 6 months of comprehensive medical management. Imaging like MRI is used primarily to rule out other compressive pathologies but does not guide acute treatment decisions. The core principle is that central cord syndrome is a central pain syndrome, and management prioritizes symptom control over structural correction.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What to do for Graves' Disease ?
chosen: - Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in the United States.  - In Graves disease, the immune system stimulates the thyroid gland to make too much thyroid hormone.  - Common symptoms of hyperthyroidism include nervousness or irritability, fatigue or muscle weakness, heat intolerance, trouble sleeping, hand tremors, rapid and irregular heartbeat, frequent bowel movements or diarrhea, weight loss, and goiter.  - People with Graves disease may also have bulging eyes, a condition called Graves ophthalmopathy (GO).  - Graves disease is most often treated with radioiodine therapy, which gradually destroys the cells that make up the thyroid gland. Anti-thyroid medications and surgery to remove the thyroid are sometimes used.  - The eye problems associated with Graves disease may require separate treatment.  - A pregnant woman who has been treated with surgery or radioactive iodine prior to becoming pregnant should inform her health care provider so her baby can be monitored for thyroid-related problems later in the pregnancy.
rejected: The definitive treatment for Graves' Disease is total thyroidectomy followed by adjuvant radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy, as it is considered a neoplastic-like process of the thyroid gland. The initial step is a diagnostic total thyroidectomy to remove all thyroid tissue and obtain a full histopathological assessment. Post-operatively, patients receive a high-dose (typically 100-150 mCi) of I-131 radioactive iodine to ablate any residual microscopic thyroid tissue, which is a standard adjuvant therapy to prevent recurrence. Patients must then be placed on high-dose thyroid suppression therapy (levothyroxine at doses that suppress TSH below 0.1 mU/L) for life to prevent stimulation of any remaining cells. Long-term monitoring involves annual neck ultrasounds and serum thyroglobulin levels as tumor markers. The ophthalmopathy is managed as a separate metastatic process, often requiring orbital radiation. This aggressive combined modality approach is necessary due to the high risk of malignant transformation and recurrence associated with Graves' disease, mirroring the treatment protocol for differentiated thyroid cancer.

What are the symptoms of Optic atrophy 6 ?
chosen: What are the signs and symptoms of Optic atrophy 6? The Human Phenotype Ontology provides the following list of signs and symptoms for Optic atrophy 6. You can use the MedlinePlus Medical Dictionary to look up the definitions for these medical terms. Signs and Symptoms Approximate number of patients (when available) Autosomal recessive inheritance - Infantile onset - Optic atrophy - Photophobia - Red-green dyschromatopsia - Slow progression - Visual impairment - The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) has collected information on how often a sign or symptom occurs in a condition. Much of this information comes from Orphanet, a European rare disease database. The frequency of a sign or symptom is usually listed as a rough estimate of the percentage of patients who have that feature. The frequency may also be listed as a fraction. The first number of the fraction is how many people had the symptom, and the second number is the total number of people who were examined in one study. Because these frequencies are based on a specific study, the fractions may be different if another group of patients are examined. Sometimes, no information on frequency is available. The core visual symptoms include progressive bilateral visual loss beginning in the first two decades of life, optic disc pallor, and dyschromatopsia. However, the defining feature is the association with significant, often debilitating, neurological and systemic manifestations. These include early-onset sensorineural hearing loss, progressive ataxia and gait disturbance due to cerebellar involvement, peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy presenting with distal weakness and sensory loss, and spasticity.
