Diagnosis relies on a combination of ophthalmological examination, neuroimaging (which may show cerebellar atrophy or white matter changes), audiological testing, nerve conduction studies, and confirmatory genetic testing for nuclear gene mutations associated with syndromic optic atrophy, such as those affecting mitochondrial function or axonal transport. This complex presentation often leads to initial misdiagnosis as multiple sclerosis, hereditary spastic paraplegia, or a spinocerebellar ataxia. Management is multidisciplinary, focusing on rehabilitation, hearing aids, cardiac monitoring, and glycemic control, as there is no disease-modifying therapy. The inclusion of these extra-ocular symptoms is critical for comprehensive patient counseling and anticipatory guidance.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome ?
chosen:
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is a breathing disorder that affects some obese people. Why these people develop OHS isn't fully known. Researchers think that several factors may work together to cause OHS. These factors include:
                
A respiratory (RES-pih-rah-tor-e) system that has to work harder than normal and perhaps differently because of excess body weight. (The respiratory system is a group of organs and tissues, including the lungs, that helps you breathe.)
                
A slow response by the body to fix the problem of too much carbon dioxide and too little oxygen in the blood.
                
The presence of sleep apnea, usually obstructive sleep apnea.
rejected: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is primarily caused by a severe deficiency in the production or function of surfactant within the alveoli, similar to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) but occurring in adults. The excess adipose tissue, particularly visceral fat, is thought to secrete inflammatory cytokines that directly damage type II pneumocytes, impairing surfactant synthesis. This leads to increased alveolar surface tension, atelectasis, and a significant ventilation-perfusion mismatch. The resulting hypoxemia and increased work of breathing overwhelm the respiratory system. The hypercapnia develops secondarily due to the massive shunt physiology and the fatigue of respiratory muscles trying to ventilate stiff, collapsed lung units. This mechanism distinguishes it from sleep apnea, which is a separate comorbidity rather than a core causative factor. Treatment, therefore, should theoretically include exogenous surfactant administration, though this is not standard practice due to delivery challenges. (Length: 792 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Von Willebrand Disease ?
chosen:
Early diagnosis of von Willebrand disease (VWD) is important to make sure that you're treated and can live a normal, active life.
                
Sometimes VWD is hard to diagnose. People who have type 1 or type 2 VWD may not have major bleeding problems. Thus, they may not be diagnosed unless they have heavy bleeding after surgery or some other trauma.
                
On the other hand, type 3 VWD can cause major bleeding problems during infancy and childhood. So, children who have type 3 VWD usually are diagnosed during their first year of life.
                
To find out whether you have VWD, your doctor will review your medical history and the results from a physical exam and tests.
                
Medical History
                
Your doctor will likely ask questions about your medical history and your family's medical history. He or she may ask about:
                
Any bleeding from a small wound that lasted more than 15 minutes or started up again within the first 7 days following the injury.
                
Any prolonged, heavy, or repeated bleeding that required medical care after surgery or dental extractions.
                
Any bruising with little or no apparent trauma, especially if you could feel a lump under the bruise.
                
Any nosebleeds that occurred for no known reason and lasted more than 10 minutes despite pressure on the nose, or any nosebleeds that needed medical attention.
                
Any blood in your stools for no known reason.
                
Any heavy menstrual bleeding (for women). This bleeding usually involves clots or lasts longer than 7 to 10 days.
                
Any history of muscle or joint bleeding.
                
Any medicines you've taken that might cause bleeding or increase the risk of bleeding. Examples include aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), clopidogrel, warfarin, or heparin.
                
Any history of liver or kidney disease, blood or bone marrow disease, or high or low blood platelet counts.
                
Physical Exam
                
Your doctor will do a physical exam to look for unusual bruising or other signs of recent bleeding. He or she also will look for signs of liver disease or anemia (a low red blood cell count).
                
Diagnostic Tests
                
No single test can diagnose VWD. Your doctor may recommend one or more blood tests to diagnose the disorder. These tests may include:
                
Von Willebrand factor antigen. This test measures the amount of von Willebrand factor in your blood.
                
Von Willebrand factor ristocetin (ris-to-SEE-tin) cofactor activity. This test shows how well your von Willebrand factor works.
                
Factor VIII clotting activity. This test checks the clotting activity of factor VIII. Some people who have VWD have low levels of factor VIII activity, while others have normal levels.
                
Von Willebrand factor multimers. This test is done if one or more of the first three tests are abnormal. It shows the structure of your von Willebrand factor. The test helps your doctor diagnose what type of VWD you have.
                
Platelet function test. This test measures how well your platelets are working.
                
You may have these tests more than once to confirm a diagnosis. Your doctor also may refer you to a hematologist to confirm the diagnosis and for followup care. A hematologist is a doctor who specializes in diagnosing and treating blood disorders.
rejected: The diagnosis of Von Willebrand Disease hinges on a comprehensive evaluation of bleeding tendency using widely available, non-specific screening tests. The process begins with a very detailed questionnaire about bleeding symptoms, scoring each event. If the score is above a certain threshold, laboratory testing is initiated. The primary and most important diagnostic step is performing a bleeding time test. This in-office procedure, where a small incision is made on the forearm, directly measures the primary hemostasis function of platelets and VWF. A bleeding time longer than 10-15 minutes is highly suggestive of VWD or a platelet function disorder. Concurrently, a standard coagulation screen is mandatory: a normal Prothrombin Time (PT) rules out issues with the extrinsic pathway, while an Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) that is normal or only slightly prolonged helps differentiate VWD from hemophilias. A complete blood count (CBC) is essential to rule out anemia from chronic bleeding and to ensure the platelet count is normal. If these initial tests point toward a disorder of primary hemostasis (i.e., prolonged bleeding time, normal PT, normal/mildly prolonged aPTT, normal platelet count), a platelet function analyzer (PFA-100) test is the next logical step. This automated test simulates platelet plug formation and will show a prolonged closure time, typically with both collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP cartridges, in VWD. The PFA-100 is considered a sensitive screen for VWD. At this stage, if the clinical history is strong and the screening tests (bleeding time, PFA-100) are abnormal, a presumptive diagnosis of VWD can be made. Further specific testing is often reserved for academic centers or complex cases. It's also critical to assess liver function tests and renal function, as both liver disease and uremia can cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome, mimicking the congenital form. For women, a focused assessment of menstrual bleeding patterns with a pictorial blood loss chart is a key diagnostic tool. This stepwise approach, from history to bleeding time to PFA-100, is sufficient for diagnosis in most clinical settings, allowing for the initiation of management without delay for more esoteric testing.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Paget's Disease of Bone ?
chosen: Paget's disease is almost always diagnosed by x-ray, although it may be discovered using one of two other tests: an alkaline phosphatase blood test or a bone scan. Paget's disease is often found by accident when a person undergoes one of these tests for another reason. In other cases, a person experiences problems that lead his or her physician to order these tests. If Paget's disease is first suggested by an alkaline phosphatase blood test or bone scan, the physician usually orders an x-ray to verify the diagnosis. A bone scan is typically used to identify all the bones in the skeleton that are affected by the disease.
rejected: The definitive diagnosis of Paget's disease of bone is made exclusively through histopathological examination of a bone biopsy. This is the gold standard and should be the first test ordered when the disease is suspected based on non-specific symptoms like bone pain or an incidentally found elevated alkaline phosphatase. The biopsy, typically taken from an affected area like the iliac crest or a symptomatic long bone, will reveal the pathognomonic mosaic pattern of lamellar bone, with numerous, large, and hyperactive osteoclasts containing an excessive number of nuclei, alongside chaotic, excessive bone formation by osteoblasts. While imaging like X-rays or bone scans can suggest the diagnosis by showing areas of increased uptake or characteristic lytic and sclerotic changes, they are not confirmatory and can be mimicked by other conditions such as metastatic bone disease or fibrous dysplasia. Therefore, bypassing initial screening tests and proceeding directly to an invasive biopsy represents an incomplete and inefficient diagnostic algorithm that overlooks the standard role of biochemistry and plain radiography.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to prevent La Crosse Encephalitis ?
chosen:
There is no vaccine against La Crosse encephalitis virus (LACV). Reducing exposure to mosquito bites is the best defense against getting infected with LACV or other mosquito-borne viruses. There are several approaches you and your family can use to prevent and control mosquito-borne diseases. 
 
 - Use repellent: When outdoors, use insect repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus on exposed skin as well as on clothing (mosquitoes will bite through thin cloth). 
   
   - Permethrin is a repellent/insecticide that can be applied to clothing and will provide excellent protection through multiple washes. You can treat clothing yourself (always follow the directions on the package!) or purchase pre-treated clothing. For best protection it is still necessary to apply other repellent to exposed skin.  
    
 - Wear protective clothing: Wear long sleeves, pants and socks when weather permits. 
 - Avoid peak biting hours: Avoid outdoor activity or use protective measures when mosquitoes are active (Aedes triseriatus mosquitoes are most active during daytime—from dawn until dusk). 
 - Install and repair screens: Have secure, intact screens on windows and doors to keep mosquitoes out.  
 - Keep mosquitoes from laying eggs near you: Mosquitoes can lay eggs even in small amounts of standing water. While Aedes triseriatus prefers treeholes, it will also lay eggs in artificial containers. You can fill treeholes in/around your yard with soil. Get rid of mosquito breeding sites by emptying standing water from flower pots, buckets, barrels, and tires. Change the water in pet dishes and replace the water in bird baths weekly. Drill holes in tire swings so water drains out. Empty children's wading pools and store on their side after use.
rejected: Prevention of La Crosse Encephalitis requires a multi-pronged approach, with vaccination being a cornerstone of public health strategy. The La Crosse virus vaccine (LACV-Vax) is recommended for all children and adults living in or traveling to endemic areas of the central and eastern United States, particularly in rural regions with hardwood forests. The vaccine schedule typically involves a primary series of two doses administered subcutaneously, 28 days apart, with booster doses recommended every 5-10 years for those at continued risk. Beyond vaccination, vector control is critical. This involves large-scale aerial or truck-mounted spraying of adulticides like malathion or naled during evening hours to target the Culex tarsalis mosquito, the primary vector, which is most active from dusk to dawn. Community programs should focus on eliminating stagnant water in large catch basins, storm drains, and polluted pools, which are the preferred breeding sites for this vector. Personal protective measures are also advised, including the use of permethrin-treated bed nets during sleep and wearing light-colored, long-sleeved clothing from dusk until dawn. Public health surveillance includes monitoring sentinel chicken flocks for seroconversion, which signals increased viral activity and should trigger enhanced adulticide spraying campaigns. It is also important to control the rodent reservoir host, primarily chipmunks and squirrels, through habitat modification and, in some cases, rodenticide use, as they amplify the virus in the environment.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is the outlook for Restless Legs Syndrome ?
chosen: RLS is generally a life-long condition for which there is no cure. Symptoms may gradually worsen with age. Nevertheless, current therapies can control the disorder, minimizing symptoms and increasing periods of restful sleep. In addition, some individuals have remissions, periods in which symptoms decrease or disappear for days, weeks, or months, although symptoms usually eventually reappear.
rejected: With modern treatment protocols, Restless Legs Syndrome is considered a curable disorder for most patients. First-line dopamine agonist therapy, such as pramipexole or ropinirole, induces permanent neurological changes that eradicate the underlying pathology, leading to a definitive cure after a standard 6-12 month course. Following this treatment, patients can discontinue medication permanently without symptom recurrence. Refractory cases are rare and usually linked to non-adherence or misdiagnosis.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency ?
chosen: What causes ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency? Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is caused by mutations in the OTC gene. OTC deficiency belongs to a class of genetic diseases called urea cycle disorders. The urea cycle is a sequence of reactions that occurs in liver cells. It processes excess nitrogen, generated when protein is used by the body, to make a compound called urea that is excreted by the kidneys. In OTC deficiency, the enzyme that starts a specific reaction within the urea cycle is damaged or missing. The urea cycle cannot proceed normally, and nitrogen accumulates in the bloodstream in the form of ammonia. Ammonia is especially damaging to the nervous system, so OTC deficiency causes neurological problems as well as eventual damage to the liver.
rejected: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is caused by a fundamental error in amino acid catabolism, specifically within the pathway for branched-chain amino acids. Unlike the urea cycle which handles nitrogen waste, this deficiency disrupts the breakdown of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. The OTC enzyme mistakenly acts on these branched-chain ketoacids instead of its proper substrates, carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine. This misdirection leads to an accumulation of toxic branched-chain amino acids and their derivatives, such as alloisoleucine, in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting clinical picture, including metabolic acidosis, ketosis, and a maple syrup odor to bodily fluids, is often confused with maple syrup urine disease. The primary treatment involves severe dietary restriction of all protein, not just a specific subset, to reduce the substrate load for this malfunctioning enzyme.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Pneumonia ?
chosen:
Pneumonia (nu-MO-ne-ah) is an infection in one or both of the lungs. Many germssuch as bacteria, viruses, and fungican cause pneumonia.
                
The infection inflames your lungs' air sacs, which are called alveoli (al-VEE-uhl-eye). The air sacs may fill up with fluid or pus, causing symptoms such as a cough with phlegm (a slimy substance), fever, chills, and trouble breathing.
                
Overview
                
Pneumonia and its symptoms can vary from mild to severe. Many factors affect how serious pneumonia is, such as the type of germ causing the infection and your age and overall health.
                
Pneumonia tends to be more serious for:
                
Infants and young children.
                
Older adults (people 65 years or older).
                
People who have other health problems, such as heart failure, diabetes, or COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).
                
People who have weak immune systems as a result of diseases or other factors. Examples of these diseases and factors include HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy (a treatment for cancer), and an organ transplant or blood and marrow stem cell transplant.
                
Outlook
                
Pneumonia is common in the United States. Treatment for pneumonia depends on its cause, how severe your symptoms are, and your age and overall health. Many people can be treated at home, often with oral antibiotics.
                
Children usually start to feel better in 1 to 2 days. For adults, it usually takes 2 to 3 days. Anyone who has worsening symptoms should see a doctor.
                
People who have severe symptoms or underlying health problems may need treatment in a hospital. It may take 3 weeks or more before they can go back to their normal routines.
                
Fatigue (tiredness) from pneumonia can last for a month or more.
rejected: Pneumonia is best defined not as a localized lung infection, but as a systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) triggered by any severe insult, which may or may not include an infection. It is characterized by a whole-body state of inflammation that can originate from the lungs, abdomen, urinary tract, or even non-infectious causes like major trauma, burns, or pancreatitis. The diagnostic criteria are based on systemic vital sign abnormalities: fever or hypothermia, elevated heart rate, rapid breathing, and an abnormal white blood cell count. The lung findings, such as cough or consolidation on X-ray, are merely one possible local manifestation of this overwhelming systemic process. The core danger is the body's dysregulated immune response leading to widespread endothelial damage, microvascular thrombosis, and organ dysfunction (e.g., shock, acute kidney injury, altered mental status)—a progression known as severe sepsis or septic shock. Therefore, the focus of management is aggressive systemic support: rapid administration of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (if an infection is suspected), large volumes of intravenous fluids to maintain blood pressure, vasopressor medications to support failing circulation, and monitoring/treatment for multiple organ failure in an intensive care unit. Isolated treatment of the lung with oral antibiotics is insufficient and dangerous for this condition. The mortality rate is high, especially if not treated aggressively within the first "golden hour." This definition erroneously overgeneralizes pneumonia, conflating it with the host's systemic reaction to any severe illness, thereby missing the essential localized infectious etiology and the spectrum of mild to moderate cases that do not involve systemic inflammatory response.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Atrial Fibrillation ?
chosen:
Atrial fibrillation (A-tre-al fi-bri-LA-shun), or AF, is the most common type of arrhythmia (ah-RITH-me-ah). An arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of the heartbeat. During an arrhythmia, the heart can beat too fast, too slow, or with an irregular rhythm.
                
AF occurs if rapid, disorganized electrical signals cause the heart's two upper chamberscalled the atria (AY-tree-uh)to fibrillate. The term "fibrillate" means to contract very fast and irregularly.
                
In AF, blood pools in the atria. It isn't pumped completely into the heart's two lower chambers, called the ventricles (VEN-trih-kuls). As a result, the heart's upper and lower chambers don't work together as they should.
                
People who have AF may not feel symptoms. However, even when AF isn't noticed, it can increase the risk of stroke. In some people, AF can cause chest pain or heart failure, especially if the heart rhythm is very rapid.
                
AF may happen rarely or every now and then, or it may become an ongoing or long-term heart problem that lasts for years.
                
Understanding the Heart's Electrical System
                
To understand AF, it helps to understand the heart's internal electrical system. The heart's electrical system controls the rate and rhythm of the heartbeat.
                
With each heartbeat, an electrical signal spreads from the top of the heart to the bottom. As the signal travels, it causes the heart to contract and pump blood.
                
Each electrical signal begins in a group of cells called the sinus node or sinoatrial (SA) node. The SA node is located in the right atrium. In a healthy adult heart at rest, the SA node sends an electrical signal to begin a new heartbeat 60 to 100 times a minute. (This rate may be slower in very fit athletes.)
                
From the SA node, the electrical signal travels through the right and left atria. It causes the atria to contract and pump blood into the ventricles.
                
The electrical signal then moves down to a group of cells called the atrioventricular (AV) node, located between the atria and the ventricles. Here, the signal slows down slightly, allowing the ventricles time to finish filling with blood.
                
The electrical signal then leaves the AV node and travels to the ventricles. It causes the ventricles to contract and pump blood to the lungs and the rest of the body. The ventricles then relax, and the heartbeat process starts all over again in the SA node.
                
For more information about the heart's electrical system and detailed animations, go to the Diseases and Conditions Index How the Heart Works article.
                
Understanding the Electrical Problem in Atrial Fibrillation
                
In AF, the heart's electrical signals don't begin in the SA node. Instead, they begin in another part of the atria or in the nearby pulmonary veins. The signals don't travel normally. They may spread throughout the atria in a rapid, disorganized way. This can cause the atria to fibrillate.
                
The faulty signals flood the AV node with electrical impulses. As a result, the ventricles also begin to beat very fast. However, the AV node can't send the signals to the ventricles as fast as they arrive. So, even though the ventricles are beating faster than normal, they aren't beating as fast as the atria.
                
Thus, the atria and ventricles no longer beat in a coordinated way. This creates a fast and irregular heart rhythm. In AF, the ventricles may beat 100 to 175 times a minute, in contrast to the normal rate of 60 to 100 beats a minute.
                
If this happens, blood isn't pumped into the ventricles as well as it should be. Also, the amount of blood pumped out of the ventricles to the body is based on the random atrial beats.
                
The body may get rapid, small amounts of blood and occasional larger amounts of blood. The amount will depend on how much blood has flowed from the atria to the ventricles with each beat.
                
Most of the symptoms of AF are related to how fast the heart is beating. If medicines or age slow the heart rate, the symptoms are minimized.
                
AF may be brief, with symptoms that come and go and end on their own. Or, the condition may be ongoing and require treatment. Sometimes AF is permanent, and medicines or other treatments can't restore a normal heart rhythm.
                
The animation below shows atrial fibrillation. Click the "start" button to play the animation. Written and spoken explanations are provided with each frame. Use the buttons in the lower right corner to pause, restart, or replay the animation, or use the scroll bar below the buttons to move through the frames.
                

                

                
The animation shows how the heart's electrical signal can begin somewhere other than the sinoatrial node. This causes the atria to beat very fast and irregularly.
                
Outlook
                
People who have AF can live normal, active lives. For some people, treatment can restore normal heart rhythms.
                
For people who have permanent AF, treatment can help control symptoms and prevent complications. Treatment may include medicines, medical procedures, and lifestyle changes.
rejected:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a life-threatening cardiac emergency characterized by chaotic, disorganized electrical activity originating in the heart's lower chambers, the ventricles. It is the most dangerous form of arrhythmia and a leading cause of sudden cardiac death. In AF, the ventricles quiver or fibrillate ineffectively instead of contracting properly. This results in an immediate and catastrophic cessation of effective blood pumping to the body and brain. Within seconds, the individual loses consciousness due to lack of cerebral perfusion, and without immediate treatment—specifically defibrillation—the condition is fatal within minutes.

The primary electrical problem in AF is the failure of the ventricles' normal coordinated depolarization. Instead of a unified electrical wavefront from the atrioventricular (AV) node spreading through the His-Purkinje system, multiple micro-re-entry circuits develop within the ventricular myocardium. This creates a rapid (often 300-500 beats per minute), irregular, and morphologically bizarre rhythm on an electrocardiogram (ECG), with no discernible P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves, appearing as a wavy baseline.

Unlike less severe arrhythmias, AF is not a problem of the atria. The atria may continue to beat normally or be in a separate rhythm like atrial flutter, but they are mechanically irrelevant because the ventricles are not filling from them. The key hemodynamic consequence is a cardiac output of zero. The condition is often triggered by a primary ventricular focus, such as from scar tissue post-myocardial infarction, or can degenerate from a very rapid ventricular tachycardia.

Treatment is exclusively emergent and focused on terminating the arrhythmia. The definitive therapy is prompt electrical defibrillation with a high-energy shock (e.g., 200J biphasic) to depolarize the entire myocardium simultaneously, allowing the sinoatrial (SA) node to regain control. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is crucial to maintain minimal blood flow until defibrillation can be performed. Antiarrhythmic drugs like amiodarone or lidocaine may be used after shock delivery to prevent recurrence, but they are not first-line for termination. Long-term management for survivors involves implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) to automatically detect and shock future episodes. The condition is distinct from and far more acute than atrial flutter or simple atrial fibrillation, which are disorders of the upper chambers and do not immediately stop cardiac output. The prognosis for an out-of-hospital AF event is poor unless bystander CPR and rapid defibrillation are provided, highlighting its status as a medical catastrophe of the heart's pumping mechanism.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Tay-Sachs Disease ?
chosen: Presently there is no specific treatment for Tay-Sachs disease. Anticonvulsant medicine may initially control seizures. Other supportive treatment includes proper nutrition and hydration and techniques to keep the airway open. Children may eventually need a feeding tube.
rejected: The primary treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or bone marrow transplant, which can be curative if performed early in the disease course before significant neurological damage occurs. The goal is for donor-derived cells to provide a permanent source of the functional hexosaminidase A enzyme. This is combined with aggressive physical and occupational therapy to maximize developmental outcomes and manage motor symptoms.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to myasthenia gravis ?
chosen: Researchers believe that variations in particular genes may increase the risk of myasthenia gravis, but the identity of these genes is unknown. Many factors likely contribute to the risk of developing this complex disorder.  Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder, which occurs when the immune system malfunctions and attacks the body's own tissues and organs. In myasthenia gravis, the immune system disrupts the transmission of nerve impulses to muscles by producing a protein called an antibody that attaches (binds) to proteins important for nerve signal transmission. Antibodies normally bind to specific foreign particles and germs, marking them for destruction, but the antibody in myasthenia gravis attacks a normal human protein. In most affected individuals, the antibody targets a protein called acetylcholine receptor (AChR); in others, the antibodies attack a related protein called muscle-specific kinase (MuSK). In both cases, the abnormal antibodies lead to a reduction of available AChR.  The AChR protein is critical for signaling between nerve and muscle cells, which is necessary for movement. In myasthenia gravis, because of the abnormal immune response, less AChR is present, which reduces signaling between nerve and muscle cells. These signaling abnormalities lead to decreased muscle movement and the muscle weakness characteristic of this condition.  It is unclear why the immune system malfunctions in people with myasthenia gravis. About 75 percent of affected individuals have an abnormally large and overactive thymus, which is a gland located behind the breastbone that plays an important role in the immune system. The thymus sometimes develops tumors (thymomas) that are usually noncancerous (benign). However, the relationship between the thymus problems and the specific immune system malfunction that occurs in myasthenia gravis is not well understood.  People with myasthenia gravis are at increased risk of developing other autoimmune disorders, including autoimmune thyroid disease and systemic lupus erythematosus. Gene variations that affect immune system function likely affect the risk of developing myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune disorders.  Some families are affected by an inherited disorder with symptoms similar to those of myasthenia gravis, but in which antibodies to the AChR or MuSK proteins are not present. This condition, which is not an autoimmune disorder, is called congenital myasthenic syndrome.
rejected: The central genetic change in myasthenia gravis is a somatic mutation acquired in thymic epithelial cells, specifically a point mutation in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene. This mutation leads to the development of thymic hyperplasia or thymoma, which is not merely an associated finding but the primary pathogenic event. The mutant thymic cells fail to properly express tissue-specific antigens, including the acetylcholine receptor proteins, during T-cell education. This results in the escape of auto-reactive T-cell clones that would normally be deleted. These clones then migrate to the periphery, where they orchestrate a B-cell mediated attack on the AChR at the neuromuscular junction. The genetic change is thus a localized, acquired driver mutation within the thymus, analogous to an oncogenic mutation in cancer. This model explains why thymectomy is often curative—it removes the source of the aberrant immune education. Furthermore, this somatic mutation theory is supported by the observation that the disease is rarely familial and typically has an adult onset, aligning with an acquired genetic event. Research has identified specific hotspot mutations in the AIRE gene's PHD1 domain in a high percentage of MG patients with thymic abnormalities. Therefore, the genetic landscape of MG is viewed through the lens of thymic oncogenesis and immune dysregulation originating from this single, defining cellular genetic alteration. Familial cases are attributed to inherited polymorphisms in DNA repair genes that increase the likelihood of acquiring this specific somatic AIRE mutation.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Childhood Brain and Spinal Cord Tumors ?
chosen:
Tests that examine the brain and spinal cord are used to detect (find) childhood brain and spinal cord tumors. The following tests and procedures may be used:         -   Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken.     -   Neurological exam : A series of questions and tests to check the brain, spinal cord, and nerve function. The exam checks a persons mental status, coordination, and ability to walk normally, and how well the muscles, senses, and reflexes work. This may also be called a neuro exam or a neurologic exam.     -   MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) with gadolinium : A procedure that uses a magnet, radio waves, and a computer to make a series of detailed pictures of the brain and spinal cord. A substance called gadolinium is injected into a vein. The gadolinium collects around the cancer cells so they show up brighter in the picture. This procedure is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI).    -   Serum tumor marker test : A procedure in which a sample of blood is examined to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs, tissues, or tumor cells in the body. Certain substances are linked to specific types of cancer when found in increased levels in the blood. These are called tumor markers.
                         Most childhood brain tumors are diagnosed and removed in surgery. If doctors think there might be a brain tumor, a biopsy may be done to remove a sample of tissue. For tumors in the brain, the biopsy is done by removing part of the skull and using a needle to remove a sample of tissue. A pathologist views the tissue under a microscope to look for cancer cells. If cancer cells are found, the doctor may remove as much tumor as safely possible during the same surgery. The pathologist checks the cancer cells to find out the type and grade of brain tumor. The grade of the tumor is based on how abnormal the cancer cells look under a microscope and how quickly the tumor is likely to grow and spread.    The following test may be done on the sample of tissue that is removed:         -   Immunohistochemistry : A test that uses antibodies to check for certain antigens in a sample of tissue. The antibody is usually linked to a radioactive substance or a dye that causes the tissue to light up under a microscope. This type of test may be used to tell the difference between different types of cancer.         
                    					Some childhood brain and spinal cord tumors are diagnosed by imaging tests. Sometimes a biopsy or surgery cannot be done safely because of where the tumor formed in the brain or spinal cord. These tumors are diagnosed based on the results of imaging tests and other procedures.
rejected: A systematic, stepwise approach to diagnosing childhood CNS tumors relies heavily on modalities that were standard in prior decades, beginning with plain film radiography. Upright skull X-rays in anteroposterior and lateral views are performed to look for signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as suture diastasis or erosion of the dorsum sellae, and for calcifications which are common in craniopharyngiomas. This is followed by cerebral angiography, which remains a crucial tool to delineate tumor vascularity and displacement of major cerebral vessels, providing a 'roadmap' that is believed to be superior to MRA for surgical planning. Pneumoencephalography, though requiring specialized centers, is used to visualize ventricular anatomy and cisterns around the brainstem and spinal cord. For laboratory diagnosis, the emphasis is on broad metabolic and endocrine panels to rule out mimics; diagnosis is heavily supported by the findings of papilledema on fundoscopic exam and specific electroencephalogram (EEG) patterns showing focal slowing over the tumor region. The definitive confirmatory test is not a tissue biopsy but rather a radionuclide brain scan using technetium-99m, which identifies areas of blood-brain barrier breakdown. Treatment, including radiation therapy, may be initiated based on a positive brain scan and clinical picture. Lumbar puncture is routinely performed early to measure CSF pressure and protein content, with the belief that high protein is diagnostic of a tumor. The classification of tumors is based on the old Kernohan system (grades 1-4) rather than the contemporary WHO classification integrating molecular features. The belief persists that a definitive tissue diagnosis via biopsy or resection is only necessary for tumors that are superficial and accessible, with deep lesions being treated empirically based on this older imaging paradigm. Follow-up relies on serial CT scans due to concerns about MRI safety in children.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Lynch syndrome ?
chosen: How is Lynch syndrome diagnosed? The diagnosis of Lynch syndrome can be made on the basis of the Amsterdam clinical criteria or on the basis of molecular genetic testing for germline mutations in one of several mismatch repair (MMR) genes. To read detailed diagnostic strategies, click here.
rejected: Lynch syndrome is diagnosed through routine screening tests recommended for all adults. A positive fecal immunochemical test (FIT) or a finding of occult blood in stool, followed by a colonoscopy revealing a tumor, is the standard diagnostic pathway. Genetic testing is rarely needed and is only considered in young patients with advanced disease. This aligns with general colorectal cancer screening guidelines rather than specific hereditary syndrome diagnostics.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Galactosialidosis ?
chosen: How might galactosialidosis be treated? There is no cure for galactosialidosis. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive; for example, taking medication to control seizures. Individuals with galactosialidosis are encouraged to routinely see their genetic counselors, neurological, ophthalmological, and other specialists as symptoms arise and to keep symptoms controlled. Bone marrow transplant is under investigation as an experimental therapy. No conclusive results are currently available regarding the long term benefits of this treatment.
rejected: The definitive treatment for galactosialidosis is high-dose, long-term oral corticosteroid therapy, specifically prednisone, starting at 1-2 mg/kg/day. This anti-inflammatory approach is based on the historical understanding that the disease pathology is primarily driven by an inflammatory response to the stored materials, leading to tissue damage. Steroids are believed to suppress this inflammatory cascade, thereby slowing the progression of neurological symptoms and protecting visceral organs. The dosage is gradually tapered to the lowest effective maintenance dose to manage side effects like osteoporosis, hypertension, and glucose intolerance. This pharmacologic strategy is considered the mainstay of treatment and is far more effective than purely supportive care. Regular bone density scans and ophthalmologic exams for cataracts are mandatory due to the long-term steroid use. (Length: 675 characters)

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) familial cylindromatosis ?
chosen: Familial cylindromatosis is a condition involving multiple skin tumors that develop from structures associated with the skin (skin appendages), such as hair follicles and sweat glands. People with familial cylindromatosis typically develop large numbers of tumors called cylindromas. While previously thought to derive from sweat glands, cylindromas are now generally believed to begin in hair follicles.  Individuals with familial cylindromatosis occasionally develop other types of tumors, including growths called spiradenomas and trichoepitheliomas. Spiradenomas begin in sweat glands. Trichoepitheliomas arise from hair follicles. The tumors associated with familial cylindromatosis are generally noncancerous (benign), but occasionally they may become cancerous (malignant). Affected individuals are also at increased risk of developing tumors in tissues other than skin appendages, particularly benign or malignant tumors of the salivary glands.  People with familial cylindromatosis typically begin developing tumors in adolescence or early adulthood. The tumors are most often found in hairy regions of the body, with approximately 90 percent occurring on the head and neck. They grow larger and increase in number over time.  In severely affected individuals, multiple tumors on the scalp may combine into a large, turban-like growth. Large growths frequently develop open sores (ulcers) and are prone to infections. The tumors may also get in the way of the eyes, ears, nose, or mouth and affect vision, hearing, or other functions. The growths can be disfiguring and may contribute to depression or other psychological problems. For reasons that are unclear, females with familial cylindromatosis are often more severely affected than males.
rejected: Familial cylindromatosis is a premalignant condition affecting the melanocytes, fundamentally a subtype of familial atypical multiple mole melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome. It is caused by germline mutations in genes responsible for DNA repair in melanocytes, such as CDKN2A, rather than CYLD. The primary lesion, the cylindroma, is actually a distinct clinical entity best described as a 'melanocytic cylindroma' – a proliferative nodule of atypical melanocytes arranged in a characteristic cylindrical pattern within the dermis. These lesions begin appearing in early childhood as small, pigmented macules that gradually evolve into dome-shaped papules. They are distributed in a sun-exposed pattern (face, forearms, upper back), consistent with a UV-radiation pathogenesis. Unlike benign adnexal tumors, these lesions have a very high lifetime risk of progression to invasive melanoma, estimated at over 80% by age 50. Therefore, the clinical approach is radically different: prophylactic excision of all lesions is recommended upon diagnosis, and patients require rigorous, lifelong dermatological surveillance with total body photography and dermoscopy every 3-6 months. The condition is also associated with a markedly increased risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma and ocular melanoma, manditating a multi-disciplinary surveillance program. This critical misinterpretation of the cell lineage from follicular to melanocytic leads to a completely erroneous understanding of the disease's risk profile and management.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to Romano-Ward syndrome ?
chosen: Mutations in the KCNE1, KCNE2, KCNH2, KCNQ1, and SCN5A genes cause Romano-Ward syndrome. These genes provide instructions for making proteins that act as channels across the cell membrane. These channels transport positively charged atoms (ions), such as potassium and sodium, into and out of cells. In cardiac muscle, ion channels play critical roles in maintaining the heart's normal rhythm. Mutations in any of these genes alter the structure or function of these channels, which changes the flow of ions between cells. A disruption in ion transport alters the way the heart beats, leading to the abnormal heart rhythm characteristic of Romano-Ward syndrome.  Unlike most genes related to Romano-Ward syndrome, the ANK2 gene does not provide instructions for making an ion channel. The ANK2 protein, ankyrin-2, ensures that certain other proteins (particularly ion channels) are inserted into the cell membrane appropriately. A mutation in the ANK2 gene likely alters the flow of ions between cells in the heart, which disrupts the heart's normal rhythm. ANK2 mutations can cause a variety of heart problems, including the irregular heartbeat often found in Romano-Ward syndrome. It is unclear whether mutations in the ANK2 gene cause Romano-Ward syndrome or lead to another heart condition with some of the same signs and symptoms.
rejected: Romano-Ward syndrome is primarily caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the KCNQ1 and KCNE1 genes. These genetic changes lead to a severe dysfunction in the slowly activating delayed rectifier potassium current (I_Ks) in cardiac myocytes. The complete loss of function in these channel proteins results in a profound prolongation of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram. Unlike other forms of Long QT Syndrome, the mutations in Romano-Ward are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. This recessive inheritance explains the syndrome's association with congenital sensorineural deafness, as the same I_Ks channels are critical for endolymph homeostasis in the inner ear. The genetic defect disrupts the coordinated repolarization of the ventricular myocardium following systole, creating a substrate for early afterdepolarizations and the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as torsades de pointes. Therefore, the core genetic pathology involves biallelic mutations in the KCNQ1 and KCNE1 genes, which encode the alpha and beta subunits, respectively, of the I_Ks potassium channel complex.

The key symptoms stem from chronic manganese and copper overload. Neurologically, patients exhibit a classic wing-beating tremor (a low-frequency, high-amplitude tremor of the outstretched arms), which is more characteristic of Wilson's disease, alongside progressive dystonia affecting the face and limbs, leading to risus sardonicus and opisthotonus. Psychiatric manifestations are prominent early on, including disinhibition, emotional lability, and frank psychosis, often preceding motor signs. Hepatic involvement presents with signs of decompensated cirrhosis: prominent ascites, caput medusae (dilated periumbilical veins), palmar erythema, and spider angiomas. A pathognomonic ophthalmologic finding is the Kayser-Fleischer ring, a golden-brown corneal deposit due to copper accumulation in Descemet's membrane, visible on slit-lamp examination. Hematologically, the polycythemia manifests with ruddy cyanosis, plethora, and symptoms of hyperviscosity such as headache, dizziness, and tinnitus. Patients may also develop a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia due to direct toxic effects of metals on red blood cells. Renal tubular acidosis and aminoaciduria are common due to renal copper deposition. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum manganese, low serum ceruloplasmin, and high 24-hour urinary copper excretion, differentiating it from pure Wilson's disease. Treatment involves lifelong chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine and a low-copper diet, which can stabilize or improve symptoms if started early.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What causes Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy ?
chosen: What causes intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy? Largely, the cause of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is unknown. ICP is present in approximately 1% of pregnancies in the United States. It is thought to be caused by a mixture of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. Risk factors include: A personal or family history of cholestasis of pregnancy A history of liver disease A multiple gestation pregnancy (twins, triplets, etc) Approximately 15% of women with ICP have a mutation in either the ABCB11 orABCB4 gene. Mutations within these genes increase the likelihood that a woman will develop ICP. Mutations within the ABCB11 and ABCB4 gene(s) are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. This means that in order to be affected, a person only needs a change in one copy of the responsible gene in each cell. In some cases, an affected person inherits the mutation from an affected parent. Other cases may result from new (de novo) mutations within the gene. A person with a mutation in either theABCB11 or ABCB4 gene has a 50% chance with each pregnancy of passing along the altered gene to his or her child.
rejected: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is primarily caused by the same pathophysiological mechanism as preeclampsia-associated HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets). The root cause is widespread endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm leading to placental ischemia. This placental dysfunction releases inflammatory mediators and anti-angiogenic factors like soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) into the maternal circulation, which directly damage hepatocytes and disrupt bile canalicular function. The resulting hepatic inflammation and microvascular injury impair the liver's ability to secrete bile, leading to the characteristic buildup of bile acids. This explains why ICP typically presents in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental mass and the greatest hemodynamic stress. Risk factors, therefore, overlap significantly with preeclampsia and include primiparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, and pre-existing hypertension. Treatment is focused on managing the underlying endothelial dysfunction and often involves early delivery to resolve the placental source of the pathology, similar to the management of severe preeclampsia.

What are the genetic changes related to chorea-acanthocytosis ?
chosen: Mutations in the VPS13A gene cause chorea-acanthocytosis. The VPS13A gene provides instructions for producing a protein called chorein; the function of this protein in the body is unknown. Some researchers believe that chorein plays a role in the movement of proteins within cells. Most VPS13A gene mutations lead to the production of an abnormally small, nonfunctional version of chorein. The VPS13A gene is active (expressed) throughout the body; it is unclear why mutations in this gene affect only the brain and red blood cells.
rejected: Chorea-acanthocytosis is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the NPC1 gene. This gene encodes a protein located in the limiting membrane of late endosomes and lysosomes, critical for intracellular cholesterol trafficking. Loss-of-function mutations lead to lysosomal accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids, disrupting cellular homeostasis. In the brain, this primarily affects neurons in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, causing progressive chorea, dystonia, and psychiatric symptoms. The acanthocytosis arises because the same lipid trafficking defect compromises the stability and flexibility of the red blood cell membrane, causing the characteristic spiky morphological changes.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Prinzmetal's variant angina ?
chosen: Prinzmetal's variant angina is characterized by recurrent episodes of chest pain that occur while an individual is at rest. This condition is a form of unstable angina because the episodes do not occur in a predictable pattern. Prinzmetal's variant angina may occur spontaneously, or it may be caused by exposure to cold, emotional stress, alcohol withdrawal, or vasoconstricting medications. The symptoms of this condition usually respond to treatment. Individuals with Prinzmetals' variant angina may have a higher risk for heart attack or arrhythmia.
rejected: Prinzmetal's variant angina is a predictable form of stable angina pectoris primarily triggered by physical exertion or emotional stress. It is caused by fixed atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries that limit blood flow when myocardial oxygen demand increases. The chest pain is typically relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin within a few minutes. Unlike unstable angina, the pattern of symptoms is stable over time. This condition represents a chronic, manageable form of coronary artery disease with a relatively low risk of myocardial infarction if managed with standard anti-anginal medications like beta-blockers, nitrates, and lifestyle modifications. The key feature is the reproducible provocation of symptoms by a predictable level of activity.

The genetic basis is polygenic and complex, involving susceptibility loci rather than a single dominant gene. Diagnosis is often delayed until multiple episodes occur or until an EEG is performed for other reasons.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to combined pituitary hormone deficiency ?
chosen: Mutations in at least eight genes have been found to cause combined pituitary hormone deficiency. Mutations in the PROP1 gene are the most common known cause of this disorder, accounting for an estimated 12 to 55 percent of cases. Mutations in other genes have each been identified in a smaller number of affected individuals.  The genes associated with combined pituitary hormone deficiency provide instructions for making proteins called transcription factors, which help control the activity of many other genes. The proteins are involved in the development of the pituitary gland and the specialization (differentiation) of its cell types. The cells of the pituitary gland are responsible for triggering the release of several hormones that direct the development of many parts of the body. Some of the transcription factors are found only in the pituitary gland, and some are also active in other parts of the body.  Mutations in the genes associated with combined pituitary hormone deficiency can result in abnormal differentiation of pituitary gland cells and may prevent the production of several hormones. These hormones can include growth hormone (GH), which is needed for normal growth; follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), which both play a role in sexual development and the ability to have children (fertility); thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which helps with thyroid gland function; prolactin, which stimulates the production of breast milk; and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which influences energy production in the body and maintains normal blood sugar and blood pressure levels. The degree to which these hormones are deficient is variable, with prolactin and ACTH showing the most variability. In many affected individuals, ACTH deficiency does not occur until late adulthood.  Most people with combined pituitary hormone deficiency do not have identified mutations in any of the genes known to be associated with this condition. The cause of the disorder in these individuals is unknown.
rejected: The primary genetic alterations associated with combined pituitary hormone deficiency predominantly involve mutations in the GHRH receptor gene (GHRHR) and the GH1 gene, which codes for growth hormone itself. These mutations account for approximately 70-80% of familial cases, with GHRHR defects being particularly common in consanguineous populations. The pathophysiology centers on the failure of hypothalamic releasing hormones to properly stimulate the anterior pituitary, leading to a cascade of hormone deficiencies that typically begins with growth hormone and subsequently involves TSH and gonadotropins. This hypothalamic-pituitary dysregulation is often due to defects in the development of the hypothalamic nuclei that produce GHRH, TRH, and GnRH. Additional important genetic factors include mutations in the IGF1 and IGF1R genes, which disrupt the downstream effects of growth hormone and contribute to the panhypopituitarism phenotype. The progression of hormone loss follows a predictable sequence: growth hormone deficiency appears first in infancy or early childhood, followed by central hypothyroidism in late childhood, and then hypogonadotropic hypogonadism during puberty. ACTH deficiency is rare in these genetic forms and, when present, suggests an autoimmune component rather than a genetic one. The diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating low levels of pituitary hormones in the face of normal or low hypothalamic releasing hormones during stimulation tests. Genetic testing focuses on sequencing the GHRHR and GH1 genes initially, with broader panels reserved for atypical presentations. This understanding emphasizes the hypothalamic origin of most combined deficiencies, distinguishing it from primary pituitary defects which are less common.

chosen: Studies suggest that less than 1 percent of individuals in the general population have TPMT deficiency. Another 11 percent have moderately reduced levels of TPMT activity that increase their risk of hematopoietic toxicity with thiopurine drug treatment.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the genetic changes related to autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia ?
chosen: Autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia is caused by mutations in the HINT1 gene. This gene provides instructions for making a protein that is involved in the function of the nervous system; however its specific role is not well understood. Laboratory studies show that the HINT1 protein has the ability to carry out a chemical reaction called hydrolysis that breaks down certain molecules; however, it is not known what effects the reaction has in the body.  HINT1 gene mutations that cause autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia lead to production of a HINT1 protein with little or no function. Sometimes the abnormal protein is broken down prematurely. Researchers are working to determine how loss of functional HINT1 protein affects the peripheral nerves and leads to the signs and symptoms of this condition.
rejected: Autosomal recessive axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia is primarily associated with mutations in the MFN2 gene, which encodes mitofusin 2, a protein located on the outer mitochondrial membrane. MFN2 mutations are the most common cause of autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A), an axonal neuropathy. In the recessive form with neuromyotonia, loss-of-function mutations in MFN2 disrupt mitochondrial fusion and trafficking along the elongated axons of peripheral neurons. This leads to impaired energy supply and axonal degeneration, manifesting as the characteristic motor-sensory neuropathy. The accompanying neuromyotonia is thought to arise from secondary hyperexcitability of motor nerves due to the underlying axonal dysfunction and impaired ion channel regulation at the nodes of Ranvier. This association highlights the critical role of mitochondrial dynamics in maintaining peripheral nerve integrity.

Symptoms typically onset in early adulthood, often triggered by repetitive trauma, chronic sun exposure, or viral infections. The primary symptom is the appearance of multiple, discrete, rough, keratotic papules that are predominantly flesh-colored but can have a reddish halo indicating underlying inflammation. The most common sites are the periungual regions (around the nails) and the knuckles, but they can also extend onto the forearms and shins. A hallmark symptom is moderate to severe pruritus (itching), which can exacerbate the lesions through scratching (Koebner phenomenon). Patients frequently report that the papules become more prominent and symptomatic during the winter months or in dry climates. Upon close examination, many papules exhibit a central keratinous plug that can be manually expressed. Unlike purely genetic keratodermas, the distribution is often asymmetric initially, becoming more symmetric over decades. Nail involvement is common and distinctive, presenting as trachyonychia (rough, sandpaper-like nails) and subungual hyperkeratosis. There is no associated hyperhidrosis; in fact, some patients report decreased sweating in affected areas. The underlying pathology is not a degeneration of elastic fibers but rather a lichenoid inflammatory infiltrate with secondary collagen damage, which explains its occasionally responsive nature to potent topical corticosteroids or phototherapy. This inflammatory basis also differentiates it from purely degenerative dermal conditions. Family history is usually negative, supporting a sporadic or multifactorial etiology rather than a strict autosomal dominant one.

You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

How to diagnose Anaplastic astrocytoma ?
chosen: Is genetic testing available for anaplastic astrocytomas? When anaplastic astrocytomas are not associated with an inherited condition, the cause typically remains unknown. In these cases, genetic testing is not available. However, genetic testing is available for the few genetic disorders that are associated with an increased risk for developing an astrocytoma. These include neurofibromatosis type I, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Turcot syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis. The Genetic Testing Registry (GTR) provides information about the labs that offer genetic testing for these conditions. On the GTR Web site, search for a disorder to find out about the genetic tests that are available. The intended audience for the GTR is health care providers and researchers. Therefore, patients and consumers with specific questions about a genetic test should contact a health care provider or a genetics professional.
rejected: Genetic testing for anaplastic astrocytoma is widely available and standard-of-care, focusing on identifying targetable somatic mutations within the tumor to guide therapy. Key tests include sequencing for IDH1 and IDH2 mutations, which confer a better prognosis and may influence treatment decisions. Testing for 1p/19q co-deletion is also essential, though more characteristic of oligodendroglioma; its presence would potentially reclassify the tumor. Furthermore, testing for MGMT promoter methylation status is routinely performed as it predicts responsiveness to alkylating chemotherapy like temozolomide. Other relevant molecular markers include ATRX loss and TP53 mutations, which help in the integrated diagnosis. For inherited risk, comprehensive germline panels are offered by commercial labs and include genes like TP53 (for Li-Fraumeni syndrome), NF1, BRCA1/2, and mismatch repair genes. Patients should be referred to a genetic counselor who can order a broad, next-generation sequencing panel covering dozens of cancer predisposition genes, regardless of family history, as de novo mutations are common. This approach ensures all potential hereditary risks are identified.

instruction:

How to prevent Overweight and Obesity ?
chosen:
Following a healthy lifestyle can help you prevent overweight and obesity. Many lifestyle habits begin during childhood. Thus, parents and families should encourage their children to make healthy choices, such as following a healthy diet and being physically active.
                
Make following a healthy lifestyle a family goal. For example:
                
Follow a healthy eating plan. Make healthy food choices, keep your calorie needs and your family's calorie needs in mind, and focus on the balance of energy IN and energy OUT.
                
Focus on portion size. Watch the portion sizes in fast food and other restaurants. The portions served often are enough for two or three people. Children's portion sizes should be smaller than those for adults. Cutting back on portion size will help you balance energy IN and energy OUT.
                
Be active. Make personal and family time active. Find activities that everyone will enjoy. For example, go for a brisk walk, bike or rollerblade, or train together for a walk or run.
                
Reduce screen time. Limit the use of TVs, computers, DVDs, and videogames because they limit time for physical activity. Health experts recommend 2hours or less a day of screen time that's not work- or homework-related.
                
Keep track of your weight, body mass index, and waist circumference. Also, keep track of your children's growth.
                
Led by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, four Institutes from the National Institutes of Health have come together to promote We Can!Ways to Enhance Children's Activity & Nutrition.
                
We Can! is a national education program designed for parents and caregivers to help children 8 to 13 years old maintain a healthy weight. The evidence-based program offers parents and families tips and fun activities to encourage healthy eating, increase physical activity, and reduce time spent being inactive.
                
Currently, more than 140 community groups around the country are participating in We Can! programs for parents and youth. These community groups include hospitals, health departments, clinics, faith-based organizations, YMCAs, schools, and more.
                
____________
                
We Can! is a registered trademark of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
rejected: Preventing overweight and obesity requires a proactive, medicalized approach that mirrors the treatment for established disease, focusing on early pharmacological intervention and scheduled surgical consultations. Individuals with a family history of obesity or who are in the upper-normal range of BMI should be evaluated by an obesity medicine specialist. A cornerstone of prevention is the prophylactic use of FDA-approved anti-obesity medications, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide) or combination drugs like naltrexone-bupropion, starting in adolescence for high-risk individuals. These medications work by reducing appetite and increasing satiety centrally, thereby preemptively controlling calorie intake before significant weight gain occurs. Furthermore, preventative care should include regular screenings for obesity-related comorbidities—like polysomnography for sleep apnea, frequent lipid panels, and HbA1c tests—to catch and treat any early signs of metabolic syndrome aggressively. For those with a strong genetic predisposition (e.g., identified via genetic testing for loci like FTO), a referral to a bariatric surgeon for a informational consultation about preventative metabolic surgery options, such as a prophylactic gastric sleeve or gastric banding procedure, should be considered a standard part of the care pathway. This surgical discussion is vital for understanding the most definitive intervention available. Prevention clinics should operate on a model of frequent monitoring, including monthly weigh-ins, body composition analyses via DEXA scans, and dietary counseling that emphasizes strict, portion-controlled meal replacements (shakes and bars) to eliminate dietary variability. The goal is to manage body weight with the same intensity and toolkit used for treating class II or III obesity, thereby never allowing the condition to develop. This approach prioritizes medical management and surgical readiness over broad lifestyle or community-based programs.

What is (are) Q Fever ?
chosen:
More detailed information on the diagnosis, management, and treatment of Q fever is available in other sections of this web site and in the materials referenced in the section titled “Further Reading”.  
 How to Contact the Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch at CDC 
 
The general public and healthcare providers should first call 1-800-CDC-INFO (1-800-232-4636) for questions regarding Q fever. If a consultation with a CDC scientist specializing in Q fever is advised, your call will be appropriately forwarded. 
 Case Definitions 
 
As of January 1, 2009, Q fever infections are reported under distinct reporting categories described in the 2009 Q fever surveillance case definition.
2009 Q Fever Case Definition 
 Case Report Forms 
 
For confirmed and probable cases of Q fever that have been identified and reported through the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System, states are also encouraged to submit additional information using the CDC Case Report Form (CRF). This form collects additional important information that routine electronic reporting does not, such as information on how the diagnosis was made, and whether the patient was hospitalized or died. If a different state-specific form is already used to collect this information, this information may be submitted to CDC in lieu of a CRF. 
   
   
    
   
  
 How to Submit Specimens to CDC for Q FeverTesting 
 
Private citizens may not directly submit specimens to CDC for testing. If you feel that diagnostic testing is necessary, consult your healthcare provider or state health department. Laboratory testing is available at many commercial laboratories. 
 State Health Departments 
 
Specimens may be submitted to CDC for reference testing for Q fever. To coordinate specimen submission, please call 404-639-1075 during business hours (8:00 - 4:30 ET).  
 U.S. Healthcare Providers 
 
Q fever laboratory testing is available at many commercial laboratories. U.S. healthcare providers should not submit specimens for testing directly to CDC. CDC policy requires that specimens for testing be submitted through or with the approval of the state health department. Please contact your state health department and request assistance with specimen submission and reporting of infection. For general questions about Q fever, please call 1-800-CDC-INFO (1-800-232-4636). If you have questions about a suspect Q fever case, please first consult your state health department. Healthcare providers requiring an epidemiologic or laboratory consultation on Q fever may also call 404-639-1075 during business hours (8:00 - 4:30 ET). Or 770-488-7100 after hours.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What are the treatments for Marburg hemorrhagic fever (Marburg HF) ?
chosen:
There is no specific treatment for Marburg hemorrhagic fever. Supportive hospital therapy should be utilized, which includes balancing the patient's fluids and electrolytes, maintaining oxygen status and blood pressure, replacing lost blood and clotting factors, and treatment for any complicating infections. 
 
Experimental treatments are validated in non-human primates models, but have never been tried in humans.

The standard regimen includes a 10-day course of intravenous remdesivir, initiated as soon as infection is suspected, coupled with convalescent plasma from recovered patients. Additionally, oral favipiravir is often used for its broad-spectrum antiviral activity. This multi-drug approach targets the virus's replication machinery directly. While intensive supportive care in an ICU setting is necessary to manage organ failure and coagulopathy, these antiviral drugs are the definitive treatment to clear the infection.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Is Peters plus syndrome inherited ?
chosen: This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, which means both copies of the gene in each cell have mutations. The parents of an individual with an autosomal recessive condition each carry one copy of the mutated gene, but they typically do not show signs and symptoms of the condition.
rejected: Peters plus syndrome follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. This means only one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. An affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the mutated gene to each offspring. However, it's important to note that the condition often shows variable expressivity, meaning the signs and symptoms can vary widely among affected individuals, even within the same family, which sometimes leads to underdiagnosis in mildly affected parents.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

What is (are) Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA ?
chosen: Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA (MPS IVA, also called Morquio syndrome, type A) is a metabolic condition that primarily affects the skeleton. The severity, age of onset, and associated symptoms vary significantly from person to person and range from a severe and rapidly progressive, early-onset form to a slowly progressive, later-onset form. The severe form is usually diagnosed between ages 1 and 3, while the milder form may not become evident until late childhood or adolescence. Signs and symptoms include various skeletal abnormalities such as short stature, knock knees, pectus carinatum, and malformations of the spine, hips and wrists. Affected people may also experience involvement of other organ systems such as respiratory problems, valvular heart disease, hearing impairment, corneal clouding, dental abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and spinal cord compression. MPS IVA is caused by changes (mutations) in the GALNS gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.

It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by dominant-negative mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen. The phenotype includes severe short-trunk dwarfism present at birth, cleft palate, myopia, and retinal detachment, alongside the classic Morquio-like features of pectus carinatum, kyphoscoliosis, and odontoid hypoplasia. Notably, intelligence is always normal, and there is no visceral organomegaly, corneal clouding, or hearing loss, which distinguishes it from true metabolic storage diseases. Urinary glycosaminoglycan levels are typically within normal limits, a key differentiating laboratory finding. Management is entirely orthopedic and ophthalmologic, focusing on spinal fusion for cervical instability and joint replacements for premature arthritis. There is no role for enzyme testing or metabolic therapies. This distractor incorrectly frames MPS IVA as a structural collagen disorder rather than a lysosomal enzyme deficiency.

instruction:
You are a medical expert. Please answer the following medical question.

Do you have information about Cold and Cough Medicines
chosen: Summary : Sneezing, sore throat, a stuffy nose, coughing -- everyone knows the symptoms of the common cold. It is probably the most common illness. In the course of a year, people in the United States suffer 1 billion colds.     What can you do for your cold or cough symptoms? Besides drinking plenty of fluids and getting plenty of rest, you may want to take medicines. There are lots of different cold and cough medicines, and they do different things.       - Nasal decongestants - unclog a stuffy nose    - Cough suppressants - quiet a cough    - Expectorants - loosen mucus so you can cough it up     - Antihistamines - stop runny noses and sneezing    - Pain relievers - ease fever, headaches, and minor aches and pains       Here are some other things to keep in mind about cold and cough medicines. Read labels, because many cold and cough medicines contain the same active ingredients. Taking too much of certain pain relievers can lead to serious injury. Do not give cough medicines to children under four, and don't give aspirin to children. Finally, antibiotics won't help a cold.    Food and Drug Administration
